The County Councils for the County Palatine of Lancaster. and the COUNTY of CHESTER.
"THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT, 1888," AND "THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT, 11394." THE WARRINGTON UNION.

IVOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that a Joint Commit- tee appointed respectively by the County Coun- cils of the County Palatine of Lancaster, and of the County of Chester, under and for the purposes of "The Local Government Act, 1888," and " The Local Govern- ment Act, 1894," or either of them, will hold an INQUIRY at the COUNTY POLICE COURT, in WARRINGTON, ON FRIDAY, the let day of JUNE, 1894, at half-past eleven o'clock in the FORENOON, and will then and there take into considerAtion :

1. The case of the township of Latchford, partly situate in the Borough of Warrington, in the Administra- tive County of Lancaster, and partly situate in the Administrative County of Chester. 2. The case of the Warrington Union Rural Sanitary District, which is situate partly in the Administrative County of Lancaster and partly in the Administrative County of Chester. 3. The desirability or otherwise of uniting the part of the Warrington Onion Rural Sanitary District situate in the Administrative County of Chester, and which has less than five elected Guardians, to an adjoining Rural Sanitary District in such County. 4. The number of Guardians and Rural District Councillors to be elected for t ach Tewnship in the Union. 5. The retirement of such Guardians and Rural Dis- trict Couneillors. 6. Any other matter and thing which under the said Act may be necessary to be inquired into, and will make such Order or Orders thereupon as may be deemed expedient. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GIVEN, that all Persons interested in all or any of the foregoing matters may attend the said Inquiry and ,-‘e heard. Dated this 19th day of Mat', 1894. FRED. C. BULTON, Clerk of the County Council for the County Palatine of Lancaster, REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the County Council for the County of Chester.

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

I hear that the Chancellor of the Exchequer will shortly announce the intention ot the Government to nbantion the Local Veto Bill for the present seA- SiOn. The announcement will not be received with any surprise even by the temperance party, it hav- ing been clear for some time that its passage this se-10u is impossible. I also learn that the second portion of the Registration Bill will be dropped.

Mr. Haldfine,Q.C., is engaged in a remarkable case before the Privy Council. That body is to con-ider the important question whether the Channel Is- lands have a constitution, and on this point Mr. Haldane, who represents Guernsey, is expected to speak for a weEk. This ought to be extremely gratifying tb the inhabitants of Guernsey, which has not hitherto distinguished itself in the realm of constitutional law, but enjoys a modest renown as a charming little island and as the home of Victor Hugo's exile for many years.

Mr. W. T. Stead, the editor of the "Review of Reviews," proposes to erect a tent in his gardAn where the cyclist may bathe and cook a meal over a spirit lamp, and sleep in a bed on a boarded floor. It would be an excellent idea if cyclists merely trav- elled in pairs, hut when they travel in thousands the accommodation will be exce,Aingly However, ;:t.ir. Stead expects his example to be fol- lowed on a very large &elle. Why should not every prosperous person have his cyclist tent? Why should not. the men at the wheel be able to find in the garden of every villa free accommodation for the night ? Tue notion suggests Arcadia and the golden age.

Mr. Pickard's resignation of the offices of presi- dent of the Miners' Federation and general,aecre- Lary of tne International Miners' Congress is due simply to the state of his health, *bleb for many months has been extremely unsatisfactory. There is no foundation for any Atitement to the effeet that Mr. Pickard is in disagreetilent with any ot his col- leagues. The hon. gentlethan thought of resiwta- tion twelve months ago, but was persuaded to abandon the idea, and • there is 'some hope among his friends now that he may again consent to retain office.

Mr. John Wilson, M P., and Mr. Woods, M.P., who presided on different days ever the recent, Inter- national Miner's Conference at Berlin, express the opinion that the Conference was,quite as satisfactory in charalter as any of its predecessors, and that, in addition it aff)rded evidence of distinct progress towards an un.lerstanding among the miners of the different countries represented. They do not anti- cipate that any united action can arise from the Conference tor a long tithe to come, but they point out that its moral eff.:et must become greater year by year from the publication of its proceedings and the information they supply as to tho'condition and wants of the. miners. Both .hon. gentlemen take exception to the report of the recent gather- ing as publi:hed in the English papers, on the ground that they give far more than due import- ance to difNrences of opinion on matters of no par- ticular morn-nt. With a solitary exceplion, they say, the delegates were actuated by thce most friendly feelings towards each other,

The Irish Unionists intend to have something li.ke a "Held day" on tiie Vote on Account. In addition to raising the question of the state of county Clare, they intend, I near, to more the reduction or the Chief Secret:lry's salary for the purpose of callinst attention to the adminiQtration of the poor 171 w under his role. In point of fact, the whole of the old charges against Mr. Morley's administration are to he stone over again, and the ghief Secretary will be called upon to traverse groun itwhich he tins covered a score of times before. --It is worth not- ing that a somewhat more harmonious spirit pre- vails now in the Irish Unionist camp. it looks very much as if the "lovers quarrel " between 411 r. T. W. Russell and the landlords will be patched up. The fact is that the Irish Conservatives may not really like Mr. Russell, hut they cannot spare him. ills defection -would mean not only the loss of the seat in South Tyrone, hut also of one or two other shaky seats which are largely dependent on the tenant farmer vate.

Wesleyan Methodist circles here, and, I am told also that throughout the country, are greatly exer- cised over the election of female, representative_to the forthcoming Birmingham Conference.. Alread) certain leaders in the denomination have taken up H very determined attitude of opposition. whilst. Mr. Price Hughes and his party, On the other.side. are prepared to test the legality. of the•case. Five years ago when an .attempt was made in connec- tion with Arneriean Methodism to elect Miss Frencis Willard and other women as representatives a whole week was • spent in discussion, and the question st•Il remains undecided on the other side of the Atlantic. The other Methodist bodies naturally take great interest in this question be- e ne of its far reaching consequences. I hear that immediately the Wesleyan Conference assembles in its repr, sentative session the whole 'question will be raised as a noint of ecclesiastical law and dis- cussed apart from v-rsonal feeling. The ground Silken by the progressive party in Methodism is that eligibility for the post, ot circuit sewrd earries in itself district representation, and a possibility of Conference representation also. Whether ecclesias- tical experts will endorse this view remains to be seen.

Asf ivy is current, that Lord Rosehery when he went to see the Queen at Windsor, on Saturday, wa driven from a first class carriage by the incmi- venient attentions of some ill-mannered people who wanted the honour of travelling with the Prime Minister, and he took refuge in a third class com- partment, in which we're seated a workman, a foot- man and two others. It is to be hoped that the talk is true, for it is far too good to be spoiled by contradiction. The only indication afforded by the occupants of the third elass carriage that they re- cognised their (listing u4hed companion was one or them. having to answer a simplK question, renlied 4' Yes my lord." The workingman comes so well out of this story that one delights to think of the Prime Minister of EnOand going to visit the Queen in hi, company, in a third class carriage. A demo- cratic age and a democratic Premier, truly.

The incident reminds one of a story of the .late Lord Shaftesbury.who on one occasion, by stress of circumstances, found himself in the unwont.t.d ut- mophere of a somewhat crowded third-class car- riago. The good earl " improved the occa,zion "by entering into instructive conYersatiou with his ei,orpanionsyinoi with such acceptability that before kfr one of.them addressed him in words to His :—" We'Lyon sPern a good sort of hloke,so put yon up to a wrinkle. Whenever you buy a new 'et. put a piece of blotting paper insie.e the lining. I'm a 'atter, end so I know. The 'at will last you twice as long."

The unwonted—probably the unprecedented— spectacle of Indies within the sacred doors of the House of Commcns was witnessed on Tuesday. to the amazement, of the few members who haPpened to he present, and to the consternation of the horni- -fl,l officials. It is -Well known that there is beside t door of the cloitrib,r, a niche with glazed win- through which favoured ladies can.one or two st a time, obtain a view of the sitting House. By sr,me accident this afternoon, the oversight usually pt over those privileged to enjoy this spectacle wa4 relaxed, and t wn ladies, apparently mother and .dsughter, cdmly availF4l themselves .of the swing- ing doors opening for Mr. Robertson to enter, passed through, and advanced towards the bar. Sir Charles Pearson was Apenking at the moment, and such members as were there gasped for breath at the apparition. The :.,peaker made no sign, and it, Was a moment or two before the frenzied officials le-rceiced whet )ad happened. Then one of them rushed frantically at these asserters of this new form of women's rights, and without any courtesy —indeed somewhat roughly—hustled the intruders out, of the doors. Yesterday there was another virtent, when for wome unexplained reason a divi- 45ion took place without the usual warning of bells res.unding in all narts of the Rouse. There is, of course, much hostile criticism of the words and actions of the four Welsh members who have constructively raised the standard of revolt. Their attitude is distinctly repudiated by most of their Welsh colleagues at Westminster. At the same time it is quite certain that a considerable number of English county members heartily agree in the pslicy of pushing Welsh Di.sestablishment, and are quite ready to make any personal sacrifice, by attending an autumn session or otherwise to force through the bill and send it, to the Lords. Those who hold this view are convinced that the passage of the bill through the Commons and its rejection by the Lords will greatly help the party in constituencies where there is a strong Noncon- formist element, and that this policy is the only policy which will confirm the outside public in the conviction that the Ministry mean business as to their programme generally. The policy which the constituencies will approve will be, to speak plainly the policy of forcing the whole programme piece by piece through the House of Commons and compell- ing the Lords to come to sucsessive decisions. In any case many Radicals feel that however out- wardly injudicious may have been the recent utter- ances in Wales, the West demand is perfectly fair, and will, by memorial or otherwise, iu a few days give expression to their opinion.

div.head: LORD ROSEBERY ON ENTERPRISE.
div.p: LORD ROSEBERY ON ENTERPRISE.

Mr. Jerome K. Jerome, the Editor of " To-day "has received the following letter under date of May 17th. Sir,—l am in receipt of your letter of yesterday, and I anticipate you wid t enjoy whit I have to say half as much as your varied writings; landscape advertising barred. In your issue of the 12th, yeu compliment Lord ltosebery on selecting his theme from the ea-.tes of "-To- day," how I would have congratulated you had lie " quoted his author." No one enjoyed Lord -Rosetiery's speech mare than I did, and if any (biota/bad previously , existed in my mind as to the effectiveness of this form of advertising, he dispelled it. Much has been made of this being an American idea, but boards have beep used in fields by my firm ten years, and by other English ad- vertisers in a small way much further bark, but like hll . eood things it is being spoilt by so many now taking it up ; this fact alone is sufficient to assure me it is tune to stay my hand and look out for" pastures new," and I would like to suggest to any" Landscape Spoiler," that if for reasons best known ti himself he is wishful to retire from the field, now is an auspicious time to declare his intention. lam fully convinced there is very little in- terest taken in the matter by the general public, and it is to them I call, and if the few who are desirous of keeping this" A beautiful World," would worry their minds more about the uglinesa and Frye% lor of streets where people have to dwell, they would be better occu- pied than in trying to gratify their present whirs, and by so doing, depriving farmers, fishermen and others from getting a little help. There has been a lot of exag- gerated rubbish written and •spoken as to wliat adver- tisers intend doing ; they have to exercise judgment as to what amount to spend on any one systern,and I que,- tion when Ladas wins the Derby if the amount of kr eains for her illustrious owner would provide with sails all the boat-owners who have applied to me. lam sorry to have disappointed t.,0 many and hen,- fitted so few. Again it is agaiost the interest of any advertiser to put up these expensive boards too closelyond my fixers lam sorry to say, have erre, i in this respect in some few instance, which will have to be rectified as my agreements expire. Th-y have orders to avoid interfering with any " nice bits of stuff," as is Liver Pool law7er once described a lovely view to me,arel this reminds me how differently landscape effects indi- viduals. I was about two years ago having lunch at the hotel at the head of Lake,Couistore and a lady and gentleman were seated at the same table. Their conver- sation was not conducted in a whisper, and I was inter- ested when she remarked to her companion—" See ! my dear, that is the Coniston Old Man," arid his answer which was brief bears out my argument', for it ran— What ! that wretched thing.' —Yours faithfully, THOMAS BEECHAM. Our readers. will readily conjecture the place of origin.

BY A LUNATIC ORNITHOLOGIST. The owlet howls " too-whoo ! too-whit r How 11O,WIS the owl " too-whit ! too-whoo !" On worm-worn beam tte owl (loth sit To howl "too-whit "the whole night -through. He bi ts where beams and rafters rot, Where moonbeams scarce 1111,q brook the gloom, To howl " too-whoo !too-whit !" t') what ? To howl " Lo-whit !too-whoo !" to whom ? His mate on worm-worn beam doth sit, :He howls to it, as it howls too. To wit, he howls " too-who-a !" to it, • To it he howls " too-whit !" to woo. Two wits has nature given to him, To wit, to hear his mate's " too-whits !" To witness where, in twilight dim, It too, with its two wits. too, sits, To its two wits he hom,ige pays, To whose" too•whoos !" he howls" too-whoos !" He teaches it to watch his ways An 6 it, too, its two wits to use. To its unseasonable howl,: He adds a whit, to wit, too-whit r Till all ttie howls of both the owls To Whitsun seasonaily fit. . For dropping their too wild" too-whoo !" A wQdtling song these owls emit,. With a refrain (in season ton) To it, to wit, " Too-whit I—to Whit !"

div.head: LIBERAL COM-ERENCE AT BIRk:INGHAM. IMPORTANT SPEECH BY LORD ROSEBERY.
div.p: LIBERAL COM-ERENCE AT BIRk:INGHAM. IMPORTANT SPEECH BY LORD ROSEBERY.

A Conference WM held in Birminaham on Wednesday for the purpose ot forming a • Midland Liberal Federa- tion, and at its close the Earl of Rosebery and Mr. Fowler delivered short addresses. Mr.Fowler,wlio spoke first, referred to the Registration Bi!hand remarlOai that the cost of elections, the cost of our Parliamentary ceri- tests—this perpetual speeding of money in order to en- able a mau to discharge a publid fluty,—was no credit the country, but was a positive deterioration to public morality. Lord Roseliery tcok the first opportunity that had presented itself to say that is was a source of grief and weakness to the G.wernment, that they should be deprived of the services of Mr. Mundelia„ They fully respected the chastity of honour which had led him to insist on his resi,gnatton being accepted until the affairs of the company with, which he was connected, were cleared up. In the evening the Earl of Rosebery ad- dressed a public meeting in the Birmingham Town Hall. He reproached the Birmingham Liberal Unionist Associ- ation, which was in reality, he said, Mr. Chamberlain, with incensistency in its aititude to various current political questions. First there was the question of dis- e•tablisliment in Wales and q-aaeland—a cause which lle Government were certainly determined to prisecute.l hen there was the question of the House of Lords. The com- ing conference at Leeds was a spontaneous movement. He thought it would not sel.arate without having pro- nounced emphatically for some limitation of the powers and prerogatives of the House of Lords. Mr. Chamber- lain's views on the questions of the Churcit Establish- ments, oneinan one vote, and the House of Lords had apparently disappeared like thin smoke in the air. His questions t himself (Lord Ito,eherv) on the occasion of his last visit to Birmingham were a direct insult. Ti follow the Birmingham Liberal Union- ist Association was to bucks the Liberal measures to which they had lons., set their seal with enthusiasm, simply in order to establish and maintain Tory government. Where was the consistency of that Association in regard to liquor traffic legislation? If the State did riot soon control the liquor traffic it was evident that the liquor traffic would control the State. The Government had not yet been able to deal with this question. They came into power with an insufficient majority to carry out their plogramme. Of late they had had in addition two little schisms. With a majority such as they had no schism was to be over-looked. One was the" alcoholic schism," in connection with which lie ridiculed the idea that the cause of Home Rule could be furthered by supplanting the Liberal Government by a Tory Administration. As to the action sf certain Welsh members, the "ecclesiastical schism," the Gov- ernment hoped before they again met the country to have t assed a measure el Welsh Disestablishment through the House of Commons. He could say nothing as to its subsequent fate, tut what he said to these, members he said to an in the Liberal party—if their, were any in their ranks who did not care for the Gov- ernment's policy, who did not trust their seal and their capacity, by all means let them turn them out. He for one would never be a Minister on sufferance.

A Dainty Dish. The following is a nice way to cook chops for invalids and others :—Have some chops cut from the loin, trim off the supeifluous fat, and spread both sides with but- ter, allowing about an ounce to each chop; place in a moderately quick oven between two plates for about twenty minutes, basting the chops once or twice in that time; before serving, pour .off the fat, mix a teaspoonful of flour with a little water, season with pepper and salt, pour over the chops, and return to the oven until it boils. Chops done in this .way are delicious, if cooked properly.
Waterproofing Tweed-cloth.

Put half a pound of sugai•-of lead and the same quan- tity of alum in powder into a bucket of hot suit water; stir at intervals for an hour. Then pour off the clear liquor into another vessel and immerse the cloth, allow- ing it to remain for four-and-twenty hours; then hang up to dry, without wringing. It will be found to be perfectly waterproof in the heaviest rain, without the slightest damp penetrating. Another way—Moisten the cloth on the wrong side with a weak solution of isin- glass, when dry apply an infusion of nutgalls. Or— Apply a solution of soap to the wrong side the cloth, when dry go over again with a solution uf alum. The first way is the best, and I would suggest that it should be well ironed and pressed wen dry.

CHAPTER XIV'. BIEGGY'S RECITAL. No future hour can rend my heart like this, Save that which breaks it. MATURIN.

The Lady Beatrice entered her own apartments through Vmse of her seamstress, and hurried into her dre ,g-room, stiangely oppressed with a heavy foreboding of evil. She was not reassured by the sight of the figure that met her startled gaze. Meggy Fleck, the housekeeper and nurse of The Evergreens, was crouching before the red fire her face buried in her hands, her attitude that of ut- ter and almost hopeless misery. The Lady Beatrice sprang to her and caught her arm in the fierceness of sudden terror. ,
What is it? " she gasped. "My husband—" Meggy Fleck slowly rose from her crouching position, and turned her face up to that of her mistress.

How that face had changed since the Lady Bea- trice had looked upon it last. Its freshness and ruddiness were gone. The cheeks that had been so smooth were seamed • with lines cut by her heavy grief. The eyes were dim with weeping, and set in dark and cavernous sockets. The whole countenance was wretchedly haggard.. The LAdy Beatrice stepped back involuntarily. "My husband? " she repeated with a low wail. He is well, my lady," replied Meggy Fleck, in a hollow voice, striving to speak calmly. "Thank God I "cried the Lady Beatrice. "And my children, Meggy ? Fay—" "Master Fay is well, and so is Master Rupert, my lady," said the housekeeper, slowly. " And Ciralda ?" exclaimed the mother, in ter- ror. "She is not ill, Meggy ? Oh, she is not dead, my bright, beautiful girl? Tell me she is not dead ! '

"She is not dead—not ill my lady," answered the housekepper, in a stilled voice. Her revulsion of feeling, on receiving this as- surance, almost overcame the Lady Beatrice. She clutched at the back of a chair, leaning heavily upon it, a wave of faintness sweeping over her.

Her tiring-woman chafed her hands in alarm. "Not ill—not dead !" said her ladyship, clasp- ing her hands above her heart. "Oh, I have been cruelly frightened ! " She drooped her glittering head to the shoulder of her attendant, and gave way to a wild, tem- pestuous burst of weeping. It was as brief as it was violent.

A moment later, she raised her bead, strug. gling for self-command, and said in a broken voice: "I can bear anything now that I know they are all well, Meggy. Your looks scared me so terri- bly! What is the trouble? Your errand con- cerns Giralda ? "
" Yes, my lady," replied the housekeeper. "Miss Giral(la is gone I " " Gone I" echoed the Lady Beatrice, in a fright- ened voice. " Gone !"

"Yes, my lady," said Meggy, avoiding the ter- rified and anguished gaze of her mistress, and speaking in fluttering, sobbing tones, Miss Giralda is gone ! I rang the bell at the usual hour this morning for the children to get up. Then as usual, an hour later, the breakfast-bell was pm& My master and the young gentlemen came to the breakfast room but Miss Giralda did not come. My master smiled and said my young lady had overslept herself for once, and bade me waken her. I went to her room, but she was not there. The bed had not been slept in." "Not slept in!" said the Lady Beatrice, hol- lowly. "No, my lady, and there was a note on the pillow." . "A note! • Then she left home deliberately. A note! Did you bring it? Give it to me !" The housekeeper drew from her bosom the little note Giralda had written to her parents before her departure, and gave it into the eager hands of her mistress.
The latter read it with burning, feverish eyes. Then her ladyship sat down in a chair and cov- ered her face with her hands.

The twin-sisters, her devoted attendants, looked at her with pitiful?, sorrowing gaze. "My noble, misguided child " exclaimed the Lady Beatrice, after a brief silence. "Knowing so well her generous, impulsive nature, I might have feared this ! Oh, I have been blind ! If I had only been frank with her yesterday! So young—so beautiful—so ignorant of the world— where is she now?"

She turned to the housekeeper, and said: "Giralda left her home last night ! Why did you not come to me with the news this morning, Meggy ? " "Because, my lady, my master said we were not to alarm you until we had tried every means to find Miss .Giralda. My master drove straight to the railway station, but the ticket agent did not remember seeing a young lady answering to her description. He said that there were several ladies who bought tickets for the night train, .and one young lady, with black hair and eyes, was booked for London on the 4.30 morning train." "It was not Giralda," said the Lady Beatrice. "Her eyes are dark blue, almost black—" She paused abruptly. "They were black at times, my lady," suggested Meggy. "Might it not have been her ? " "Herd in London, as ignorant of the world as baby, as beautiful as an angel—oh, I hope not ! " cried the Lady Beatrice in anguish. "It is no place for her. She had a:few pounds in her purse. I have taught her to dread London. Perhaps— nay, she must have gone to some country town to solicit a situation as governess. She spoke to me. about wanting to go out as a governess." "We found some papers, or scraps of papers, in her room, my lady," said Meggy. "She had partly burned them. She must have taken them from my master's study. There was a TiniCS, and two or three other (lady papers—" " She has been studying them," interrupted the Laiy Beatrice. "Perhaps some advertisement attracted her attenton, and she has gone to answer it. Mary, bring me yesterday's dailies. You will find them in my boudoir." The woman hurried to execute the errand, re- turning with the journals. Her ladyship scanned their columns keenly. "'A nursery governess wanted,'" she read, aloud. "She did not answer that, for the adver- tiser lives in London. 1 know that my child can not have come to Landon, after all my teachings. Ab ! what is this ? " and she started abruptly. " A secretary and companion wanted by Lord Trevelyan ! Giralda could not have ' gone to Trevelyan ! " and the face of the Lady Bea- trice was convulsed with an awful fear. "No, no! Surely the good God who has so long shielded us would have kept her feet from straying into such a pit! She cannot have sought out her fa- ther's enezny—the being who would crush her and all whom she loves with utter remorselessness ! Some adverse fate cannot be compelling my child to bring ruin and destruction upon her family!" "No, indeed!" exclaimed the housekeep:T, with a positiveness that contributed greatly to reassure the Lady Beatrice. "That child is no nurse for an old man, and she would realize the fact. Miss Oiralda has a rare lot of good sense, my lady. She wouldn't go trying for a situation where an elderly woman was wanted. Ignorant of the world as she is, she'd know better than that, my lady." " I believe she would," said her ladyship, bright- ening. "The child could not have gone there. I must lose my faith in a watchful Providence to believe that. Let me look at the other advertise- ments." She looked them all over, but could not see one that was likely to attract her daughter's attention, and she finally dropped the papers, saying : "She has possibly sought souse country town, thinking to support herself as music-teacher or daily governess. My poor, mistaken darling ! She is, without doubt, weeping herself asleep to- night, homesick and sorrowful, yet resolute in her attempts to earn her bread, while 1, her mother, am decked out in costly jewels, and shine the belle of the ball-room ! Oh ! it' is hard ! I said truly to my children that I am an actress ! "—and she spoke ,bitterly—" only the stage on which I play is wider 'and lan.rer than the hoards of a theatre " She was silent a moment, and then resumed: "When does the next train leave, Muggy?" "At three in the morning, my lady." It And it is twelve now," declared the Lady Bea- trice, consulting the tiny watch, ha larger than a silver sixpence, which, set with jewels, dangled from her diamond brooch. " The company must have gone to the supper-room, or be about going. ' I shall be missed. 1 must go down, even if my heart is breaking. My father will be hurt at my absence, and Lord Adlowe may suspect something' of my seczet I For 44 4u:.*41.4.4 kitice X :2111,4 go &war _
" You look like death, my lady," said the seam- stress, sopping a cambric handkerchief with co- logr. 3, and proceeding to rub the cheeks of her mistress.

"It's no use, Mary," said the Lady Beatrice. "The blood has all gone back to my heart. Never mind my looks. Lay out my wrappings. I shall go back with Meggy. Both the women looked dismayed. "Oh, my lady," said the seamstress, implor- ingly, "you will only ruin my master and your- self if you go! That policeman or detective— I know he is one, even if his clothes are plain—is still hanging about and watching the house." "I will cheat him," said her ladyship, after a moment's rapid thought. "I will put on my opera cloak and hood, and go out as one of the guests. Meggy, you had better leave ths house early, and go to the station by a circuitous route. Do not try to dissuade me from going. I mum go. It I was ever wanted at home, I am now when this cloud rests upon it. I must consult with. my husband in regard to the best course to pursue. I can do nothing without his advice and knowledge, for a slight misstep now would ruin him and me. Oh, Giralda I " she added, with a moaning cry, "you little knew what trouble your generous self-sacrilice would bring upon us!" The women made no further attempt to persuade her ladyship to forego her projected visit to The Evergreens, submitting in silence to .her better judgment arc! the prompting of her instincts. "One word more, Meggy," said her ladyship. "Send a carriage for me at a quarter to three. Tell the cabman to call for Lady Pierce. There is no such lady, you know. I will enter the carriage then, and drive to the depot. That is all, I think."

She paused a moment, to summon up her coolness and fortitude, and then gathered up her long and shining train, and set out on her return to the con- servatory by way she had come. The terrace was deserted as she crossed it and approached the floral palace. Lord Adlowe was standing on the marble steps, a bouquet of marvellous beauty in his hands. He looked searchingly at the countenance of the Lady Beatrice as she came near. She looked like a being of ice, incapable of emo- tion or feeling. Her manner was instinct with haughtiness, her bearing cold and quiet. Her eyes met those of his lordship, and he was startled at their glowing brilliance. It was almost incredible that this cold and haughty belle could have been the impassioned, anguished creature of a brief while before. "All alone, Lord Adlowe ? " she asked lightly. "Are you star-gazing ? " "I was only awaiting your ladyship's return," said Adlowe, bowing politely. "Lord Hain pton has been here in search of you. Supper is about to be announced, and the dancers are impatient to get through with it in order to commence their exercise. May I escort you to the supper- room ? "

The Lady Beatrice accepted his arm, saying: "I was called to see a poor woman who needed sympathy and help. Thanks for waiting for me, my lord. And now let us join the candidates for supper. They moved towards the drawing:room. "You will take my bouquet ? ' asked Adlowe bending towards her. "I see you have lost your own. We are almost betrothed, you know, Lady Beatrice, and you cannot refuse my flowers, the language of which is love." The Lady Beatrice dared not refuse the offering. She accepted them in her character of belle, but the wifely love and self-e steem of her other charac- ter made her cheeks burn as she did so.

"Your ladyship will give me the first waltz ? " asked Lord Adlowe, as they emerged into the drawing-room. "I shall not dance to-night," replied the Lady Beatrice. "As hostess, I must devote my time to my guests, and see that all the timid young ladies, the spinsters, and wall-flowers are provided with partners. Do not urge me, Lord Adlowe. 1 cannot dance."
At this juncture, Lord Hampton, pale with sup- pressed anxiety at the singular ahsence of his daughter from the scene of festivities, espied through the throng the Lady Beatrice and her suitor.

The sight was an immense relief to him. He had feared and dreaded some development of the mystery enveloping her ladyship. He had thought of seeking her in her rooms. He had had an idea in his inmost heart, but half acknowledged to himself, that she might have effected one of her mysterious absences or silences—he knew not what to term them,

His face brightened at once, and he offered his arm to a dowager duchess, the no1:1,!:-t guest of the evening, excepting the scion of royalty, and pro- ceeded to lead her to the supper-room. Most of the guests had marked the absence of their hostess, and her return to the drawing-rooms, leaning on Adlowe's arm, excited speculation at once. It was immediately rumored that "she had been on the trrace tete-d -tete with her lover, Lord Adlowe, who had seized the first opportunity after his return to renew his suit for her hand, all the world' knowing that his lordship had loved her ever since she first entered society."
Adlowe's manner went far to provoke the opinion also that his suit was favored by her ladyship. He had an al. of suppressed jubilance which was thought to spring from recent encourag6mcnt.

The Lady Beatrice, cold and brilliant as usual, did nothing to favour the opinion. She was gra- cious and smiling in the supper-rooms, although she half thought her heart was breaking, and that her glances must be wild and strange. Supper over, the dancing begun. Neither the Lady Beatrice nor Lord Adlowe danced. The formed performed her duties as hostess with rare grace. None of her guests—not even the plainest or most timid—had time to feel neglected. The hours wore on. After two, the carriages began to arrive for the early-goers. After half-past two, there was a con- stant succession of announcements of carriages, although many of the untiring young people had no thought of departing before dawn. The Lady Beatrice flitted about among her guests; and finally, eluding the watchful glances of Lord AdlOwe, stole through the conservatory to the terrace, and thence by the private way to her own rooms. Her attendant was there alone. Meggy Fleck had been gone an hour. The Lady Beatrice hurriedly exchanged her amber robe for one of pearl-hued satin, her seam- stress suggesting the change. "That amber dress might be recognised as you go ont, my lady,' she said. " Lord Adlowe, or the earl `would know it at once. Meggy took a long cloak and bonnet to the station for you to travel in. Oh, my lady, I hope you'll get off unseen by that detective, or any one else' and that you'll gain some clew to where poor Miss Giralda has gone, the dear, sweet lambi" The earl's daughter threw over her dress a long White opera cloak, drawing the hood over her face in such a Manner as .to completely conceal the latter. '
"Thu know what to do, Mary," she said. "Do not let my absence be suspected. Goad- bye." She wrung the hard of her weeping attendant, and unloekiog the door passed out into the great

It fortunately happened to be deserted. She glided to the dressing•room unseen, but had scarcely gained the portal when the servant an- nounced the carriage of " Lady Pierce." The Lady Beatrice descended the staircase, and passed out of the hall, gaining the carriage unre- cognised. The cabman drove off at once, another carriage sweeping into its place. The earl's daughter looked out of the window and marked the person she had deemed a detective. He was leanin4 against the area railing conversing with a liveried foutiwin. He seemed merely some passer who had stopped to listen to the music and to watch the dancers through the uncurtained windows.

But the Lady Beatrice was not deceived by ap- pearances. She knew that his presence so con- tinually on the street, so often before Hampton House, meant harm to her. The necessity for • perfect secrecy—the mystery of her life—ms.de her prompt to recognise danger. " Outwitted again, Mr. Detective !" she mur- mured. " You can tell your employer, Lord Ad- lowe, that he is not yet on the track of my secret." She leaned back on the seat, and the cab whirled out of the street into a more. quiet one, on its way to the Victoria station.

My DEAREST NELLIE, The most popular material of the moment is erepon. These differ CM, siderably from those whieh obtaitted last year, and they exi-t in a large variety. The prettiest are soft, with a thick shot rib; an old ro,,e colour shot with white is quite ideal. °theta tlwre are with a very coarse rugged surface in a mixruro o sill; and wool ; some show a combination of cotton and wool, but those with silk hang with the most couvinciug grace. The crocodile crepon with large circles has been banish-al, and in its stead r,-igns a Parisian erepen whir infieitesitnal little bumps all over it. Titia, however effective, is rather harsh in texture, and in crepon, as in every oiler fabric, you may today pay your money and take your choice. A fascinating tea gown is in e, open of a pale turquoine ahade, beautifully finished and lined throughout. All rnund the skirt is an ample frill of lace, headed hy bands of insertion, this also ornamenting in a tlviah fashion the bodice and full- puffed sleeves. A second brilliant example is made in rich golden yellow-and-erearn shot brocade, with Watteau back and c'oaely fitting side pieces richly trimmed with n;ffide of white lace and knots of shot brocaded rihbon. A third charming gown is of ohi-roae crepon, with soft cape-like lea ,s of lace and Watteau, the draped front being so arranged that it can be removed, and a fresh one huttoeti in at a minute's notice. A blouse for dinner wear which I have jest seen is made of blue-grey crepon, with full sleeves, epaulettes, and eravatends in guipure lace.

The most exquisite brocades are to-day used to make the tea jacket, while old lace playa its decorative part, and paste buckles are adopted with enthusiasm. A white satin brocaded jacket I know well boasts an accordion-pleated pink chiffon shirt fastened with diamond studs; this is a veritable edition de luxe of its kind, and a tea jackes no less magnificent is made of one of the new chiee silks in white striped with black, the surface strewn with pink rosebuds, and this dis- plays a vest and frills of green chiffon with an applique of very fine lace I,:t in transparently. Ilsre is a dewription of a Paris home dress : Round skirt, low bodice, and puffed upper sleeves in pick cloth, enhanced with full bertha and ba:que, together with pointed lapels, also in cloth, but elaborately embroidered with silk of a darker shade, and edged with bands of skunk. A similar work adorns the plastron, with straight collar, likewise the long close sleeves, and graduated tabs on the skirt.

The mediumeized hat is a thing almost unknown in fashionable quarters this season, the opposite extremes of the diminutive toque and the huge "picture" hat being worn to the exc!irdon of all other shapes, save, of course, for travelling, boat- ing, Stet. he most conspicuous point in the millinery of the day is undotibtedty the audacity of the cernbinations of vlours. Bright green straw with blue velvet-, and black flowers; beetroot red combined with pink and brown; heliotrope With magenta, and yellow with purple—such garish mixtures as these, with scores of others equally astonishing, are to be seen every day. Coloured straws are, indeed, very popular, and, trimmed discreetly, are exceedingly pretty. A charming little bat, for example, is of rough nut- meg Ntraw in a pa;e she.de of pink, and h close- &Able-, with a slightly pointed crown. The brim is formed of a sort of ruche of creem lace, in wide') clusters of black violets nestle, and at the left site a smartly tied leJw of black moire ribbon —the faveurite trimming of the ueason—with just two p'nk roses, is placed. Another is to (Sem and chestnut straw, trimmed with wide chestnut silk ribbon, a wreath of black roses and pink roses under the brine, resting OIL :he hair,. with black strings.

div.head: Princess and the Miner.
div.p: The Princess and the Miner.

In 1865. two years after she catne to England, th Princess .of Wales was says "Little Folks," talt,t) to see Botallack, the most famous tin mine in Cornwall. Tie Prince of Wales and Hy.' late Duke of Sutherland were of the patty, which was shown over the mine hy "Captain "Jan, one of the overseers. In his excite- ment " Captain " Jan had forgotten his gloves, an omission that was brought to his mind the first time he was about t) lead the Princess over the rough floor of a tunnel. He did not tare to offer her his gloveless hand, and-to beg the loan of the Prince's or the Duke's gloA es was also impossible. So 'he pulled a newspaper, winch he happened to have with him, out of his pocket, and, wrapping his ri,2llt hand in it, offered it to the Princess. Naturally thit.king the paper was held out fir her to read, she tried to look at it. Fairly cornered " Captain " Jan had to explain matters, and after a hearty laugh, in which the whole party joined, the Princess took the bare hand•nf the honest miner.

div.head: SOME LARGE INCOMES.
div.p: SOME LARGE INCOMES.
GROUND RENTS AND MINERAL ROYALTIES.

The Earl of Derby draws from his tenant farmers up- wards of one hundred and seventy thousand pounds a year. This is supplemented by his Liverpool property. This fortunate family also owns nearly all the town of Bury. The total inc me of the. Earl of Derby is close on three hundred and fifty thousand pounds a year. The Earl of Sefton's family, in addition to Ltverpool estates , producing forty-three thousand pounds a year, and ground rents seventy-five thousand pounds more, re- ceived two hundred and fifty-one thousand pounds fer three hundred and seventy acres of land required by the corporation for a public park,. Earl Vane has one h0,,- dred thousand pounds a year, in addition to his mil royalties, which extend over twelve thousand acre,. Coal is worth to the Earl of Fi'.zwilliam• one husiirt d thousand pounds a year, in addition to another one Win- dred and seventy-six thousand pounds, the value of his estates in Yorkshire and Irleand. The Marquis of Lon- donderry, who sells his coal wholesale and retail, his a rent-roll of one hundred and eighty-three thousand pounds a year. The Marquis of Salisbury's London property is said-to bring him in seventy thousand p,unds a. year. The Marquis's other estates produce thirty-live thousand pounds per annum. The Duke of 130,:iyonshite owns one hundred and ninety-three thousand three hun- dred and fifteen acres of l,thd, prodacing a revenue a one hundred and seventy-five thousand pounds a year. Thsa Duke of Hamilton's mining royalties amount to vale hundred and fourteen t hoesand pounds a year. His other estates brhig in seventy-three thousand pounds per annum. The Duke of Norfolk has an income of three hundred and sixty-nine thousand pounds a year,and the Duke of Northumb uland one hundred and seventy-six thousand pounds. ,

div.head: " TRUE BORN ENGLISHMAN."
div.p: THE " TRUE BORN ENGLISHMAN."

From the Celt, most probably, the Englishman gained his quickness and elearnesis of v-rception, his imagina• tion,his wit and humour, his sociability,his family love, his reverence,- and, perhaps, his aristocratic tendentie:'. His deliberateness, accuracy, directness, providence, a.. venturous disposition ,patient labour,silence and reserve, may, as Dr. Nicholas thinks, be due to the Germatiii portion of his ancestry. But where he derived watty cf his other characteristics it is hard to say. Truth,fidelit3 , and sincerity are rn't generally regarded at; the saliecr, virtues of the 'Celt ; though it would be flattery to say that they are peculiar to the Teuton. Hospitality, courage, and individuality,through all its forms of st,rn resolve and self•assertion are, however common to both stocks, though public benevolence, or organised charity has been regarded by the ablest of the advocates of the "Celtic theorv,"almost "an idiosyncracy of the English." It is certain, however, that the modern English have in few respects the exact characteristics of the modern Germans,or of the Saxons or Swabian stocks,fiom wiech they spring. Mice admixture has done moth to aVer them. Laws,religion,isolation,have had their influence; while, imquestionably. the opportunity which they ha ye had of leisurely watching, at their convenience, the tar- moil of the w•irld outside, has done much to impart a tone to their national habits, and a conservatism, tt-ing the term not in its political sense, to the life of a " True. Born .Englishman," not only in his own country, but wherever he has takeol up his home, on every coast, and in every city, from China to Peru.—Cassell's "Peoples of the World,''.

THE SHOOTING OF MINERS AT OTRAIJ.

TERRIBLE EFFECTS OF THE MANNLICHER RIFLE. A correspondent resident nelr the scene of the great strike of Moravian miners sends to the "'Newcastle Chronicle" the following acceuht of the events which . have happened there : . The- workmeu of the collieries in Polish Ostrau have gone out on striksein large numbers—according to latest • • reports from 10,000 to 15,000. The strike began in a few Silesian mines belonging to the Northere Railway Company, throueh dissatiefaction with a new sick fund , law, which demanded higher payments and altered .the !triode of relief. In the beginning of May the strike was limited to only a few pits, but gained ground in conse- quence ef Socialist agitation and insufficient authorita- tive protection and at the same time the watchword " eight hours' ;hat was given out. In reslity, the ' working time in the collieries since the strike of 1891 was only eight hours, with going down and coming up 10 hours, but the Workmen now demand that the up and down going must he included in th • eight hours. On Thursday' morning, a number Of workmen wanted to storm the Trinity Pit, in the mistaken idea that work was going on—in fact, about 50 men came to the morn- ing shift, but the menagement would not allow them to start, in consequence nf the threatening attitude of the workmen in the neighbourhood. Of the scenes which • took place the following is a short report :—At half-past 6 a.m. about 1,000 workmen advanced en the high road in regular order, and tried to force their way to the col- liery. The Gendarmes Sergeant Mark, with eight gen- • darrees, who constitute the police force of Polish °stray, were sent, by order of the district chief Dobrowsky, to meet the workmen and demand them to disperse. The leaders of the men declared that they were determined to storm the pits, as work was being carried on. The sergeant left it free to them to select a deputation to convince themselves that such ss'a,s not the case. As the masses for all this still advanced, the sergeent with his eight msn barred the way to the min.e. about 100 metres above the pit, and called to the workmen that if they coetinued to aelvance he must firm upon them, wet that they would only reach the mine over his corpse. Suddenly the ems; d pressed forward against the gendarmes swinging their sticks, and shouting " Hurrah." The sergeant saw that they (tee gendarmes) were in great danger, and commanded " Piro." The gendarmes gave one volley against the stormers and at once several fell dead,and others sank shrieking together. Still the workmen pressed forward. Then the gendartries fired other two volleys, and at last the strikers fled with frightful wailings and lamen- tations. The shots had a fearful result-8 dead and many wounded, covered the road ; two severely Wounded died during the transport to the hospital, in. which 26 heavily wounded were brought; 9 others, also severely wounded, were taken to their homes. Two priests distributed the sacrament for the dying to the severely wounded, of whom several will perhaps not recover. Me manager of the hospital, Dr. Swoboda, assisted by a regimee"tal doctor, dressed their wounds. The most of the killed and wounded are youths of 18 to 26 ; only a few are from 30 to 40; 2 are married ; one has 5, the other 1 child. The wounds are all very severe. The sergeant of gendarmes Mark reports:—A.bout 1,500 strikers wished to force their way to the pit, led on by a workman named Kolar. I told them to defend their resles as they would, but not by violence, as they weeld by such only damage their fellow workmen. They enswered they must see if the men had gone down the pit. I said, " What ca n it matter to you if men are at work ? Per:saps they are men with families, who must (sem bread for he same—leave them alone. You can strike if you like. All discussion was useless. The striking workmen declared they must all get to the pit. I a eswered. " You shall not t so long as I live I will not allow it." I then placed my gendarmes in position at she yard ga!e. Kolar and those standing with him as- sumed a threatening dernmenur. Kelar tree his shirt 'recast cpen, calling "Fire ! What ties it matter to me?" et the same time he threw hiS hat in the air. • This was the •critical moment. At L.nee the mazses stormed against rice gates, and I was obliged to command "Fire." For all my excitement I saw how Kolar fell to the ground, but afterwards it was found that he had taken the precaution to fall, and to remain on the ground until the shooting was over. Then he arose and ran away. Another report says :—The number of wounded by the collision is more than was at first supposed. Twenty-five shots were given in all out of the Mannlicher repeating rifis, and a total et 50 dead and wounded was the result. A mass of 1,000 workmen advanced to storm the Trinity Pits The sergeant called out to them —" Only over my corpse will von get in." The leader of the workmen, Kolar, tore his shirt open, crying, "Shoot at me and kill me. What does it matter for my miserable life ? " and Kolar, through throwing himself to the ground, escaped unhurt. Two volleys were given against the stormers, who retreated, but were pressed forward by those in the hinder ranks, and the eight gendarmes, thinking they were being again attacked, gave a third volley, many of the fleeing workmen being- shet in the lack. They could•naither retreat to the right nor the left, as the road was narrow and very steep. Nearly every shot wounded two men standing behind ore? another. Friday passed over in peaces hut the strike is rapidly gaining ground. The interment of the work- men killed in the collision took place during the night of May 11, in all' quietness. The coffins were carried by soldiers. The churchyard was oceuriied by military, and no disturbance took place in the whole district. Mourners were not allowed, and the hour of interment was kept secret. Nine of the killed have no relations in ()strafe as they are strangers. ' One cduld not be recog- nised at all. the Priest held the funeral service, and the District Chief and officers of the troops followed the bodies to the grave. Later on, during the forenoon when the miners asked when the men were to be ireer- red, and were told that they km been leried during the night, great agitation' prevailed again, but was soon quietened. It may he added that the man Kolar, who tdaved a part in which discretion was fully as promi- nent FIR vatoursehee-since been arrested. fie headed a- di,litation to his employer, the latter having promised a safe conduct. The authoritits, however, inter- vened ; and, in spite of the coalownees pleadings, Kolar wee removed to prison.

Genrat o,i-en Williams started his horse Pensioner in rho De Trafford Ilandirap, and the animal was well backed. It finished third, and immediately after pass- ing. the post dropped down and expired. An examina-- Von has been made by exrrirts, and it is now declared tAat Pensioner had been pGisoned. The vineyards ct William the Second are situated in the most renowned localities along the Rhino Ake Eleckheim, Erbach, and llatteinheim, where is pro- lue,ed the famous white wine known by the name of Steinberger Cabinet. It was a case of this famous wine which was sent recently by the Kaiser to Bismarck on • he latter's birthday anniversary.

div.p: DEATH OF DR. MACKIE.

Dr.lfaekie, founder;and for many years proprietor and editor of the Warrington " Guardia n," died after tlifigering illness on Monday. The deceased gentle- ▪ n was horn in Dundee, on the 22nd November, , and was 68 years of age. His father waa ager of large flag mills in Dundee, and was well o`gn as an inventor in connection with the flax 'P▪ m fling trade. While aporenticed to a I".rtir trader Dr. :,,4ckie studied to qualify himself to enter the G4s- a.,°N, University, with the obi.ct of becoming a minister the Church of Scotland, but he ultimately became the Er2l!_ proprietor of the Belton "Advertiser "and in 18532 oecame the proprietor of the Warrington "Guardian.' "r many years Dr. Mackie threw hi_nseifheartily into Eir3cal. educational, and social movements, arid de- ered numerous lectures to workingmen, for whose • lefit he also established " The Workmen's Club." He Enbli,hed several small lyoks and pamphlets, but his 'Jest known work was entitled " An Editor's Holiday," rich is descriptive of his journey to Italy and France. ' 12 was well known as a debater and on one occasion a public debate with the late Mr. Bradlaugh. Dr. ,74cifie spent much of his time in his early days on vari- discoveriea connected with machinery,and patented 'A▪ t! invention for setting type by automatic machinery. FLone time durine, the Crimean War the soldiers were Irally starving, although food was in plenty some six es away. Dr. Mackie suggested to the Government m.e despatch of two or three thousand navvies to make a Ilitltzisay to connect the men arid the food. The wisdom suggestion was at once apparent,and tccoruingly tal!,Saniuel Morton Pete) and his men were gnat out, the I,llWay was made and a letter acknowledging the source h°lll which this spirit of practical sympathy emanated, ,Ift'en preserved in the Warrington Free Library. Dr. 18',,ie unsuccessfully contested the city of Perth in to'o, at a vacancy caused by the sitting member going t.,..the House of Lords on the death of his father. Ile ,Ze_d his luck a second time by putting up for the Mont- P"trghs, where two Liberals were in the field. But 1,3 Efforts were unsuccessful. His services in connec- a-,T With the Manchester Ship Canal were both import- .3..4L and onerous, and considering that circumstance, it ,a singular co,incidence that he should have hreathed 4_l'B last on the day of the offilial opening of the great noundertaking. He gave evidence on committees,lectured laa the subject, attended numerous public meetings that d reference to it. He was for several years, a useful ..4• enther of the Warrington Hoard of Guardians. He was ()Bete(' Mayor of Warrington on the 9th November,lBBs. ...011 the Ist February of the following year he resigned O ;I_, der distressing circumstances, having been struck ttVn with paralysis. From that time to the day of his math, little improvement took place in his mental or Si' condition. Occasionally, he so far gained au di- -11.4.`„nt atrength to take a walk in the Pork, but a few B,Ths ago his condition became so serious as to call for al medical treatment. Medical skill and the mast /3a• teciful attendance however, proved ot no avail, for he '144 became worse and died on Monday.

div.head: QUEEN'S VISIT TO
div.p: THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO
M INC fIESTER.
IMPOSING ROYAL CEREMONY.

The Manchester Ship Canal, into which many ships have, as a matter of fact, entered and discharged cargo since Jenuary, was formally opened by her Majesty the Queen' osi Monday afternoon, in presence of Prince and Pi incess Henry of Bettenberg, Princess Leiningen, mem- brae of both Houses of Parliament, official represeeta- tives ot the County Palatine, the Boroughs of Manchester and Selfotd, the, Army, the Navy, and the Church, and tens of thousands of private citizens of all reeks, from the upper ten to the loser millions. The visit practi- cslly itivelved a series of ceremonies, that at the Ship Canal being the most splendid and novel. The weather, though cold and threatening, was on the whole fair for the multitudes who had been pouring in horn the thickly recurring., towns which distinguish this part of Lanca- shire. The crowds were packed in certain central epaces as it by hydraulic force, but as the route was a very long one there was a long-drawn distribution • of humanity. This gigantic line cl crowd, without a single gap from beginning to end, was a remarkable featnre of the eels- bretion, end it is said that the Queen was particularly impressed by the fact. The estimate from an officer of police that there were two millions of people in the strecte did not seem so very extravagant to any one who had driven in the Royal procession from Landon-road Station to the Canal -Docks, arid via Salford and the Deanegate district to the Exchange Station. . The festivities of the day were in progress in minor matters for homes before the arrival of the Queen. Troops were marching in the streets, anti benes were playing at various stations. Albert-square was the gayest of these. The Town Hall by this time looked as (nark as if it had weathered the eenturies,but the beauti- ful Prince Consort Statue and canopy had been made clean and bright for the occasion. Indeed, until noon the marble fieure of Albert the Good bee been draped with jsaleus care. A couple of cavalry bands pliiyed for !an hour, while the ladies and gentlemen on the open stand in front of the hall were cooled by the biting. enirth-caster. The 8-ate carriages of the High Sheriff and 'Lord Mayor, with other open landaus, conveeing the numbers of the Reception Committee, departed in pro- cessienal order to meet the Queen, and by this timeall the troops were in position and the thoroughtares clear. On emerging from the approach to the station,the Queen loeked upon endless lines of upturned faces, and upon house fronts where, at every balcony, window, stand, and often house-top, were people waving handkerchiefs in concert with the roar of the crowds below. Festoons of artificial flowers were stretched across the streets,and from the Venetian masts ; the warehouses and shops had their independent decorations ; flags danced every- where. At the Manchester Infirmary, within the first five minutes of the progress, there was a grand stand, where the uniformed nurses created a striking effect. The weather had changed, however, for the worse ; the intermittent sunshine of the forenoon had given way to a settled gloorn,and it was cold enough for snow. There- fore AS soon as the precession of police, military, and carriages had passed, the crowds broke up. The mounted police led the way, with Mr. Malcolm Wood, the Chief Constable,' in his richly silvered uniforn, preceedine the carriaves of the Lord Mayor. the High Sheriff, and the Aldermen. Then came the advance guard, and the lead- ing. troop of Yeoman Cavalry aeiead of the first Real carriage—horsed by four bays, and containing the , Queen,wearing her usual black, with a little white in her bonnet ; Princess Beatrice, in a fawn-coloured mantle; land Princess Leinineen and Prince Heney of Batten- leer,. There were hve other Queen's carriages, Earl Spencer Minister in Attendance, and Lord Carrington, as Len; Chamberlain, riding in one of therm was the Mistress of the Robes. The scarlet uniforms and white plumed helmets of the yeomanry were much admired by this crowd, though the less showy Hussar escort was, of course, a much smarter sample of English cavalry. • The short journey to the Town Hall, in its heartiness of reception high and low, was but a foretaste of what followed, but Piccadilly and Manket-street were prob- ably more densely thronged than any other thorough- fare. The best military spectacle was probably in Albert-equare, and it was a very fine sight when the Queen's carriage entered, and the troops salute& The address, which hael been formally adopted by the City . Ceuncil an hour and a half previously, was delivered to the Queen. After the customary assurances of devotion, Ste— tele there was a reference to the visit paid by her Majesty with the Prince Consort, and attention was called to the memorial statue, opposite which the Qwen was sitting in her open carriage. The address men- Moved the assistance rendered by the Municipality of Manchester to the ship canal scheme. In exchange for this document the Queen handed over the following reply: I thank you for rour loyal and dutiful address. The . immense undertaking which I this day open has filled me with, admiration. Exceptional engineering as well as other difficulties have been overcome, and the cone- meree of the world has been brought into direct coin- munirettien by sea with your great city and its neiehbourhood. I trust that Manchester may never cease to be prosperous arid thrive, and that all classes of my subjects may share in the benefits attending the suceees of this most important enterprise. The procession set under way without more than five minutes' halt, leaving, however, one policeman unhorsed, and one soldier in what seemed to be a fit. The reute was now by Mount-street, past the site of the Peterloo massacre, and capitally-decorated Oxford-st. At the Municipel School of Art, Cavendish-etreet, Dr. Ward, the principal of Owens College, and other learned Professors. in their academical robes, issued from a hewer of flowers and shrubs, ard begged the Queen's acceptance of an address. Earl Spencer. as Chancellor of the Victoria University, Reproached the Royal carriage, and formally presented Dr. Ward. Her Mejesty made the following reply to the addreee of the College : T thank you for your loyal and dutiful address. It is with great satisfaction that I hear of the strenuous efforts made by Owens College and its allied institutions to promote the came, of learning and scientific research in the city of Manchester and its neighbourhood. I earnestly hope that success may attend the efforts which have been made by all engaged in the management of ()wens College, to whom the character to which it has attained must be attributed. The crowd were a little thinner in Stret- ford, where the road was lined by the County Connenthulary. The waifs and strays under Superintend- ent Bent. were a most touching assembly of forlorn child- ren, jobilantly happy, however, in their big stand, awl their setergy compelled notice from all. The Queen and Princess Beatrice made a point of acknowledging their greeting, and did the same a little further on at a halt et, the Deaf and Dainb Asylum. Between the Town Hall and the new road heading to the Trefford Wide; there had been a shower of rain, but it was noticed that as the Royal cortege clattered down to the Pavilion the sun made a feeble attempt to smile. It is true there was no more rains but it really has not been quite success wea- ther at any time during this long busy day. file ships in the canal were mustered at the Salford Docks end ; with their bunting flying from the stern, they gave the direct tone te Ude novel seaport gala. The gorgeous standard was run up over the Pavilien as the troops sal- uted, the bands played the National Anthem, and the Royal party went on board the Enehantress yacht lying alongside, the gunboats and tenders being moored on the . other side of the water. The Queen seated herself aft ! on a raised dais, with a background of choice flowers, sent, from the Botanical Garden, and Lori •Egerton (chairman) and other directors were introduced to the qu,reerdeck, add Lady Mitford, his lordship's sister, (save the Queen a bouquet. The directers pegged her Majesty in review order, each name being announced, and Lord Egerton then presented the necessary address on teshalf of the Ship Canal. This like its predecessor ' Albert-square, was an affair of money and art, in • Royal blue Levant morocco, emblematic in its leaves and borderinge of the enterprise in which navvies began and sailors finished the work. There are dolphins, anchors, ! monograms, neptinees, mermaids, and views of canal ' scenery and machinery. The text embalmed in these beautifully illuminated pages, is not too long. In five paragraph, the Directors convey thanks, welcome devoted loyalty, end information about the scheme, of which the following links her Majesty with the locality: The Manchester Ship Canal follows as nearly as pos- sible the ancient river boundary between your Majesty's

div.head: I ITE EXAMINER SATTTPDA f, MAY 26, 1894. SEEING TUE QUEEN.
div.p: I ITE EXAMINER SATTTPDA f, MAY 26, 1894. SEEING TUE QUEEN.

Duchy of Lancaster and the county of Giester for a dig- twice of thirty five and a half mile.. Its construction has occupied a period of seven years, and it may claim to rank as one of the greatest engineering achievements of your Majesty's beneficient and prosper- ous reign. The Queen's reply was in the following term,: :

It is with great pleasure that I receive your address, and am able to be present at the opening of the Man- chester Ship Canal. . I recognise in this great and impor- tant undertaking, and the admirable engineering skill with which it has been constructed, further evidence of the increasing energy and enterprise of my. subjects. I trust that the increased facilities to be afforded by it for direct commercial intercourse by sea with the trade of the world, will not fail to be of the greatest advantage to the busy and industrious population . of Manchester and the neighbouring district, and I earnestly pray that by God's blessing this work may contribute to the.well- being and happiness of all classes of my subjects in the United Kingdom. Amongst the presentations now made were Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, Mr. Marshall Stevens, manager, and Mr. Whitworth. secretary of the company. Next in succession the Lord Mayor of Manchester and the Mayor of Salford were summoned, bidden to kneel, tapped on the shoulder with the Royal sword, and commanded to rise as Sir Anthony Marshall and Sir William Bailey. This public: bestowal of honours was unexpected, and was hailed with much applanse. The Quein expressed delight at the dererations of the streets, and the enthusiasm of the crowds, and the new knights kissed hands on . retiring. The Enchantress was some time in getting an offing, but the paddle wheels • began to revolve at last, and followed by a somewhat ponderous pleasure steamer set apart for the Ship Canal Company's guests, she steamed slowly down the Canal, Mr. Leader Williams, by royal request, pointing out to the Queen the chief points of mechanical value. It is known that her Majesty has always been personally interested in this great work, and she was now particularly struck with the statement that the same power which moves the huge swing bridge carry- I ing the Trafford-road over to Salford, also works the Mode Wheel Locks, though the two are a mile apart. This, however, is one of the triumphs of hydraulic en- gineering, and in a little while, by pressing a button, as she sat on her chair on deck, the Queen set in motion the machinery which caused the mignty gates to swing as softly open almost as a lady's fan. This was the formal ceremony of the day, and great was the cheering, sing- ine, cannon firing and music. On her return to the landing stage, the Enchantress was followed by Mr. Platt's beautiful yacht Norseman, before whose advance the Trafford Swing Bridge, said to be the largest ever made revolved upon its centre, allowing her to pass through. On leaving the docks the Royal procession crossed this bridge and halted at Ordsall Park, where Sir William and Lady Bailey and the Corporation of Sal- ford awaited it. At this point the grand stand for the wives and friends of the Salford Town Council, School Beard, Board of Guardians, and Overseers was placed, arid midway between two fl,iral arches was a dais glori- fied with the regulation scarlet cloth, and garnished with fi,svors. and shrubs grown in the public parks. Upon this platform the newly-knighted Mayor, in his robes of offi •e, scarcely concealing his Court dress, supported by the Recorder and Town Clerk, presented with courtly solemnity an illuminated address in a silver basktt of elaborate design. The Mayor, Aldermen, and burgesses iipon this scroll poured out their feelings in three para- graphs, adroitly rounding off the first by a statement which left the Queeta in no doubt that the principal docks of this great Canal are in the borough of Salford. The children, to the number of 25,000, who, by the special i,rra ngement of the Mayor, were massed opposite, were a very charming feature of the crowds in this district, and the Queen smilingly acknowledged their shrilly exuberant greetings. To the Salford address the Queen replied: I receive with satisfaction your loyal and dutiful address, and sincerely hope that the Borough of Salford may enjoy every advantage which it may be expected to derive from the opening of the Manchester Ship Canal.

The school children, and crowds of the industrial classes, were very conspicuous along the Salford route, and at the D.ansgate end of it, where the statue of Oliver Cromwell stands with a white wreath at his feet. This afternoon the bells of the cathedral seemed to ring out a God-speed. It was dusk now, the illuminations were already twinkling, and the Royal train was ten minutes late in starting. All the. notabilities were on the plat- form to see the Queen off—Lvrd Sefton,Lord St ilt,ridge, the new Knights, the Lord Chamberlain, tho Generals, and a host of fashionably-dressed ladies. The Queen sat- in her saloon,looking thoroughly pleased with every- thing. Her Majesty looks in good health, but on her arrival at London-road it was thought that she was not in the hest of spirits. The extraordinary extent of the decorations and the memorable seven miles and three- quarters of unbroken crowd had, however, acted like a charm ; and the Royal countenance was wreathed in smiles when, a somewhat arduous duty dorP, she made her final bow to my lords,ladies, and gentlemen deferen- tially bending low at the edge of the platform.

div.head: MORE HONOURS.
div.p: MORE HONOURS.

Thn Queen has intimated her intention to confer the honour of knighthood upon Mr. Joseph Leigh, M.P., for Stockport, and Mr. Alderman Leech, Deputy Mayor of Manchester Directors of the Ship Canal Cmrany. The Curt(rt Circular issued on Tuesday night contained a long description of the Queen's visit tr Manchester on Mon- day. After speaking of the pr )cesion through the streets and the proceedings on Board the Enchantress the following sentence was added :—" The Queen was deeply gratified by the very great and enthusiastic dis- play of loyalty with which Her IVlsj sty was received during her long drive through Manchester and Salford, the decorations of which she greatly admired." WARRINGTON AND THE OPENING OF THE CANAL.

At Warrington on Monday, most of the works and business establishments were closed during the greater pin of the day. There was, however, no public display in honour of the occasion with the exception of flags hoisted upon the Town Hall and one or two other public buildings. The Town Hall flag was a new one,and was USt3ti for the first time. It is much lsrger than the old one, and bears the borough arms in the cow re,with the words in large letters " Borough of Warriegton." Al- thotieh there was no public ceremony in Warrington, thoesAnds of Warringteniaes went to Manchester to swell the enormous crowds already there to welcome the Queen. A good number went by the London and North- Wie,tern from Bank Quay Station,but by far the greater number journeyed from the Central Station. At this station the " record " with regard to the number of pas- sengers was soon broken. Up to three o'clock no fewer than 3,000 persons had been sent away. and during the day it is estimated that more than 5,000 persons had taken excursion tickets,which were isseed at ls.6d.each. Although the resources of the officials, who were assitred by a staff from Stockport, were taxed to the utmost, very little delay was experienced in the despstch of the xprees trains. A large number of " specisls " were also requisitioned,as well as a Warrington relief traiNunder the direction of Mr. W. 11. Rigbey, the stationmaster. At night the scene at the Manchester Central Station was of a most animated character. No sooner had her Majesty left the city than great numbers of excursionists from Liverpool and Warrington made their way te the Oat ion, and quickly filled each succeeding train. As soon as a train was found to be full it was despatched, and another took its place. This course was continued throughout the night, and it was after one o'clock in the morning before the last train bringing Warrington and Liverpool pleasure-seekers steamed into the .Central Station. Fortunately no accident of any kind is reported, and the traffic arrangements appear to have passed off without a hitch.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

At about noon on Friday the" Norseman "arrived at Runcorn on her way to Manchester, closely followed by the" Enchantress" and the two gunboats " Speedy " and "Seagull." The Ship Canal Company's premises in the nf ighbourhood were hung with a profusion of bunt- ing whist several flags of larger proportions floated in various parts of the buildings. The progress of the vessels up the canal was watched by several hundred people on the banks. On Monday about one hundred or more persons travelled from Runcorn station to Man- chester for the purpose of viewing the opening ceremony by her Majest.c. A large number of Ruueornians took advantage of the cheap boAings from Widnes to jour- ney thither, and accordingly cross.d the bridge. The returning of the above named vessels exlited consider- able interest on Wednesday morning. Tory arrived at Runcorn at about eleven o'clock, their progress being very slow by some means. The " Enchantress " followed the "Speedy" at a respectable distance and the rear was brought up by the "Seagull," which,on reaching Rivedere, or between the swing bridge and Runcorn bridge, moored alongside the wall for several minutes and then afterwards continued her course at an increased pace. A large number of people congregated on the banks of the canal to get a sight of the boats.

div.head: INTERESTING TO CANARY FANCIERS.
div.p: INTERESTING TO CANARY FANCIERS.

A " congris de serinephiles," or congress of canary fanciers,is to be held shortly in Paris. It is well known that the Parisians are particularly fone of the sweet warbler with the yellow plumage, and even in the poor- eEt quarters one generally sees glore than one in a cage on a window sill. It is estimated that the total number to be found in the French capital is over one hundred thotwand, and that they eat 10,000 francs worth of chickweed a day,which is bought at the central markets and distributed by hawkers. In the western suburbs of Suresnes and Courbevcie are vast tracts of land specially, set apart for the cultivation of that herb. A public ex- hi hit ion of specimens is to be held at the Bird Market,lec- tures on canary breeding are to be delivered in the Hall of the Association of Learned Societies, and prizes will be given for the best birds at a competition to be held in the Palais Royal.
