div.head: TRIP WITH TIIE CORPORATION.
div.p: A TRIP WITH TIIE CORPORATION.
BY LUKE BLUNT.

Vehicles had been engaged to convey the party from the Town Hall to Latchford locks, where we went to embark on boatd the Helvetia. At Knutsford-road bridge there was a number or spec- tators, whom one of the party endeavoured to en- courage into cheering. But the move was received with a distressing ch,illiness, which froze it at its birth. These spectators must have been ratepayers for they gazed at us in a wondering, silent way from the commencement, and when the gentleman alluded to, waved his handkerchief and showed "Hooray," they simply drew more into themselves and looked so icy that had it been a hot day one could have refreshed and cooled himself by a eight of them.

Upon arriving at the Helvetia the party were received by Mr. •F. Monks and Councillor P. W. Monks. Just before we steamed away it was an- nounced that Mr. Birtles would photograph the party from the lock. At this there ensued quite a little panic. Ladies made frantic" pads" at their heads to see that those pretty hair arrangements described as "Brighton buns," were safe, and then pursed their lips into little winning smiles, and gazed fixedly at the sky. And some of the gentlemen threw themselves into icaposing:y languid postures, leaning on the bulwarks with one arm, and the other extended with a cigar between the thumb and index finger. Generally their faces assumed quite a Spynx-like stolidity of expression—an ex- pression of no particular meaning in some .cases, in others unnaturally angelic, or quite untruly de- praved,and I regret to say almost criminal in a few. But there: one always makes his face tell "stories". when he is being photographed. When this task was over the respected commander ot the Helvetia, Captain Monks, mounted his wheel-house and away we steamed up the great waterway.AShrewd north east wind was blowing, which quickly induced the gentlemen ta turn up their coat collars, and the ladies to withdraw into the war-nth of their wraps.. Weather prophets—and the whole company seemed to be more or less endowed in that direction—were unanimously of opinion that rain would arrive in time to ruin the great pageant .in which we were going to take part., for a special berth near the Royal yacht had been engaged for the Ilelvetia,and the vessel was profusely decorated with bunting. We steamed quickly past the alternating scenes of bare fields anct rugged bulks, and snug lithe farm- steads nestling amid orchards where the trees seemed actually to shiver in the bleak wind. We "pottered" about the deck to Keep ourselves warm, occasionally inverting our nose into the engine room to sniff the.warm air, and look with envy at t,he throbbing engines, and feel almost ready to go down and offer to help, even if it Were only to the extent of standingaround and seeing that the engines did not overwork themselves.

At length however,we came to Mode Wheel locks where was to be seen the first sight of the great show. All about the footways of the lock, and along the embankment were rows of poles, about which fluttered brilliant streamers, whose bright hues con- trasted strongly with the leaden sunless sky. From here to our berth at Old Traff)rd, was a short jour- ney. and we were soon moored opposite the Royal landing stage. The time was something between the hours of three and tour. At any rate, the Queen was not expected to arrive for an hour and a half, andqn the interim there was plenty to do. The hold had been fitted up into a capital refreshment saloon,and so we were able to spend some little time in catering for the delectation of the" inner man." But in addition to this there was much to be seen. Away along the docks on each side of the canal ' were colossal grand stands, carpeted with red baize, and decorated with brilliant buntings. and let at the small pries of a guinea a seat! At the end of all the pier heads had been erected large tressle looking firework designs, seeming now with the wind moaning through them like 80 many uncom- fortable skeletons that had been suddenly un- earthed, but which were destined to become later on, one of the most gorgeous pyrotechnic spectacles ever seen in Manchester. Almost directly opposite our mooring lay the Itlyal yacht Enchantress, wait- ing at the Royal landing stage for her Majesty to embark. As the time wore on, the excitement be- came intense. Away on Trafford Bridge and al- most everywhere within the eye's range, w-le to be seen people watching and waiting, and struggl- ing; they were even on the roofs of outhouses and other buillings, some of the more daring spirits having gained the altitude of house gables. Every minute that passed now, increased the fever; people began to wander about absent-mindedly,sed offer irrelevant and illogical answers to questions, and betray all the symptoms of nervous tension that I should think a man experiences ten minutes before getting married. At, length squires began to gallop from Trafford Bridge down to the Royal landing stage,and the echoes of mighty cheers came floating on the breeze to tell us the Queen was on her way. Royal attendants began to make their appearance, and were cheered spasmodically by the crowds. At length a voice from near our mast heed shouted excitedly "She's here! she's here ! " The voice was that of one of our Councillors who, in his enthusiasm bad risked much to soar with his loyalty as far as he could with safety get. I had seen him there almost an hour, and as the intense excitement grew lie had seemed to draw himself up like a ball with surpressed feeling, and decrease in bulk, until now with a shout he was standing at, his full height with one foot on the rigging and the other leg and an arm waving to his cheers. We had hut turned our eyes on him for a moment. when a cheer such as I never heard before came rolling and echoing like one mighty vaice. It came like electricity along Traff )I.d-road. Now it, is taken up at the Bridge I—Another moment and the Royal carriage rolls in view from the Bridge, and the cheer in a trice has travelled along the erstwhile silent-stands • it seems for a second to vibrate on the water, and then it is over on our side, taken up lustily by the Helvetia, and then by other boats berthed in the vicinity. There is a great bustling going on near the Enchantress, and the people are cheering continuously. But we cannot discern any- thing definite. Half an hour passes in this manner, and then the Queen is descried sitting under an awning on the deck of the Enchantress, with a lady standing erect on each side of her. More and more cheers follow. Then the Enchantress draws a little

div.head: nearer. We can easily make out her Majesty with her sombre attire—the small black cap and black dress.
div.p: nearer. We can easily make out her Majesty with her sombre attire—the small black cap and black dress.

The Royal yacht now steamed away to Mode Wheel, where the ceremony was to be completed. The Queen soon returned and disembarked at the Royal stage, and drove away to the station. Our company made their way to the road; and now for the first time we realized the great magnitude of the crowd. Wherever the human vision could reach—except in the air—there was to be seen dense crowds of human beings—on stands, in windows, on house tops, and packed in solid blocks along each side of the road they were to be observed as far as could be seen, until away in the distance their upturned faces looked like myriads of little specks. Of the fight we had, when the procession had passed, to gain the Central Station, let us not speak. But rather let us dwell for a moment on the scene about the railway station. Upon arriving there I felt almost "dog beat," and endeav6mred to obtain refreshment in neighbourieg restaurants. But it wasn't any good to try. In all the places I went into there was no tea, no coffee, no anything hut just soda water. It was the only beverage to be obtained —no one seemed to drink it; and yet I would have recomtnend-d it to half the people I met I At length I made my way to the station platform; and there the fun commenced. People were streaming in by thousands; and so great was the crush that women were fainting away on every hand, and men were doing the equivelant—using strong language. A crush would come from one end of the platform, and in a moment you were carried off your legsand swept as though by a great wave to the other end. There you would shake yourself down for a moment, and then the next instant another rush of frantic passengers, perhaps struggling to get to No. 1 platform would carry you away again. In due course I got washed up on the middle platform where the Liverpool and Warrington trains start. I made a wild rush from coach to coach but they were all full—people were heaped up together like parcels. At length in the midst of my despair there came a great ray of hope. I had come to a carriage where almost all were talking Welsh. In a second I was at the carriage window, asking with deep earnest cuss :
"Is there anyone here• named Jones P" And eight voices all answered, "Yes, my nanfe vas 'hone."
"Qqick " I said "there's a person very ill in the booking-office—says he's a relation of yours." " Ttstr, tsar, whoeffor can it be?" "I think he's dying—wants to make a deposi- tion."

"Efrans!" ejaculated the eight—and then they all rushed off to the booking-office. The next moment the train started, and I bad al- most half a carriage to myself. I admit. it was a wrong thing to do, but then it was only lay fighting one could get into the train, and its much nicer to fight With ingenuity than fists. It was after mid- night when this occurred and there were thousands of people then waiting about the station. Before I had been in the train five minutes I received a great shock. On feeling for my right hand trousers pocket I found it right in front closer scrutiny showed that my clothes,were almost "hack to front" and the horrid thought rushen upon me that I liad been " twisted" by the crush! I sat for some moments almost in a swoon, and then bracing up courage enough to examine myFelf, I found it was only the clothes that had been twisted! And the discovery lifted a great load from my mind. It would have been a terrible thing after that crush to have set about taking thingseasy,and then sudden- ly to have feund one's self a twisted man!

div.head: MR. JOHN MORLEY ON POLITICAL AFF SIRS.
div.p: MR. JOHN MORLEY ON POLITICAL AFF SIRS.

Mr. John Morley, M.P., speaking to his constituents on Monday night at Newcastle, said they had suffered a great loss through the retirement of Mr. Gladstone, but the torch that he had lighted must be carried on. Mr. Goschen said the Liberal party were being torn by a disruption of interests. It was quite true that many different interests were struggling for priority. Why not ? But whatever rivalry there might be there was one common interest—they did not believe in turning ministers out simply because they would not give prior- ity to any one of these. competitive measures. Common sense in politics must win in he long run. He did not quarrel with the friends who made these rival claims, hut the Government must decide this question of priority. The Government had. done their best to fulfil their pledges. They had carried the Home Rule Bill through toe House of Commons, and they had carried one great measure—the Parish Councils ICl—which would de more than any bill since the Reform Bill of 1832 to quicken public life. He held that the power of the House of U.irds should he strictly limited, and that speeches in Parliament should be much shorter. He said that Ireland was more tranquil now than she had been for 20 years past ; but he had not adopted the Unionist form of government in Ireland, for during his term of office there had not been one man tried under the Coer- cion Act. England must not forget the condition on which tranquility in Ireland had been secured. That condition was that there should be no paltering with the Irish demand. Failure to give that demand a prominent place would be perilous for the Government. He toliched upon the Registration Bill and the Budget proposakand referring to the Independent Labour party, said the poi.licv of labour representatives in making war on the Liberal party was insanity and suicide. In fact there was much ground to be cleared by the Liberal party before the industrial population could take their des- tinies into their own hands.

div.head: IS THIS BOYCOTTING?
div.p: IS THIS BOYCOTTING?

The extremity to which scitne agents ol the licensed victuallers are prepared to go in the effort to (Mend the interests of " the Trade " has says the " Daily News," in a particular case, reached dangerous lengths. A circular has been issued by one of the Trade Associa- tions, drawing the attentian of publicans all over the country to the vote upon the Budget Resolutions given by a member of the Government who has intimate rela- tions with a well-known firm supplying certain materials to the clerical departments of breweries and public- hAuses. The persons addressed are urged to have no dealings with the firm in question. This is a gross breach of the privileges of the House, involving serious pnalties. Impunity results from disinclination of the m-rnber attacked to take notice of such methods of warfare. But th-r.- is talk of altion being volunteered from an independent quarter.
Mr. Isaac Pitman, of Bah, the veteran shorthand writer, on Tuesday morning, received a lett,r from Lord Rosebery saying the Q leen had been , pleased to confer upon him the honour of knighthood.

div.head: THINGS IIEA.RD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS IIEA.RD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

There was some lively speaking at the annual meeting of the Warrington Football Club last week. The balance hheet was not as satis- factory as usual, and of course that of itself was sufficient to raise a discussion as to the best way to improve the finances of the club. Many items came under consideration, and the principal po:nts for criticism appeared to be the railway fares, and the hotel expenses, and refreshments. A pro- posal by Mr. Evans was intended to go in the direction of curtailing expenses. This was the dis- banding of the second team—really the third team. This wasrun at a cost'of between.E6o and£7o,and Evans urged that no substan,ial benefit was derived from it. The proposal however met with a strong opposition, chi,-fiy for the playing members of the club, and it was overwhelmingly defeated.

The Most important alteration in the rules was that which provided thatno playing member except , the captains of the first and" A" teams should be , placed upon the Committee, Mr. S. Wright J.P.,who brought this motion forward, was subjected to fre- (pent interruptions from the players who resented it strongly. His motion slightly modified by allow- ing touch judges to be placed upon the committee was in the end carried unanimously, This resolu- tion had the effect of causing a postpenenent of the : meeting Lecause the committee could not then be elected, owing to several playing members having been nominated. A surprise of the meeting VMS the election of Fair Turner to the captainship of the first team, as it was publicly announced a few weeks ago that he was retiring from active service after being so many years a member of the team. Ile has evidently changed his mind, and instead of retiring, be will be at the head of affairs next season.

The meeting of the Board of Guardians was a very short one last week, the work of looking after the Union being very light. .In fact beyond the ordinary routine work, there was scarcely any- thing to be dene. The Chairman and the. Clert: to to the Guardians have been honoured with an invi- tition to attend the festivities at Manci.bl4ter ;on Monday in connection with the "opening P•l4 e ship Canal. This shows that the Company /Wye not forgotten Warrington altogether although they are so backward in the making of the docka.

I A reduction in the rates now-a-days is a very rare occurrence, the tendency being rather the other way. The members of the Warrington Highway Board however last week passed a resolution to have a sevenpenny highway rate, instead of an eightpenny rate as heretofore. This will be good news for those out of the borough, and it is to be hoped the rate will provide money sufficient to pay all expenses. The Highway Board is evidently de- termined to make the rate as low as possible before it becomes defunct as it very soon will do, and set an example to the District Council when that body c,lmes into exigence.

I have alluded before to the dreadful nuisance, caused in the neighbourhood of Wilderspool-road, by the stench from the stagnant water of the old river bend. From what I can gather there is small chance just yet of an abatement being brought about. It seems that some years ago the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority secured the right of de- positing the sewage of Stockton Beath into this part of the river, and when the Ship Canal Com- pany took over the bend, I understand that the task fell upon them of supplying some other place for the deposit of this sewage. This has not yet been done, and I have heard during the week that the Canal Company have notified to the Warring- ton Corporation their intention of not unduly hurrying themselves. Consequently, there is likely to be " some fun," derived from the matter—not,of course,by the inhabitants of Wilderspool. The Cor- poration have decided to invite the co-operation of other authorities concerned in endeavouring to compel the company to move a little more quickly. Messrs. Greenall and Co. have already written the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority urging them to take some steps in the matter; but as we all know, a Hurst Sanitary Authority is not an over-hasty body. It proceeds deliberately. It is quite cer- tain, hcwever, that if something be not done quickly the nuisance at Wilderspool is likely to be a serious danger to the public health.

Speaking of the Ship Canal reminds me that I have had assurances from mem- bers of the I 'orporation, that the Company do not intend to make the docks. It is recognized that in this event, IVarrington will stand a very poor chance, in Parliament, of forcing the hand of the Company, and consequently an agitation is already shapnig itself among certain members of the Cor- portion, for securing Parliamentary powers to the BorolLzli, to construct its own docks. For my part I am rather doubtful if such an agitation will suc- ceed. The entbusium about the Ship Canal is al- ready cooling in Warrington, and I rather think LT will be quite below zero by the time such a scheme finds its way into the Council.

The other day I hears a pretty little story about certain members of a particular local body, This particular hod y—l prefer not to disclose its name— indulges annually in a picnic, and for the purpose of arranging the details of the present year's outing a committee of four was appointed. It was essen- tial, it seems,for the deputation to make its journey in a vehicle. registered to hold four. When three of the deputation arrived at the spot where the cab had been ordered to wait, lo and behold! they dis- covered seated in the vehicle, a lively colleague, who had not been appointed on the deputation. It was explained to him, in words unmistakable in impnrt, if not felicitious in choice, that when the fourth rson arrived he would have to vacate his seat. llowever,when the fourth individual did "put in" an appearance he was requested by his intruding colleague, to " put out " his comely figure on the box with the driver. This request was at length reluc tantly complied with, and the journey commenced. But the mater did not end here. The intrusive individual was praised to an astounding degree upon his possegsion of what was described as "colossal cheek." But he did not take to this flat- tery kindly, and when, after the party had adjourned to a certain building not a hundred miles from the Town n all, and partaken of refreshment, he began to ie with his companions in the exchange of doubtful compliments. So vigorous, I hear, became this exchange between the one of" colossal cheek," and another, that only a timely interference by mutual friends ~•revented them going to busi- ness on the transfiguration of each others features. MERLIN.

div.p: unjust." That was in 1885 ; now there is no man more frantically eager than Mr. CMAMBERLAIN to oust from power a Government which is bent upon passing a Welsh Disestablisiiment Bill. A few years ago he asked his countrymen in his most indignantly eloquent style if they were going to submit to an " oligarchy which is a mere accident of birth"; now he lavishes his warmest praise on the patriotism and wisdom of the hereditary legis- lators. And so it is almost through the whole chapter of current politics. On graduated taxa- tion, on registration and electoral reform, on temperance legislation, and even largely on the Irish question itself the present actions of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN are entirely opposed to his previous declarations. It is hard to think that the men of Birmingham, who were once in the foremost ranks of advanced Radicalism, will blindly follow him in a wholesale recantation of political faith. If, after Lord RaSEBERY'S trenchant speech and after the course of propaganda which the Midland Federation will no doubt set on foot, they elect to still follow Mr. CHAMBEELAIN they will ,do so with their eyes open and they may be regarded, at all events for some years to come, as a force lost to Liberalism.

Mr. MORLEY is pre-etninent amongst politicians for the fine literary finish of his speeches, and that delivered at Newcastle in no way falls below his usual standard. We do not think there has been any handsomer eulogium of Mr. GLADSTONE than that pronounced by Mr. MORLEY. Since 1886,the late PRI3LIER and the present CHIEF SECRETARY of Ireland have, in a special sense, worked together in politics, and hence it is easy to understand with what sincerity Mr. MORLEY declares that " the loss of that daily companion will for some of us rob Parlia,meatary life of its most sovereign attraction." The staple of the speech was a review of the work of the Government and an enunciation of the principles that guided them. He naturally spoke with some satisfaction of the improved state of Ireland, but he was care- ful to point out that the only guarantee for the permanent peace and contentment of the sister Isle is to be found in conceding the just claims of its inhabitants.

Friendly Societies DURING last week the Friendly and Societies were much in Old Age Pensions. evidence. The Manchester Unity of Oddfellows have been in conference at Northampton, the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds at Hull, and the Order of Druids at Macclesfield to say nothing of smaller bodies which met at other places. It is satisfactory to note that nearly all of these socie- ties report a steady increase in numbers in spite of the fact that the past year, with its black record of strikes and lock-outs and depressed trade, has been a trying one for such organisa- tions. Of course, most of the business dealt with had relation to the inner workings and manage- ment of the Societies themselves, but it is signi- ficant enough to note that, of the larger and more general subjects of discussion, the ques- tion of old age pensions held a prominent position It is clear that the men at the head of these great Friendly Societies view this question with mixed feelings. The Grand Master of the Oddfellows declared that the superannuation problem is still unsolved, and at present it seemed an almost hope less task. In the Manchester Unity alone it ap- pears that there are close upon twenty-six thou- sand veterans ever sixty-five years of age, and in order to secure them anything like adequate super- annuation the large sum of .C 337,324 per year would be required. Under these circumstances, it seems hardly the wise and politic thing to renounce in an uncompromising way anything in the nature of State aid. There is a constantly growing feeling in the community at large that the veterans of in- dustry should be provided for when old and helP- less in some other way than through the pauper's dole, and if the task is found to be too large for voluntary societies it will be the duty of the State to step into the breach. It seems to us that the line taken by Mr. WALKER, the Grand Master of the Druids, is the right one to follow in this great matter. The Friendly Societies being the first in the field are entitled to every encouragement and help to solve the problem, but if they find it insol- uble with the forces at their disposal, they should, as Mr. WALKER says) " am a by every legitimate means any scheme. by whomsoever instituted,that would give their aged and deserving poor a life more enjoyable than that of the parish work- house, a life free from the stigma of common pauperism, a life in which the dignity of man- hood would continue as the just and equitable re- ward of true citizenship."

LOCAL NEWS.
COMING EVENTS.

A continuation of the opening services in connection with the newly-erected St. John's Presbyterian Church, Victoria-road, will be held on Sunday. The Rev. J. Pulford Williams (pastor) will preach at both morning and evening services. Collections will be taken on be- half of the building fund. The celebrated Welsh preacher, Rev. Heber Evans, D.D., will conduct the anniversary services of the Bethe-,da Coagregational Sabbath school on Sunday. On Monday evening the Rev. Silas K. Hcking, of Southport, will deliver a lecture on "Mind your P's and Q's. Further particulars will be found in our advertis- ing columns.

div.head: FIRE AT WIDNES.
div.p: FIRE AT WIDNES.

Shortly before eight o'clock on Monday evenißg, the shop of Mr. J. Worsham, draper, Albert-road, was dis- covered to be on --fire. The doers were at once forced open and by the aid of willing neighbours the fIAMFS were very soon mastered. The Widnes Fire Brigade ar- rived on the scene and rendered great assistance. The stock was insured. TILH MAINTRNANCE OF RUNCORN THOROITONFARRS.

At the meeting of the Cheshire County Council last week, it was deeided to increase the sum of £2OO to £4OO, towards the maintenance and repair of Halton- road, Bridge-street, High-street, over Waterloo Bridge, and Station-road, subject to its being kept in a condition satisfactory to the County Surveyor, and to the Com- missioners furnishing that official,for the information of the Cornn-iilt-e, with a detailed account, showing the actual sum spent on the road. RuNcoati CYCLING CLUB.

The Wednesday riders of this club had an enjoyable spin on Wedneseay afternoon to Liverpool, from whence they sailed .to New Brighton. There was a fair mustei, and a start was made from the Devonshire Square at two o'clocic. On arriving at Liverpool they partook of tea previous to eml.,arking on the steamer for New Brightcn. A pleasant sail was experienced and a jovial evening spent. They arrived home about ten o'clock,all having ttoroughly enjoyed themselves.

THE PROPOSED DIVISION OF RUNCORN INTO WARDS. It will OP remembe:red that an inquiry into this sub- was held by a committee of the Cheshire County Council at Runcorn a few weeks ago. This Committee at the lase, meeting of the County Council, recommended that the application of trio Runcorn Commissioners,viz , that the township he div:ded into six wards, each ward to be represented. by three members, be granted. The recommendation of the Committee was adopted, and it was (acitied that the order of the Council should come into operation on the Bth- Novtmber ; but that ail pr )- ceedings preliminary or relating to the iirst election of members should commence at °mg.

div.head: HE EXA MIN E , SAT Y, MAY 26, 1894.
div.p: HE EXA MIN E , SAT Y, MAY 26, 1894.
CHARRED ON SUSPICION AT RUNCORN.

Oa Thursday morning at the Runc-)rn Police Court before Metsrs. P. Speakman and F. J. Norman,Elizabeth Allman of Vicar-street was charged on suspicion with having stolen two pairs of boots, value 203.—P.C. Rich- ardoion testified to arresting the prisoner at Widnes who on being charged at Runcorn admitted to stealing the boots from the London Boot Company, Church-street, Runcorn.—Superintendent Atherton applied for a re- mand until Saturday as several pledge tickets were found upon her person. fhe remand was granted.
CHARGE OF UNLAWFCIL POSSE.3SION AT RUNCORN.

Martin Gilligan. labourer, of no settled abode, was charged at the Runcorn Police Court, before Messrs. I'. Speakman and F. J. Norman, on Thursday morning with being in unlawful possession of a rabbit and a snare on tip 9th February.—P.C. Williams stated that he mut the prisoner coming down Halton-road, on the day men- tioned and noticing that one of his pockets was rather bulky he stopped and searched him. He found in. his possession one rabbit, recently killed, and one snare.— Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or fourteen days' imprisonment in default of payment. COMPLIMENTARY CONCERT AT WIDNES.

On Monday evening a complimentary concert was given in the Alexandra Theatre to a large and apprecia- tive audience. The programme was opened by Gossage's Prize Band giving a selection in an admirable manner. Songs were then given by the following :—Madarrie Emily Young, Miss Hr.ttie Mawdsley, Messrs. C. H. Hooker, W. Gordon, A. Evans, P. J. Kenyon and A. J. Paton. The second part was opened by a selection by the Widnes Subscription Prize Band, which was executed in excellent style. The Widnes Kentucky Minstrels then supplied the remainder of the programme consisting of songs, choruses, &c. SERIOUS WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES.

On Monday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Coun. W. W. a)ssage, John Cooghan, of 4, Mary-st., Moss Bank, was charged with unlawfully wounding ..Thn Fitzgerald, on Saturday, the 19th inst. It appears that prosecutor went to prisoner's house and broke some windows. Cooglian was brought from his work and found the prosecutor in the yard at the hack of his house, and it is alleged that there the prisoner struck Fitzgerald on the heal with a poker, thcred3y inflicting a serious wound. As the prosecutor was unable to at. tend court, the case was remanded for seven days, prirn soner bemg allowed out on bail.
WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUE SPORTS.

The Widnes athletic sports will take place on the 8,.h and 9th of June, as reference to-our advertising column will show. Aa usual there has been arranged a great number of important events, among which there are the Northern Counties championship, 120 yards hurdle, bicycle and flat race handicaps, 100 yards and one mile scratch races, and a tug of war. There will also be a half mile flat race handicap, open only to employes of the United Alkali Company, Limited. Prospectus and form of entry may be had on application to Mr. Jarni!s Walter Davies, secretary, Farnworth, Widnes, and we would draw the attention of those intending to take part in the sports to the fact that the entries close on June 4th. THE NEw PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH AT RUNCORN: OPENING
IMPROVED POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS AT RUNCORN.

The following improved postal arrangements for Run- corn commence on Monday next :—An early morning collection will be made at 530 a.m., from all letter boxes in Runcorn. (including Higher Runcorn) to con- nect with deliveries in Runcorn and Widnes at 7 a.m, in Liverpool at 11.30 a.m., and in Warrington at 11 59 a.m. An additional collection will be made at 12.30 p m., to connect with deliveries in Runcorn at 2 15 p.m. in Liverpool at 4.0 p.m., and in Warrington at 3.15 p.m. The wall boxes in Greenway-road, Lord-street, and Railway Station will in future be cleared at 8.0 p.m. for the night mail. A delivery of parcels will be made at 2.15 p.m.

ALLEGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Coun. W. W. Gossage, Thomas Henry Jones, of no fixed abode, was charged on remand with breaking into the dwelling- house of Mr. Fred Younge, 21,Deacon-road, early on the 12th inst. ,and stealing therefrom a, metal teapot,a basket, a towel, lib. of currants, and a small quantity of groce- ries. The prisoner effected an entrance to the house by prising the kitchen window with a steel cleaver. He was apprehended at Ashton-in-Makerfield, and several of the articles were found in his possession. The prisoner was committed for trial at the next Liverpool ASiiZOS.— Prisoner was further charged with staling a bicycle value £l2 10s., the property of John Ed win Hughes, of 23, Deacon-road,on the same morning. The machine was stolen from a shed in prosecutor's yard. Prisoner was apprehended at Ashton-in-Makerfield with the bicycle in his possession. He was committed for trial om this charge also.

This well-known and talented combination are open- ing a five days' visit at the Runcorn Public Hall on Mon- day evening next. As they have on three previous occasions visited Runcorn it is hardly necessary to dwell at length on their merits. Suffice it to say then that the reputation which they possessed when last they were in Runcorn, two and a half years ago, has been consider- ably improved and to day they stand amongst the first- rate dioramic and choral companies. An admirable pro- gramme has been arranged, an entire change both musical and pictorial, taking place nightly. Oa Monday night there will be views of" Old Ireland ; on Tuesday of" A trip to the Ile of Man;" on Wednesday of" Aus- tralia," on Thursday, "Canada ;" on Friday afternoon "Italy;" and in the evening" America." Mr. Joshua Dysot, will personally explain the views, and at inter- vals his numerous choir and band will contribute selec- tions of appropriate music, recitations, and laughable sketches..
SUDDEN DEATH OE AN EARLESTOWN TRADESMAN.

Dir.Williana Chambers,tailor and draper,of Earles- town, died at his residence, Crow-lane, Newton, on Wednesday morning, after two days' illness. The deceased attended service at the Wesleyan Chapel on :--unday, but some time during the night was taken ill, and Dr.Mouncey was called in,who found him suffering from English cholera. Although every attention was paid to him he did not recover, and died as stated. Ile was 51 years of age, and nine months ago was predeceased by his wife. A family of six children have been left. BAPTIST CHURCH, EARLESTOWII.

The annual services in aid of the Sunday School connected with the above place of worship were held in the chapel on Sunday. The Rev. George Hammond of Liverpool, and formerly of Prescot, conducted the morning and evening services, and interesting and instructive sermons were preached. At each service special hymns were sung by tho choir and children, in the evening the anthem; "Behold ; how good and joyful," being pleasingly rendered, the has solo being given by Mr. %V. Limond. In the afternoon the service of song, en- titled " Dot, and her treasures," was very effic:iently rendered by the children and choir, the various items being received with evident satisfaction by the large audience present. Mr. S. Harvey con- ducted, and Mr. E.I-lulme gave the connective read- ings, whilst Mr. E. Eckersley ably presided at the organ. The collections throughout the day amoun- ted to £32.
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board room of the Town Hall, on Tues- day afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., C.C. There were also present the Revs. Dean Finegan, and Father Clarke; Dr. O'Keefe, Messrs. J. W. Wareing, Major D. 149(vis, R. Shaw, B. Brown, C. E. Barlow, S. Quinn, C. Flynn, and G.H. Danby (clork).

DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that during the month of April there had been eight applications for free places, which were granted, and 21 prosecutions before the magistrates. They also recommended that they be authorised to send children who are deaf, dumb or blind, to the Deaf and Dumb Schools, at Boston Spar, Manches- ter, or Liverpool, and the Blind Asylurr in Liverpool, on the terms set forth in their respective lett-rs. The minutes were passed on the motion of Father Clarke and Major Wareing.

div.head: SERVICES.
div.p: SERVICES.

The opening services in connection with the St. John's New Presbyterian Church, Runcorn, were held on Sun- day morning and evening in the newly-constructed schoolroom. The congregations on both occasions were numerous and the proceedings were of an exceedingly bright and cheerful mature. Powerful discourses were delivered in the morning and evening by the Rev. John Thomas, 8.A., of Liverpool, whose remarks were lis- tened to with close attention.—On Monday evening an- other service was held, the preacher being the Rev. J. Puleston Jones, M.A., of Bangor, who gave a most instrucdve and interesting sermon to a fairly large assembly. At all the services special hymns and anthems were sung, and collections made on behalf of the Wilding fund._

div.head: CHILD THIEVES AT WIDNES.
div.p: CHILD THIEVES AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Petty Sessior,s, hefort? Mr. J. Brock and Ald?rinan Timinis, three %%oaten Ann Corrigan, Mary Coles, and Johanna F,llan, and a man named Patrick Quin, were all charged in cuHiodc with receiving a large quantity of timber, valued at £2, well knowing it to have been stolen by their children from Mr. J. P. Kershaw's timber yard, Tanhouse-law., on Tuesday. On Wednesday the houses of all the prisoners were searched, and some of the stolen timber was found in each of them. The children of the prisoners (whose ages range-from five to nine years) were called as witnesses by the police, and acknowledged taking the timber to their parents. The Chairman said the parents were the parties to blame in these cases. It was per- fectly evident that they were willing enough to receive anything their children stol,.—They would each have to pay 103. or go to gaol for fourteen days with hard labour. A BATCII OF ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES.

Thomas Giffin°ly, of Moon-stret, was taken to the Accident Hospital on Saturday, suffering from a fracture of the left wrist and other severe injuries sustained by falling from a plank at Me,srs. Muspratt's works. The unfortunate man fell a di,tance of twenty-five feetp—On Saturday a lad named William Hignett, of Dock-street, was admitted into the Accident Hospital suffering from scalds to his arms and hands received at the Widnes Resin Works, by a bucket of black resin falling on him. Under the care of Dr. Hutchinson he is now progressing favourably.—A child named Thomas Steele, of Martley- street, was, on Saturday, playing in Male,loy-street when a flag fell on him causing a scalp wound. Be was taken to the Accident Hospital and under the care of Dr. Donnelly, is now doing well.—An explosion occurred at Bolton's Copper Works on Monday, by which a man named William Carr, 31, sustained a wound on the left hip and severe contusions on the right arm. He was 'taken to the Accident Hospital and attended by Dr. Hutchinson. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CRIFRed, WIDNES.

On Friday evening, at this church, there was a crowded attendance to witness the several presentations to be made to the Rev. R. G. Hughes, on his leaving Widnes. He has had the pastorate of the above place for about 10 years, but now he is removing to New- castle-on-Tyne. The following mementos were pre- sented: A purse containing 60 guineas, by the congrega- tion and friends; a handsorme Bible, by some lady friends ; three handsome theological volumes, by Mr. and Mrs. Halsall ; two handsome photographs in plush frames, of ladies and gentlemen of the congregation, by Mr. Pickthall ; and an elegant inkstand with gold pen, by the young inen connected with the church. Thanks were rendered to the donors by Mr. Hughes, who spoke with deep emotion. Mr. Hughes has also been presented by the Widnes police with a group of themselves hand- somely framed in oak as a token of respect.—On Sunday evening Mr. Hughes preached his farewell sermon. There was a large congregation. IF YOU WANT a reliable is. 110 pair of Kid Gloves, write to JONES'S 59, 61. and 63, Brunswick-r•ad. Liverpool. Post Free.—See General Advertisement for other btrgains.—.Advt. JUVENILE THIEVES AT RUNCORN: EXTRAORDINARY STATEMENTS BY MOTHERS.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Thursday morning before Messrs. P. Sp-akman and F. J. N.rman, three boys named William Henry Cray, ford,James Carrollo.nd 'Thomas McDonald, all ot' whom reside in Fryer-street, Runcorn, were charged with having stolen a quantity of timber valued 6d., the property of the Manchester Ship Canal Company on the 23rd inst.—P.C. Richardson stated that at about nine o'clock on Wednesday night he was on d ity at Old Quay entry when he saw the prisoners breaking a fence down belonging to the Canal Company, and tying the wood into bundles. He went towards them, and when they saw Ym they dropped their bundles and ran away. Witness caught them and took them to the Police Station where, when charged with the theft, Crawford replied "We did'nt take it all from the canal ; we took some from Wigg's works." The other two lads confirmed this as3ertion.—When the parents of the prisoners were spoken to regarding the conduct of their boys, Crawford's mother said that her husband had left her threo years,and she had to send her children out to get sticks and coal. Carroll's mcther con- cluded licr statement by saying that they could not starve and—"we will have .sticks and coal."—Mr.Speak- man severely admonished the women for so speaking and warned them that if the children were again brought up, and similar assertions were made they would prob- ably find themselves in a very serious position after- wards. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTIE.

The usual monthly meeting of this Committee took place on Tuesday evening in the Board room. Town Hall, Runcorn, the following gentlemen being present : Messrs. W. Handley (in the chair), W. Hankinson, J, Grice, W. Pope, arid J. a Jones, librarian.—The last named gentleman presented his monthly report and financial statement. The first showed that the library had been opened twenty-one days during the month of April, in the course of which period 1,772 books had been issued, the following being the classification of the same :—Lending : Theology, 24: Philosophy, 8 ; Science, 87 : History, Sze.. 96 ; Poetry. 15 ; Fiction, 1363 ; Mis- cellaneous. 141 ; making a total for the lending depart- ment of 1740, which with 32 from the reference depart- ment brings the number up to 1772. These figures show a decrease of 14 in the lending and 11 in the refer- ence departments. The report and financial statement were adopted. The librarian also reported the follow- ing gifts :—J. E. Langshaw, Birkenhead, "Finns, and Fern culture," " How to grow Roses " (Ryder),Carlyle's " Hero and Hero Worship," " Nights with Ben Brierley," and Shirely Hibbert's " Rustic Adornments for Homes of Taste." Anonymously : White's "Shipbuilding with plates," " Shinbnilding in Wood and Iron," R. Murra)'s " Steamships " (1863) and Sutherland's " Shipbuilder's Association, 1775." Library reports had been received ' from Preston, Barking and Hove ; from the Lifeboat Crew Division of the Sons of .Temperance : " The Son of Temperance."—A letter was read by Mr. J. D. Jones from Mr. W. Sowerby, stating that his removal from Runcorn to Fleetwood necessitated his removal tr,an the [Committee. He very much regretted having to sever his connection with the Library as the work which he had done whilst connected with it bad always afforded him the greatest pleasure.—lt was moved, seconded and carried that the resignation of Mr. Sowerby be accepted, and that a letter of thanks for his services be addressed to him.

div.head: THINGS HEA RD AND SEEN AT
div.p: THINGS HEA RD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT,

Mr. J. F. Moulton, the respected headmaster at Greenway-road Board School, Runcorn, is to be con- gratulated upon the successful results of his teach- ing in connection with the evening classes. The outcome of the examinations should certainly Rive him much gratification, seeing that out of thirty- two candidates who sat for arithmetic only four failed; whilst in geography only one failed out of thirteen. The examinations in English grammar and handwriting do not produce such favourable results, however, as twenty-four out of fifty-one failed in the former subject and four out of fifteen in the latter. These statistics, nevertheless, are a convincing proof of the hard work which he has done for the scholars within the past session, and there is not the least doubt that if those who attend the classes will only do so regularly, and will try to give their utmost attention to the remarks of their tutors, that the school will at the end of the next session find its reputation considerably raised.

The Committee of the Cheshire County COUtleil, which visited Runcorn some weeks ago to hear the application of the Commissioners to divide Runcorn into wards, have decided in favour al the applica- tion and at the last meeting of the Council they re- commended that Runcorn should be divided into six wards, each ward to be represented by three mem- bers. This recommendation was accepted by the Council, whose order will come into operation in November next. All preliminary proceedings which have relation to the electiop of members, or any other subject, may be commenced forthwith. The Council also resolved to set aside £4OO instead of £2OO tor the purpose of maintaining and repairing Halton-road, Bridge-st., High •st., over Waterloo Bridge, and Station-road.

Quite a flutter of excitement was occasioned amongst the inhabitant.; of Runcorn when it wa.: known that we were to have an opportunity of viewing three of her Mijest3's vessels as they passed down the canal to Nlanchester to take part in the official opening ceremony. Just before one o'clock they arrived, the " Norseman " leading the way, followed by the Admiralty yacht" Enchan- tress,' and the two gunboats" Speedy" and"Seligull." The canal bank was alrnostcrowded witt interested spectators, some of whom raised cheers for the sailors on board the handsome vessels—which were heartily acknowledged. The return of the boats was also watched by large numbers on the bank on Tuesda3 morning.

The Presbyterians of Runcorn have now left their old chapel aid worshipped for the first time in their new chapel school on Sunday last. The, ser- vices were exceedingly heurty and cheerful and were enjoyed by all. The erection of the church proceeds apace and when the work is completed,the building will be a very handsome one, and one which the Presbyterians will surely be proud to possess. In order that the work [Right go oU un- interruptedly, liberal subscriptions to the fund are sorely needed, and it is hoped that the earnest appeals of the promoters will be responded to in a manner worthy of the cause.

The question of the provi3ion of a graving dock or otherwise by the Manchester Ship Canal Company still remains in abeyance. In the meantime, how- ever, signs of great impatience are becoming visible among the local shipwrights.who regard the appar • ent sluggishness of the Ship Canal directors in none too favourable a light. It is now more than three weeks since the Law Clerk to the Improvement Commissioners corresponded with the company upon the matter, but up to the present, it is under- Fitood that no communication bearing on the sub- ject has since been received. Of course the Directors have had a somewhat anxious time lately and have been kept rather bu•;y, but now that the calm is at hand they might be induced to consider the ques- tion forthwith.

Our local Rugby Football club has certainly held its head high during the past season. The review published in last Friiay's issue of the Runcorn " Examiner " shows an exceedingly creditable per- formance on the part of the Champions who only lost five matches out of a total of 39 played. Seven were drawn, and 27 won,a record of which the pos- sessors ought surely to feel very proud of. The " A" team have been even more successful, having gone throu,h the whole of their fixtures without once sustaining defeat. The number of matches played was 34. Of these 30 were WOll and the remaining four drawn. This is a feat which is deservinz• or the highest possible praise, and it is hoped that the players will not want for this hut that their quali- ties, and the hard work they have dit,chargeo will be fully recognised. The members of the latter team will shortly be presented with the medals which they won as champions of the Liverpool and Dis- trict Rugby Junior League. It is expected that the occasion will be made to take the form of a F.vicial gathering for the benefit of the team.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTAL

This committee tecommand-ed. that Miss Alice Saunders (vice Miss M. E. div.head: ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT.
div.p: THE ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT.

The sub-ccmmittee appointed to inquire into the charges made against the School Management Committee presented their repart, in which they stated that they had considered the matter very carefully, having held three meetings and heard evidence on both sides, and they were unanimously of (+pinion that the schools were not" [mismanaged," but that their management reflected the highest credit upon the School Management Com- mittee and their executive officer.—Mr. Lewis said he was not satirtied with the report. It touched upon +natters that had no connection with his charges, while most vital points were omitted altogether. Therefore, he gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board he should call attention to the unsatisfactory nature of the report, and more a resolution.—The repert was adopted on the motion of Maim. Waring and Mr. Shaw, only Mr. Lewis voting against.

E. Cutting, T. 0. Taylor and E. Davidson. The last-named gentleman also conducted special services on Sunday morning and evening. GRAVE CHARGE AGAINST A FRODSHAM BM—At the Frodshain Police Cour: on Tuesday. before Dr. Steele, a youth refined William Booth, aged 18 years, and living at Iron Dish, Frodsham Lordship, was charged on re- mand with a ;s tufting Elizabeth Andrews, aged 12 years, of Ship-street, Fro isham, on the 17th May. The prisoner denied having been at the place where the complainant said the assau't was committed, and as the girl's statement was not sufficiently corroborated the charge was dismissed.—Mr. Burton, solicitor of Run- corn, appeared for the prisoner: HELP FOR THE CHURCH MISSIONARY SOCIETY.-00- quent sermons were preached on behalf of the above society on Sunday morning and evening in the Parish church, Frodsharn by th Rev. J. Wood, who for 37 years has laboured with much success as a missionary in 'West Afric t. The congreations were large and the offertories liberal.-0a Mond iy evening the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blogg, presided over the annual meeting held under the auspices of the Society at the Town Hall. There was a large gathering and after a few pithy re- ma ks by the Chairman in praise of the Society, the Rev. J. Wood, detailed a few of his experiences whilst working in Africa. These narratives proved exceedingly interesting and often amusing. Collections were taken in aid of the Church Missionary Fund. THE FENCING-IN OF FRODSHAM HILLS.—A Manchester correspondent writes :—For seine time past I have been in the habit of paying a visit each Whit Monday to the quiet hut much sought after little town of Frodsham, and enjoying a ramble upon the mist delightful Over- ton Hills, but I very much regret to notice how patches of these hills are beginning to be fenced in, to the exclu- sion of the public. While walking along the road at the foot of one of the hills on Monday last, my attention was drawn to a portion of the foot of the hill that had been levelled off for some distance back from the road. and I asked a villager who was passing by at the time, what these preparations meant, and if some buildings were to be erected on the spot, and he made reply, "Ay, there's a house to be built, and they're going to fence in a piece o' yon hill." I strolled on further, and found that an iron fencing roaring right up the hill from the bottom to the top had been erected, which, enclosing a large space of land, was a persistent witness of a desire to curtail the rights of the public. On making inquiry I was informed that this fence had been erected some time. The people say that these hills belong to the lord of the manor, but there does appear to he a screw 1 iose some- where when land which has been open to and used by the public as a pleasure resort from time immemorial can be fenced off for bu ilding or other purposes. I think that this is a matter that should be taken up and fought by the Frodshani people in their own interests, as with- out a doubt the visitors • who End their way to this old- world spot contribute largely to the benefit of the town, and as it is a case that affects a large number of people who visit these hills annually the publicity given to my few remarks might be the -first step to prevent the ap- propriation that is going on.
FRACAS BETWEEN BUTCHERS.

At St. Helens on Tuesday. before Alderman M`li ryde and Mr. W. J. Thomson, William Turner, a butcher, of Ciaughton-st., was charged with committing a breach of the peace, and with assaulting Police-constable Henry Richards. He pleaded guilty, but said he did not know what he was doing. The officer, who appeared with his eye bandaged, :RAM that at twenty minutes past six on Monday night Turner was fighting with another butcher, named William Crosby, in Canslield-5".% %.% itness went between to separate them, when ['timer struck him in the eye. lie was in plain clothes, but Purner knew he was a constable. Witness's eye was cut, and was closed altogether that morning. Turner was under the influ- ence of drink at the time.—For the breach of the peace, Turner was bound over for three months, and for the assault he was fined 20A. and costs, or fourteen days.

div.p: FASHIONABLE* WEDDING AT PRESCOT.

On Wednesday afternoon, at half-past two o'clock,the wedding of Mr. George Cope, son of the late Mr. Thos. Cope, Parkside, riuytnn, and Beatrice,the third daughter of Dr. Egtrzoo F. Hall, of Ashtrees, Prescot, was cele- brated in Prescot Parish Church, which was florally de- corated for the occasion. Tne 10v. Canon Mitchell officiated, assisted by the Rev. R. Freeman. The bride was given away by her father, and wore a travelling dress of sapphire blue cloth, white moire vest,and three- cornered hat (Louis XV. style), carrying a bouquet of white eKotics. She was attend.-d by four bridesmaids— the Misses Lillian Kate and Ethel flail (sisters), and Jennie and Alice Cope (sis'er of the bridegroom), who were attired in costumes of sh it fa wn cloth,black moire lace, and hats to mateh,and carried bouquets of shaded roses. Mr. Charles Cope acted as best man. Amongst tr F. numerous guests wen, Mr. J. ft. Willox, MV , Mrs. Willox (mother of the bridegroom), Mr. and Mrs. Alexa- nder, the Misses Cope, Dr. and Mr.,. div.head: RIVAL INSURANCE AGENTS AT WIDNES.
div.p: RIVAL INSURANCE AGENTS AT WIDNES.
CROSS-SUMMONSES FOR ASSAULT.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. J. Brock and Alderman Timmis, Thomas Bolton, residing in Liverpool, was t,urntroned by James Parkinson, 2, Okell-street, Runcorn, for afsaulting hi' aon the 22nd inst. Across-summons was taken out by Bolton. Parkinson was represented by Mr. J. W. Knowles, and Bolton by Mr. J. P. Mearns, of St. Helens. In opening the case Mr. Knowles said Parkinson was the local superintendent for the Leeds and Gorieral Society, and Bolton was an inspector for the Pearl Insurance Company. Parkinson had been pushing business in Widnes for the last fort night, and Bolton appeared to have been very joalous of Parkinson, and on the 1611 inst. he threatened Parkinson in Runcorn. On Tuesday last the two men met by appointment in the house of a Mrs. Tracy, and a man named Murphy was appointed to act as arbitrator, to decide as to the claims of the respective insurance companies. It was arranged that each should have ten minutes in which to state their case, and Parkinson wanted Bolton to commence the debate, but after a few minutes argument Bolton caught hold of Parkinson's collar and hit him once on the nose and once in the chest. His nose bled freely.— Parkinson was called, and bore out his solicitor's state- ment.—Cross-,-xamined : I knew that Mrs. Tracy had already been insured in the Pearl Company, and that it had been reported to her that if she died the company would not pay any money, and we wanted her to insure with Us as well. The Pearl Company was in Wi.ines before the Leeds and General. —Mr. Mearns : And FM.I have been trying to kidnap their customers ?—No.—Witness had been in Widnes for a fortni.ht, and the company had been rep- resented in Widnes for only six weeks. He had been in the employ of other insurance companies, but the Pearl. —Mr. Mearns's case wits that Parkinson was tha aggres- sor, and that he had first knocked one of Bolton's teeth out before the latter struck Parkinson in self defence.— Jahn Murphy, Bridge-street. Whines, who was the arbi- trator between the two men in Mrs. Tracy's House, said there was a row, and Parkinson struck the first blow. He struck II lton in the mouth.—Both parties were bound over ti keep the peace for three months, them- selves in £lO and two sureties of £5 each,with the alter- native of fourteen days' imprisonment, with hard labour.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT A. GLASSWORK
div.p: ACCIDENT AT A. GLASSWORK
NARROW ESCAPE!: OF VirORKNIEN.

About tsn o'olock on Saturday night, the roof of one of the glassrnaking " houses" at Messrs.Pilking- ton's Sheet Glassworks, Sr. Helens, fell in, but for- tunately a number of employes who were at work had received timely warning, and had just got out of the " house " when the collapse took place. The particular portion of the works where the accident hap- pened is near the c,rner of Watson-itreet and Grove-st., and is the oldest of the buildings, evidently being the first " house" erected early in this century, when these great works were founded. The roof of the" house " was constructed of timber principals tied with iron rods, which rested on the walk—a span of perhaps 40ft. Un- derneath it, were holes in which men swing glass which is in course of manufacture. One of the officials, it is said, heard a cracking of the roof, and called the men out. They, ton, obserVed danger, and hurried off, just in time to escape being buried in the debris. The damage will not, it is believed, exceed £lOO.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT NEWTON.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT NEWTON.

On Tuesday evening at, the Congregational Schoolroom ,Newton after the ordinary meeting of the Young People's SoCiety of Christian Endeavour, an interesting presentation was made to Miss Holmes who mince its inception has been intimately connected with the Sniety, but who,is now leaving the neighbourhood. The presentation was made by the Rev. James Al!att., who said they had heard with the deepest regret of her removal from the district, and he con,equent severance of her Con- nection with the Y.P.S.C.E. She had spared no pains to promote its interest from the first, and her pencil had been freely used in producing artistic designs for effective service at the Society's social meetings. As one of the delegates to the London Goivention this year, it was felt that she worthily represented the spirit of Christianity, to the condi- tion of which their Societies everyw here attach( d the supremest importance. The junior society of which she had lately had entire charge had giv,i) a warmer tiff,ction to its work, and had been drawn into closer sympathy in its aims and purposes, and now both sections united in asking her accept- ance of the gold brooch, with the monogram Y.P.S.C.E., as a small token of their loving esteem and best wishes. (Applause.) Miss Holmes suitably acknowledged the gift.

div.head: DARESBITRY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBITRY HIGHWAY BOARD.

The annual meeting of this Board was held on Thursday afternoon, in the Boardroom, Daresbitry. There were present : Mr. S. Burgess (chairman), Messrs. W. Pierpoint, W. Long, J. Darbyshire, Dar- lington, Maddock, Johnson, Tickle, Aaron, Clark, and Beswick ; Mr. Linaker (clerk), and Mr. Swin- ton (surveyor).

ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The Clerk announced that it was necessary for the Board to elect a chairman and a vice-chairman for the year. Mr. Tickle proposed, and Mr. Aaron seconded that Mr. Smith Burgess be appointed chairman.—Mr. Burgess thought that as the Board was only likely to exist for another year it was not necessary to appoint another chairman in place of Mr. J. Charton Parr. Be proposed that Mr. Parr be re-elected.—Mr. Wm. Pier- point said there was this to be considered, that it was the last year they would have the opportunity of cen- ferring the honour upon Mr. Burgess, but on the other hand, there was the question whether it would not be better for the Board to continue with Mr. Parr as chair- man.—Mr. Long said he thought he was the person who proposed that Mr. Parr's resignation should not be accepted at last year's annual meeting, in the hope that Mr. Parr would be able to resume his duties on the Beard. His health had not, however, recovered, and he thought it would be better to appoint a new chairman. —The Clerk said Mr. Parr expressed his opinion at the last election of chairman when he said he thought it would be better for the Board to elect as chairman a man who would be able to regularly attend to his duties. —Mr. Burgess ultimately withdrew his motion, and he was unanimously elected chairman. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Parr for his services to the Board. For the position of vice-chairman, Mr. Darbyshire proposed, and Mr. Johnson seconded that Mr. Lone be appointed. —Mr. Long refused to serve, as he was of opinion that the tendency of the times was to have elected represen- tatives in such positions. He proposed that Mr. Hall be elected.—Mr. 1.1 ..rgess proposed Mr. Bradford for the position, Mr. Tickle seconded the latter proposal, and it was carried. The Finance Committee was also re- elected.

div.head: MR. AARON'S MOTION.
div.p: MR. AARON'S MOTION.

Mr. Aaron moved that in future, land picked stones purchased by the Board be paid for at the rate of nine shillings per ton, instead of eight shillings as at present. He contended that at present farmers were under-paid for supplying broken stones.—Mr.Tickle secondrd.—Mr. Johnson also spoke in favour of the motion.—Mr.Darby- shire was of opinion that the stones should be broken by the Board, and moved an amendment that farmers receive 83. per ton for unbroken stones.—Mr.Dariington seconded.—Mr. Aaron wished to withdraw his motion, but he was told he could not. On the am..ndinent being put to the. meeting it was carried unanimously.—Mr. Aaron gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that farmers be paid 143. instead of 124. per day for team horses. AN IMPROVEMENT AT LATCHFORD.

Mr. W. Pierpoint said as waywarden for Latchford, he had been requested to ask that the Board take into consideration a little improvement needed to a footpath in Latchford, caused by the.making of the Manchester Ship Canal. The improvement required was on the approach road to the high level bridge at Acker's•lane. He did not think the footpath would cost the Board above £s.—The Surveyor said the improvement was needed, and he did not think it would cost more than £s.—lt was decided to carry out the improvement.
THE BOARD AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The hoard's Ship Canal Committee reported that Mr. Leader Williams and several others representing the Canal Company had met them. The Committee pre- sented to the deput ttion several matters relating to road improvements &c. in connection with.the Canal,and the Canal Company had promised to catrv,out the whole of the requirements of the Eloar4;._ThOurVeyor reported that several of the Board's requirements had already been carried out by the Canal CAnnany. Mr. J. Darby- shire said that if the Committee did not stick closely to the Canal Company with their recommendations they would be put aside and not carried into effect. Mr. Pierpnint thought that although the Canal Company were rather slow in carrying out their recominendations, they would eventually do so. Several members expressed their satisfaction at the promptness with w hicli the swing bridges were turned in some parts of the Board's district.

MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AND THE DEMANDS OF THE MINERS.

div.head: EIGHT HOURS DAY AND THE LIMIT-
div.p: THE EIGHT HOURS DAY AND THE LIMIT-
ATION OF OUTPUT.

On Saturday evening at Northwicb, the mem- bers of the North %vie!) and District Amalgamated Society of Salt Workers, Rock Salt Miners, Alkali Workers, Mechanics, and General Labourers presented to Mr. J. T. Brunner M.P., a gold pencil case and an illuminated address as an expression of gratitude for the generous support which he rendered to them during the coal crisis of 1893,when for a considerable length of time he contributed £2O per week towards the relief of those who were thrown out of employment. After the address had been read by Mr. W. Ta.rwood, the secretary, Mr. Brunner said that that which he didi last autumn,lie was in a measure compelled to do by his admiration of the way in which they beam the suffer- ings brought upon them. Turning to the Employere Liability Bill, he might say he had been for years advocatieg a very generous extension of the liabilities. of employers, so much se that he held that very injury caused ti a man engaged in works bringing profit to an employer ought to be part of the cost of the eperations,. just as inevitably as an injury to a piece of machinery (applause). The leaders of the great Minere' Federation, and some other colliers' organisations had pressed very- strongly of late for a legal limitation of their hours of labour at the hands of the House of Commons. He believed that the members of the House of Commons were rather less convinced than frightened into taking this action. It seemed to him that if Parliament was to interfere with the labour of grown men, and decide the maximum hours to be worked, Parliament ought to begin not with the men who worked five days a week, but with those who worked seven. (applause). For that reason, lie was determined to vote against the Miners' Eight Hours Bill ; but he would support with all his heart a measure for the limitation of the hours of labour of those who worked seven days per week (applause). Much had been said at the International Congress in Berlin that week about the necessity of limiting the output of coal ; but the fact seemed to be lost sight of that such a limitation meant a limitation of the output of almost everything made in England. If the Miners' Federation had their way and limited the output in order to raise prices, and thereby es they hoped, their wages, ,1 they were extremely likely to limit the output of coal to sueh an extent that it would be practically impossible to get slack to carry on the great manufactures of the country. Again, the Federation had often cleimel that there should be no stacking of coal, but if the colliery owner was forbidden to stack when there was only a small demand it also would mean a forcible stoppage ot the production of slack. He claimed that periecay innocent men employed at Northwich, Widnes, Et. Helens, and in all the great iron producing counties 'should not be punished by the Miners' Federation, and for this reason he meant to resist their policy -to Lb* utmost. With regard to the important qeeivien of protecting those who were bound to work seven days a week, he had found, as far as he had been able to extend his inquiriee,that the number of men in Great Britain and Ireland working seven days a week and twelve hours a day was larger than the number of colliers. Therefore it was a very much more important matter for Parlia- ment to take in hand, and on Tuesday next he intended asking the Home Secretary to instruct his inspectors to make inquiries in all the tacteries as to the number so employed, and he hoped that the result would be the extension of an Eight Hours Act to include men work- ing tinder such conditions (applause). He urged them to stick to their own union, and to show that he believed,in what he preached he might say that he believed lie was the only man in the world who has ever stopped his works and, in his own time, called his men together and asked them to join a trades union (applause).

div.head: MEETING OF HE RUNCORN SONS OF
div.p: MEETING OF HE RUNCORN SONS OF
TEMPE RAN CE.

The fortnightly meeting of this organization was held on Saturday evening, Mr. David Smith presid• lag. Alter the usual business had been transacted, Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, who represented the Cheshire Grand Division of the Order at the 39 no dal seS- sien of the National Division of Great Britain and Ireland recently held at Newcastle-on-Tyne, presented a report of the proceedings at the Conference. He stated that there were 240 representatives from all parts of the kingdom. On Saturday the 12th inst. there was a grand reception tea and public meeting in the Loraine Hall. At rite public meeting to advocate the claims of the order, Mr. John Dixon, W.G., occupied the chair. There was-a large attendance of members and the general public. The speakers were the leaders of the movement, Messrs. J. Sanderson (York), William Whiteman (London), and C. H. Gorringe (Landen). It was stated by the speakers that 27 years had elapsed since they had held their National Division meetings in Newcastle. They were then very feeble folks. But now they had a, position in the country. No one had any need to bury his individuality in order to work with them. On Sunday the officers aud members held a grand church parade. They met at the Central Station, and headed by a brass band and the beautiful baueer of the order, walked in procession through the princi,:al streets of the city. This was a demonstration of Large propor- tions, the members walking three abreast. They then attended Divine service at St. Nicholas's Cathedral„ the preacher on the occasion being the Rev. Can-on Lloyd, M.A. The sacred edifice was full. He said they were representatives of a vast co-operative combination, one that had spread very largely up and d iwn th 3 country in the last few years, and one that was destined, if he mistook not, to spread still more. If it was founded on selfishness it would come to nothine ; if selfiehness came in it would not hold together. In conclusion he said that they had done well in coming to tha house of prayer. On the Sunday afternoon, two meetings were held in the open air. At teese there was an immense gathering of working men, eloquent addresses being given by Mr. L. Hawley (London), Mr. E. Lougher (Merthyr Tydvi)), Mr. William Whiteman (London) Councillor Hudd trt (S dford), an I others. At tile busi- ness meetings in the week—Monday, Tuesday, Wednen. day—many matters affecting the order were discussed. The various reports were read by the offieere FroEn the statistics submtted, the results of the list yea-'s effort had been most encouraeing. The increase in the adult branch was 1.271 members, making a total adult mem- bership of 30,882, while the work of the juvenile portion of their institutio)4 showed an Mere-see of 1,255, making a total of cadet membership of 11,749. The death rate was low, being 8 per 1,000 me:nbers. It was decided to hold the next annual meeting in Glaseeiv. Mr. Bis- brown, in conclusion, hoped tat the tneet:ne iast held would give a stinmlus to the cause they hal so much at heart and that eventually their efforts would be crowned with success.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A MANCLIESTER YOUNo WOMAN IN TROUBLE.,

A respectably dressed young woman belonging to Manchester, named Florence Jones, was charged at the Borough Court on Tuesday morning with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street, and further charged with doing wilful damage to a window at the ftaM's Head Hotel, to th,! extent of 30s. William mp.pp, zi barman, said the prisoner called at the Ram's Head Hotel the previous day and asked to be served with drirdc. As she was drunk he refused to serve her, and afterwards had to eject her. Si. returned several times and was ej cted. The last time she was- put out she put her fist through the window. PC. Clough said he was in c,inpany with Constable Chrimes when he saw the Prisoner, who was drunk. ej-cted from the Ram's Head Hotel, and also saw her break a pane of glas,, value 30s. h 6" was walking away when witness stopped her. P.C. Chritnes corroborated. Inspector James said the pris- oner was drunk when brought to the police station. The magistrates ordered the prisoner to pay the damage 30s. and find her for being drunk, or in default 30 days' imprisonment.

CARRYING A GUN WITHOUT A LICENCE. • William Henry Tongue, 4 Admiral-st., and James Wil- son Seb.field, 6, Florence-st., were each charged at the Warringb n Borough Court on Friday, with carrying a gun without a licence on April 21. Tonga], did not Spp' ar at the court. P.C. Meaccck Water' that on the abeve date he and Detective Ede were on the railway in Latchford, near the footh,ll field, on the look-nut for trespassers. They saw the two defendants carrying nuns near the Black Bear canal. When he and Dt• c'ive Ede went towards them, they hurried away,hut witness took Tongue into custody. Schofield 5140 gave his name asJames Wilson. The officers after getting Townie's name arid address' followed Schofield to his hniase, and when they arrived there, he gave the name of Schofi,ld. Later on in the evening witness went again to Sch.field's house. and asked for his licence, and he produced a licence dated 21st April,in the name of Jnzeph Schofield. Detective Ede gave corroborative evidence. Inspector Spinks said that he had male ing.iiries and discovered that a woman had obtained a licence in the name of Jos. Schofield on the above date, which was the same date that he was seen home by the nfficers.—The defendant said that Joseph Scho6ld was his real name, hal he was always known as James Wilson Schofield on the canal where b. worked. fle would have got a licence earlier, but he had been " on crutches " and could not get one. The magistrates fine 3 each defendant ss. and costs.

Witness shouted to defendant, but instead of slackening his speed, he stoed up in the wag- onette and whipped the horse to urge it on. He would be driving at the rate of 13 or 14 miles an hour. Wit- ness followed defendant to the c hialse in company with Sergeant Cheney.—Josenli flighiam gave evidence as to seeing the defendant driving at a turious rate.— The defendant contended that tli• horse he skai driving would not go more than five miles an hour, and called two witnesses to corroborate his statement.—A fine of 53., including cost,. was imposed. THE LAD WITH TRH BULKY POCKETS.—George Wade, eleven years of age was again broullit before the magis- trates and charged with stealing from the stall in the market of Mr. James Halliwell on the 1611 in,t. a tea cloth and two handkerchiefs. The defendant was brought before the magit,tra'es the previous Thursday when he was charged with having the articles narn.,l in his possession, supposed to have been stolen. A remand was then granted for further inquiries to be made. P.C. Barnett gave evidence as to notking the lad's bulks' pockets, and detaining him. His answers not being satisfactory, the lad was taken to the police station. From inquiries since made it was found that the articles taken from the defendant's pockets were the property of Mr. James Halliwell, a stalllinider in the market. On tieing charged with the offence the lad said " I found them underneath a tll Vtlqz`re the Jews stand."—James Palliwell identified the articles as his property.—The Chief Constable said the lad received six strokes with the hirchrod a short time ago for assisting in robbiry, a boy ftf some cigarettes and cigars.
