MONDAY.

The House of Commons reassembled on Monday. Sir W. HAncounT, replying to Sir C. Dilku, said he •• would mention Friday week as the day for the U,,anda debate." The Parochial Elf ctors (Registration Acceleration) Bill was read a second time and referred to a Sdect Com- mittee. The House then vent into Committee of Supply. In a discussion on Post-office votes Mr. Arnol.l Morley promised to consider a sugt.restion m4de hy Mr. Burns that post-office bilikling,s throughout the country shunt] be placed under the supervision of the local medical offi- cers of health.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commans on Tuesday eveninr, the second reading of the Scotch Local G.vernment Bid was tormally moved by Sir G. 0. TRETELYAN, who, in reply- ing' at the close ot the debate to the criticisms of several members on the Onnrsition side, said the till could in flomMittee be mule more w•ceptable Vian it was at present. The bill was read a second time without a division, and was referred to the Standing Committee on Scotch Bills.

div.head: WEDNE4MAY.
div.p: WEDNE4MAY.

The House Com,nons went into Committee on Wed- nesday on the Cruelty to Children Bill. Mr. G. ItuAsell moved the omission of cla.:.se 4, wh;th proposed that in a case where a person had been e nvicted of cruelty to a child he should at the o!)tion of th-e magistrate, if he was an habitual drunkard,be sent. either to a retreat for inebriates or to an asylum or wcrktiouse. Sir H. WEn- t•TER said he should he prepared to insert an a mendmeNt that a magistrate should only exercise Oda option in eases where persons were prepare t, pay the expense. Mr. REID suggested that the am'-ndm-nt should 1-ie with- drawn now arid the sot jeet reconsidered between the present time and the report, and in this S r H. Webster concurred. The clanae mai, after some turther discus- sion, agreed to. On chose 6, providing for the punish- ment of persons allowing a child of which they had thi. custody to be in any street or plane for any purnose forbidden by the wincipal At', Mr..flopProod m wed an amendment to insert the word "willull)." before "allow- ing." The amendment was rej,cted by 130 to 27. Flay- ing rased through Committee, the hill was report-A to the House, and order.d for third reading. Committee on the &ion Hours Act (1892) Amendment Bill was then resumed on the motion of Mr. PROVAND, who explained that the purpose of the bill was merely to limit the hours of young persona to eleven per day, and sixty per week. Near half-past five Mr. T. H. BOL- TON, who had previously spokPn in opposition to the bill, moved that progress he ',ported. Mr. PRovAND appealed to the hon. in,mber not to press his mu): ion. Mr. TOMLINSON Ask- d if the Goverment thought that the bill was a pract,cd working measure. Mr. G. Russßm, said the Government had considerrd the bill and supported the second readln:. Mr. TOMLINSON re- plied that this was not the second reading. The time for suspending debate had now arrived, and further proceedings on the hill ha,l to be ajiirne. The Merchandise Marks ets (1887 and 1891) Amend- ment (Cutlery) Bill was refe,red t, a S dect Commit'ee. Mr. Holland moved that the Ra'ing of Machinory Bill hP referred to the Sanding Committee,hut ohj,ction h-ing taken the motion had to stand over. On the molon of Mr. Maden the Cotton Trade (Forty-eight Hours) Bill was deferred till June 13. ,

div.head: HAYDOCK INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE HAYDOCK INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL.
ALLEGED RISKS OFI INFECTION.

At the meeting of the St. Helens l-/ealth Commit- tee on Wednesday, Connelllor Burch!),ll rererred to the rumour that an undertaker had himself to place the corpse of a patient who had died from smallpox in the Haydnelc Hospital into the coffin and bring it out of such hospital. It l'ked ridiculous to have an isolation hospital, and yft to allow an undertaker to come into contact with a corpse of that deseription. Ho considered steps ourYht to he taken to have such bodies put into Vie coffins tic someone who was isolated in the building, and not to allow ourside persons to do that sett of werk.—Dr. Robert Jon said it was quite true that the 'undertaker did assist, and he had hem cautioned.— Alderman Gamble asked if that was the case in which the committee were asked to pay the funeral tecnenaes.—Dr. Robertsnn said that vras so. It was a St. Helens pauper case removed out of the district of the Present Guardians. hut there was an arrinaement whereby the St. Helens Corporation would be refunded any reasenable cnst by the guardians.—The Chairman said that if the Corpora- tion were eruin gto bury they should make it a decent funeral, and not try and make patients more pauper than they were.—lt was decided not to pass the account until inquiries had been made.

Apropos of the engagement of Lord Silishurv's fourth son, it is said that the Cecils are form of nicknames. Lord William, "the cler(iFm 4n son," k known to his intimates as " Fish "; the voiml-st of the fl ,clc, Lord Hugh. asi " Linicv ''; and Vie bridezroom elect, Lard Edward, as " N,ggs." The daughter; of the family, clever and charming, are not distinguished by their beauty, and someone who was a hit of awa in a merry moment, christened them "The Silishury Plains." A special conference of the Miners' Federation has been called for next Tuesday to consider the wages question in view of the demands of the Sent!bh coalosorwrs. Mr. Pickard, Mx., denies the report that he had resigned the presidency of the Federation. lie had "contemplated resignation, but had not gone further than that."

GENERAL BOOTH'S FARM COLONY.
ALLEGED UNFAIR COMPETITION.

The traders in and growersof agrieultural produce in the neighbourhond of General Booth's farm colony at tladleigh have met and framed a memorial in whieh. they appeal to the public against the alleged grievous injury they have suffered through what the describe as the unfair competition of the Salvation Army, which competition, they assert, is only rendered possible by the receipt of charitable donations intended for v, re different purposes. The memorialists quote from Gem- eral Booth's appeal for fends to show that he obtained the tine sum of £lOO,OOO by virtue of a scheme a pro- minent feature of which was the avoidance of raisin., one class at the cost of another, and ruining by under- selling those who already kept their feet with diffi,eilte. It is alleged that the General has absolutely broken faith with the public, and lan turned the farm colony into a vast trading emporium, seltna produce ~at prices which exclude all possibility of successful competition by others. Atteelied to the memorial are statements by hawkers, growers, labourers, and others, whose names and addresses are given ; from which it appears that , labourers hitherto dependent, on garden produce for rent have now no market, and traders of long standing find their business eilier entirely destroyed or greatly dam- age ,1 by unfair cutting. The -following communication has been received by the Press Association from the Governor of the Salvation Army colony :—"The memorial referred to in vour issue of yesterday has not been sent to us, and we have so far failed to obtain either a repv of it or the signa- tures attached. If the memorialiFts cansider they have any real grievance it is very strange that the matter should never have been mentioned to me. It is quite true that during the past few days hills have been ex- hibited in the neighbourhood calling 'won the residence ' to give informatioe as to the effect of the Salvation Army on the trade of the district, adding that forms may be filled up at the various Post Officers, and I have no Cinuht that as a consequence some of the persons who have made complaints have a. di,tnt idea that in some way the Post Offiee officials are collecting and formulat- ing statements against WI, thus aiving the gossip of the neighbourhood hs apoearanee of actual facts. Sofara I can judge, the memorial mak two veer& complaints First, that we enter into unfair competition by under- selling with the growers of trait and veaetatiles in the locality; and, second, that we have r'amaged the neigh- bnurlinod in some undefined way. In reply, permit me to say that, first, we de not sell, and never have sold,our products under current market prices ; second, as a general rule, especially does this apply to our fruit and ves,,,etables. We have obtained higher prices for our goods than those actually prevailing in the neiahbourheod,and a number of local hawkers have been glad to purshase those goods for 119 at prices named. Third, we are not hawkers; nearly all our busine.s is wholesale, and we do not come into competition with the hawkers in the locality. lamat a loss to understand, therefore, how we can have ruined them. The goods we send to Lon-- don are sold in the leading mark,ts by first-class sales- men at 'prices current for the day. As to the general efrct of the colony on the neiahhourhood, I can only say that the value of land for miles around has enormousls- advanced sinee our advent. There is Soarrelv in house to be hired, though building is proceeding in all direc- tions. The population has considerably increased wages are higher, and in every respect the neighbourhood has been develeped and improved ; I sympathise very mach with some of my neighbours. though I do not know that they are among the signatories of the memorial, who undoubtedly suffered, as we did, in last years terrible drought ; but surely they do not suppose that misrenre- se.nticg the Salvation Army will mend the weather ?"

div.head: COLD WEATHER.
div.p: THE COLD WEATHER.
SERIOUS DAMAGE TO CROPS.

The recent spell of cold weather, though unusual for the time of year, is not without several precedents in the past twenty or thirty years. It is hut two years since a destructive frost recurred over England even in the middle of June. In 1891 a spell of severe cold was experienced between the 18 Ii and 21st of May, with snow in many parts of the country. In 1837 a similar state of things occurred between tie 20 h and 22nd of May, the conditions being greatly aggravated on this occasion' tw a strong gale, which swept over the coun- try trom the westward and north-westward. In 1885 a c.;ld•we,k occurred between the 17th and 23rd of •the month, with a sharp ground frost over England on the night of the 18h. In May, 1877, some very low tem- peratures were observed between the 20th and alth, while in 1873 a destructive frost occurred on the 20th of the month. the exposed thermometer at Harpenden, near St. Albans. falling to a minimum of 19 degrees. Going back still further, we need only recall to mind the 22ed of May, 1867, when, for the only time on record, the Derby was run in a snowstorm. The frost of the present wef k came unfortunately at a time when vege- tation was in an unusually advanced stage, so that the damage to the crops has been greater than in some of the other cases we have quoted. In nearly every in- stance, however, mention is made of serious havoconore particularly among the young potato plants.

div.head: WARRINGTON M IC [PAL
div.p: WARRINGTON M IC [PAL
FINANCE.

As some public curiosity wrri aroused by the offer of £5,000 made last week by the gentleman desig- nated as Mr. B. our representative called upon Coun- cillor Shaw Green to ask him if the offer would be acceptahle. " Oh, certainly," said the Councillor in reply to the question, " For myself I will gladly accept the offer and do my best to get the committee to accept it as soon as we are in a position to proceed, if after reading what I have to say it is repeated. I must first ask you to let me remove erroneous impressions, that are conveyed by the twisting of my words of a previous interview, and also to combat the notion that the Council does not know its strengib and power. I told you I had the duty of submitting to the Council the resolution that we.should al( Par- liament to give us power to compel the balers of gas annuities to sell them to us, and I added that when we go again we shall have full information as to what has been done elsewhere and we shail' strive for all that ought to be got. Now Mr. B. says these words signify that we did not strive for all that could then have been got. I think when I have finished,. bAh Mr. B. and the ratepayers will , be convinced that not only did we strive but that we were eminently successful. "In our Bill, the only financial question was the Waterworks purchase. This purchase was sane- tioned and the term for the repayment of the capi- tal was cut down from what we asked to the full term of the Publie Health Act, viz. : 60 years. This Mr. B. 'states was not long enough, and if we had only gone the right way about it, and employed "proper" counsel, we should have obtained much better terms. Ido not know what acquaintance Mr. B. has with the Parliamentary Bar, hut this much I do know : our leader was a most able mem- ber of it, and that he put our case in the best pos- sible way. We got, as before stated, 60 years, with the first five years abated. Now, I have repeatealy said that we made a big fight, rind that we did well. I will now prove that statement up to the hilt. Nay, I will go further, and say that if Mr. B. had been there with the best counsel that money could pro- cure, no more could have been got. Careful search has satisfied me that since 1882 no other town has got better terra, and the great majority of the applications since that date have not done nearly so well. The bulk have only had 50 years allowed them." ,

" Why do you draw the line at 1882?" " For a very simple, hut very imp ,rtant reason, and had Mr. B. known it a good deal that has been said would never have 1),7,en uttered. Ido not regret it, however, for it is well to get erroneous . impressions put right and false ideas eradicated. Besides it has given the ratepayers the opportunity to ascertain some important facts in the financial departments, that probably could not have been learned so well in any other manner. The reason is that in 1882 a select committee of the House of Commons reported with reference to private nets similar to ours: —that "the Committee have in no ' case permitted the repayment of a loan to be ; extended beyond the period of 60 years,which is the maximum period sanctioned by the Public Health Act. . . . They recommend that means should be taken to secure in future a strict adherence to this maximum," and the same Committee reported in 1885 again, upon the same subject as follows: "that the Committee where it seemed to them prier icable have still further reduced these periods believing it to be the desire of the House that municipal improvements, even when they assume a more prominent character, should he defrayed in periods not exceeding at the utmost GO yearA,which the 17omn3ittee think might reaso.qably be reduced still further." Having had this in mind I think I have proved my assertion that in our own case with this ' disposition on the part of the Committee of the House we had to make a big fight to get what we did, viz. : the utmost the House would agree to." - "Then how do you account for Bradford getting 108 years?"

"I have ascertained the circumstances. They are too long to detail, but shortly, a private act obtained many years ago contained no proviAon for repay- ment, and when a fresh application was made. special and peculiar terms were allowed them. Stockport, I am informed had a similar act, and was also allowed very specia: terms." "has Wfirrington ever bad any better terms than 60 years ?"

_ . . "Yes, in connection with our Gas Act. We con- solidated our sewage loans, when we purchased the Gas Works and we got 50 years for the repayment of these, but for the Gas Works we were allowed 75 years. Now compare this 75 years with the recent terms sanctioned for the purchase of Gas Works. The present allowance will not average 40 years end you will see what favourable terms we have obtained. Your readers will I think now better understand my statement that • when we do go to Parliament again we shall strive for all that ought to be got, and we shall hope to be amOng those as suggested by Mr. B. whcm God helps for knowing how to help themselves." "But Mr. B. stated last week that Warrington is paying £2,132 per annum in interest more than it should. Is this so?"

" ! Emphatically no! lam sorry to have to refer to the question again, but as it is thus ren- dered necessary, I hope it will not be found tediwus. Mr. B. makes the astoundinr, statement that we are losing 7s. 61. upon each "..ClOO borrowed. He is clear enough on many other matters, but it. is not surprising to find him tripping here—only another proof that clever men, for want of a little more knowledge are oft led astray. Now what are the facts. - Mr. B. says Nottingham gets its money at 3 p-r cent.interest at a premium of 2i,or at the rate of ..E2 18s. 6d. per cent.;and that Warrington is paying £36-.11,,a diffeeence as cempared with Nottingham of 7s. 61, in favour of the latter town. The one feature about this statement is that. it, is not true. Warrington is not paying £3 6s. ld, it is only paying £3 ss, and £3 2s. 61,, and this is the in- terest that should be taken if a comparison is to be made, because as I shall tell you further the annuities cannot be brought into a comparative statement at all. "Then let. me ask : How much of its stock did Nottingham sell at £lO2 10s. so as to get at the interest it is actually paying? We cannot argue without having the precise figures, before us. Let me also show you how the want of a little information has can •ed Mr. B. to get astray. I have before referred to our water and gas annuities. The former 1 have explained are irredeemable at present and have very cmisigler- ably improved in value so muth PO that calculating the, present capital value of those still outstanding though we have paid off over 26 thousand pounds we are only say the odd six to the good. At the same time however it must be added we are saved the payment. of the annuity itself. With respect to the water annuities these are of two kinds. Annui- ties in lieu of the preference shares and annuities in lieu of the ordinary shares. The former of these cannot be compulsorily redeemed until 1921 and the latter which is by far the larger part until Ist Jarman, 1896. These dates were a part of our bar- Eain with the company when we bought and it is hardly likely that Mr. B. could have known this. The maximum price is fixed at 30 years' purchase and as we have not to begin our sinking funds un- til 1896 the ratepayers will understand why they were made compulsorily redeemable at the same date. _ _

"We have put down the capital value of these in our accqunts at the maximum redemption price and Mr. B. has jug taken this maximum price and calculated the amount of annuity and will fix upon the total and so get the .£3 64. Id. hut to argue from this that Warrington is losing .£2,132 per annum and suggesting that the Warrington ratepayers are suffering thereby is misleading more especially after what I have pre- viously said about the steps we are taking to deal with the subject:' "What are those steps ? "

"1 have repeatedly said we are going for a de- benture stock. It might be well to amplify that statement a little. We have three important finan- cial issues before us. One is to get the parliamen- tary power to compel the holders of gas annuities to sell them to its. This can only be done upon proper terms and we must be prepared to face a demand for extreme prices but and, here I speak for myself only, we shall seek to make a reasonable bargain. We want power to issue a debenture stock and thereby find the money to redeem these and the water annuities that become redeemable in 1896. Then further we want to consolidate a large number of small loans and equate them." " Won't you include your money borrowed upon bond in the debenture stock?"

" Most certainly. But as these are bcrrowed subject to six months' notice from either side there is no difficulty in coming to terms with the holders. It has taken some time to make the necessary pre- parations, for it is a most important and somewhat expensive matter going to Parliament; and the Council will endeavour to provide in its Bill for all that it may want for some time to come. In say- ing this I want you to understand that we have been getting ready for a long time, and we are fully alive to our duty and responsibility. It will also take some time to get it through Parliament, and as we cannot hope to do so before the middle of 1895, you will understand we shall all have to exercise some patience. Then when all is ready to issue the stock, the holders of the annuities and many of the bond holders will in my opinion be glad to take it in exchange. "I have now given you my reason for stating that we are not asleep nor dreaming, but that we are all thoroughly awake to, and aware of all that we ought to do, and I think I shall satisfy all thinking people that we are grappling first with our finances, and having put them on a satisfactory footing, there will be full opportunity to deal with other matters. These other matters are not being left alone. The Corporation is com- posed of committees, each seeing to its own depart- ment, and the Street Improvement Committee is fully sensible of all that is expected from it,.. and those who do not know the activity of its members will probably accept my statement that their plans are ready and negotiations are constantly going on for the improvement of our thoroughfares. "I admit Warrington is old-fashioned, but re- membering it as I do from a boy,l venture to assert without fear of contradiction, that with the constant expense of keeping pace with its rapid growth, the improvements that have taken place are achievements of which we may be proud, for , they have been done without in any way imperill- ing its financial condition. " We cannot compete with a new-world town, laid out as some are, but we have greatH advantages which we are seeking to maintain and improve, and above all we are a warm-hearted people, ever ready to welcome and cordially accept new corners, and it is our boast that, I, those who do so in course of time become so thoroughly satisfied with us and so consciously part and parcel of us that they are tempted to forget they ever knew another place. To encourage them in this feeling to make it. worth while bringing new capital and new busi- ness to the town should be the object of all those who seek to direct its destinies and pre.erve and improve its splendid opportunities, and t think I have shown you that this aka is paramount in the minds of the present members of the Corpora- tion.

div.p: Mr. Byrne, of Mersey-btreet, has lately returned from a sojourn of nearly twelve mouths, in South Africa. Mr. Byrne previous to his visit to the dark continent," was connected with the Prudential Assurance Company, in Warrington, and waS ordered to take the voyage for the benefit of his health.

"Durban is the place where I made my stay chiefly," said Mr. Byrne in speaking to one of our representatives about his travels, "and a very beautiful place it is. The harbour in• which the port stands is protected from the sea board by a very iemarkabie bar, and a breakwater. I suppose it is one of the moat difficult bars in the world to cross. • Even in calm weather the wa% es break over it as though a gale were blowing and the danger to vessels crossing it is extremely great. No really large ships can cross it, and the smaller ones, chiefly coasters. are compelled to carry a pilot, either coaling in or going out, or risk a penaity of .£20." "What did you think of the town and the climate ?"

"The climate is simply delightful. Although very hot, the beat is not oppressive. The atmos- phere is bright and dry; tutu invigorating, and it seemed to we that a man could not remain long in low spirits if he wished to. Tile town itself is very healthy, and has a beautiful situation. Vegetation of a tropical kind grows in abundance. . Apart from its natural beauties I cannot say much else for it." " IS business not brig'it there for immigrants?'

" Not now. ,Situations no doubt are wThith hav- ing when the can be got ; but they are very difficult to obtain. Au Englishman cannot linu .emp.uvment unless he is a 8 killed artizain or unless he is engaged to take a position of trust. Al! un- skilled labouring is dune chiefly by the coolies ; they are the porters and pointsmen on the railways; drive the cars, brush the streets, and all that-sort oi ltis coloured labour that is beginning to ruin the place in ,fact. Shiploads of coolies are brought over by Government who undertake to find them work for live years,at the lapse t:if which period they are tree to get what employment they like. Natal is consequently over-run with these people, very considerably to the detriment of the settlers. Their labour is very cheap. I think Goiernment pay them about 4d. a day, and feed them; but as they live almost entirely on meal this does not cost much.. When employed by civilian they receive about LI per month." "And how is white labour remunented

" Well, skilled labourers receive about ..el4 per month, but it costs 255. j.ar week to live out of that. Shop assistants get about the same wage, and they are in every way much better off than their fellows in England. During the year they get '23 .day holidays, as well as the weekly half- holiday and Sunday, and they suspend business at five in the evening. They get a fortnight's holiday every year, too, and after being with an employer about five years they receive perhaps three months holiday WhiCil enables them to come home." "is the difference in caste recognized much ?" "Oh yes ! Coloured people are compelled to retire by a 'curfew at nine o'clock at night. It they are caught out after that hour they are marched off to jail by the police. Even if you send a coloured servant on an errand after that hour at night he will be " run in" unless he holds a per- tint from his master. If a coloured servant runs away from his employment and is captured he frequently receives a fortnight's or a mouth's im- prisonment with hard labour, and is then compelled to return to his master. They are not allowed to touch intoxicating liquors, and it .is a criminal offence for a civiliar to give them liquor or for a publican to sell it to them. There is one class of coloured people who are allowed out alter nine. These are the"boys"—all coloured men are called boys —who draw vehicles called rickshas. They are very light vehiclas between a juveniles "mail cart," and a gig I should say, and they take the place of traps and buggies. The "boys" win) draw them wid run at a spanking trot for three miles at a spin. They are specially licensed and are on duty until 12 o'clock, but are ciim!Jel led to wear a badge." "And how do the white people manage for even- ing entertainment?" "That's one of the most distressing features of the town. The only public place of amusement is a theatre which is open three months in the year,and genurally " run" by a third rate Variety Company . whose lowest figure of admission is 28. Apart from this there is no other attraction. People have to either remain at home during theevenings, or go to a canteen or saloon. It is either drunkenness or temperance, and if a man takes to the form,u- it soon brings him down. In the first place the clim- ate is not the one to allow a man to go to excesses, and in the second place the price ot the beer and liquors spells ruin as a rub.% You cannot obtain a bottle of stoat under a shilling." " And how does the law deal with defaulters?"

e' Very harshly indeed. If a man looks crooked he is likely to be run in. If lid is inebriated he is kept in ougtody for the night and released tie next morning upon a payment of 10s. to the officer in charge. If the charge is more serious he is brought It fore a magistrate. In cases were fines cannot be paid the culprits are sentenced to a term of impri- sonment and are sent to work on the breakwater. Here they are under public scrutiny,and are attired in convict garb, which makes the punishment ver3 hard.to woitemen. Coloured prisoners are kept separate from the white prisoners, and so here caste is recognised again. The prisoners are guarded by coloured policemen, who are under the control of white policemen.° • "And what sort. of a place is Durban for a man who is " down on his luck as the saying goes ?"- " Simply woeful! A man can easily starve to cleat h there, There are no workhouses or charity institutions. Food you cannot get without begging unless vou sell your belongings at shamefully low prices. For shelter you have either to sleep in the open or in a prison cell, where you will 1).3 turned out the next morning with an empty stomach. A man down on his luck does not in much sym- pathy—less even than he does n England. It he leaves the town and commences to beg, the farmers will not even look at him, unless he is on horseback and then, strange to say they will invariably take him in and provide food and shelter for him."

div.p: WARRINGTON RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Rugby Football Cillb Wa6 held in the Workingmen's Club in the Alarlitt Place, last Thursday evening. There was a very large attendance of members, and the chair was occupied by the prosident, Mr. P. Davies. SECRZTARY'S REPORT.

After a few preliminary remarks by the Chairman, the Secretary's report, which appeared in our last issue, was adopted on the motion of Mr. Tinnion, seconded by Mr. Hayes. ' TREASURER'S REPORT. __ _ _

The adoption of the treasurer's report, which also ap- peared in our last issue, was proposed by Mr. Jeffery, seconded by Mr. Jolley.—Mr. Tiunion said that he would like to say something about the treasurer's report. He did not think that. they could call the balance a satisfac- tory balance at all. There were many items which they could not blame their treasurer for, as ha had simply to follow the guidance of the committea. But there were a great many items which looked formidable compared with last year. The balance this year was an adverse one. He wished to cal; attention to the extraordinary expenditure,-and to see if something could not be done in future to curtail that expense. Among the items of ex- penditure, he noticed that refreshment to players, &e., was £124 more than last year. £124 almost accounted for the whole of the adverse balance. If they • did not impress upon t4.e committee which was to be elected for ! matt year, that they should seriously take into considers- ! tion the responsibility of cutting down the expenditure, with a few years like the past, they would soon be in the Bankruptcy Court, In his opinion, Warrington Rugby football was rather past its hey-day, and required care- ful marh“ement on the part of the committee and officers to keep its head above water. He thought they ought to try to get a better balance next year than they had for the past.—The Chairman thought that it was a seri- ous matter th-it they were £l2O worse off than they were last year, when the balance was £1.44, and now only £23. There had been a great deal 'spent in railway fares, and there was also an item for the relief fund of nearly £5O. They had had several extraordinary items during the past year which they probably would not have dur- ing the coming year. They ought to be careful with the expenditure ho a ever, in the interests of the Rugby game. G. Smith thought Mr. Tinniou was justified in call- ing the attention of the meeting to the matter. There was need tor careful management indeed. (Haar, hear.) They must not disguise the fact that they had had during the pa.st yaar, the best year with regard to " gate !' money. During the coming year, he was sorry to say that he thought the expenditure in painting, repairs,&e.. would not be decreased, but that it would be iacreased. Every penny which had been spent on the graund had been absolutely necessary. Among the expenditure IIf; noticed that there was LNG spent in railway fares,whice was a very high one. With united action, he thought that item could be reduced. He was considerably as- tonished at the increased number of players taken away, more than was absolutely necessary. He could uncle,- stand a player going, but he could not understand a reserve man being determined to go. Then the hotel ! expenses was a very large item indeed. Rethought that this could be lessened considerably. He was howevei sure that next year they would have a better balance to show than their present balance sheet showed.—The treasurer's'repart was then put to the meeting and adapted unanimously. ! IS A SECOND TEAM NECESSARY 2

After the adoption of the secretary and treasurer's reports, a number ot special resolutions were con- sidered. The first resolution was proposed by Mr. .J. Evans, who moved that the second team be disbanded. He said there were several reasons against running the second team, which was practically the third team. When the third team was started, almost all the high class clubs in the county ran third teams, and there was then no difficulty in arranging matches. Now however, there was not a single club which had persevered in the- attempt to ran a third team. It was therefore with ver., great ditliculty that they arranged matches,and obtained players to t,ke part in the matches. Some tilne ageethe sub-committee which managed the second team came te•' the general committee, sod confessed that it was int- pefsible to go on any further if they called the team the third team, and they accordingly obtained the cor-e sent of the committee to change its rtl me to the War- ringtoii Excelsior, thus practically sailing under false coleurs. If they referred to the fixttire card they would • see that there were 27 matches to be played. In the , secretary's repert they would tied that only 17 matches . were played-- a drop of ten clubs. Out of the 17 matches, ten were played away. The cost of the team Or rail- way fares, teas and refreshments had been £4l 185.101., and added to that was the insurauce of £1.6 10s. which made a total of £5B at. iod, With other extras fie was sure that the team would cost somewhere near £7O. He was therefore sure that it • would be bast to drop the team. ' They, reaped no benefit either financially or in the way of producing players. In the old days, some good men were found in the team,but the tendency seemed to tie to recruit the team from junior clubs. If the expense. of the third team was spared the Warrington F.C. some- thing more might be done to assist the junior clubs.— Mr. Dinwiddie seconded the resolution. It seemed to Min that it, was not right that seven matches should cost £7O, for that was what it amounted to, for only seven matches were played at home. Beyond that,if they could not get decent clubs to play the team it made the chili useless as far as they were concerned.—Mr. J Smith op- posed the motiod. He thought • that Mr. Evans had entirely misrepresented the senond team. He wanted to know what the " A" team would have done at times if there had been no second team. They had sometimes taken as many as six, seven, and eight of the second team players to meet such clubs as St. Helens Rees, Lan- caster, and the like, and yet hat won cernforta,bly. As for the fixtures they otitained,lte wanted to know whether Pendleton Trinity and Droylesden Hornets were not re- spectable clubs. If they trusted to the junior clubs for players, they would have great difficulty in obtaining them. He therefore, thought that the secoed tetni should still be run,a nd he wohld oppose the motion.—Mr. Critchley supported :lie motion, an thought that the team was not worth the expense incurred.—Mr. J. E. Warren said that he could understand Mr. Smith in his support a the second team. No one had worked harder for it tban he had done. But he would remind Mr. Smith that some of the matches played with the second team had bean obtained by misrepresentation. Droy- lestlen Hornets fully understood that they were playint, the "A" team. Be believed that if the players of the second team were distributed among the junior clubs of the town,there would be a far better recruiting ground than there at present existed.—Mr. F. Wallington would be sorry to see the second team dis6anded. The second team would provide a far greater reserve than haying to look among the clubs throughout the town. He thoueht it an honour to belong to the Warrington F.C., and he thought the players would consider it so too. The tak- ing away of players from junior clubs tendered to break up those clubs, and they might to assure a player of a• chance of permanently playing when he joined the club. —The Chairman said that lie thought they ought to listen to the trustees of the club when they were in favour of lessening the expenditure. Mr. Evans was a • trnstee, and Mr. G. Smith bad also warned them of the increased expenditure. Ile therefore thought that when a team cost £7O for only seven home matches,they ought, to save that expense.—After some further discussion ,the motion was put to the meeting, but was defeated by a large majority.
DISGRACEFUL ATTACK ON WARRING- TON CYCLISTS.

A very disoweful affair occurred on the Chester Road, near Fro isham, on Whit-Nlonday evening. A number of •%Varringt on cyclists had been on a visit to North Wales and were returning during the even- ing. A batch of three, :Messrs. Fair, Buxton, and Mountield, were leading by a considerable distance, and when they arrived near Frodshatn they en- countered what can most appropriately be described as a "gang "of strange cyclists, who, without provocation commenced to obstruct the Warringtonians. The'latter bore this treatnymt as long as they could, but in the end One of them -expressed his annoyance in terms that might not have been scrupulously politl,but-which were decidedly justifiable. At this, the strangers dismounted and without further ado set about pulling the three wheelmen from their machine?. As might be expected from athle.ic young twM, the three Warringtoniatis re- sente-I this rough treatment by endeavouring to give as much as they received. The attacking party was, how- ever, more than a dozen strong, and consequently the Warringtonians were overpowered. Mr. Buxton seems to have come in for the roughest handling. He was knocked to the ground by tour of the ruffians,' who kicked his prostrate hody until he was bruised in a pain- ful mariner, and it is possible he would have beeei more seriously iiijured had not Mr. Mounfield at a timely moment dragged him to his feet. Mr. Fair, whaliap- pened to have in his possession a policeman's whistle, blew a shrill alarm, whereupon their assailants mounted their machines and rode on in the direction of Chester. Mr. Buxton was conveyed to a neighbouring 'cottage where his injuries were attended. But in the meantime, the ruffians who had made the assault had met another hatch of the Warrington party, three or four in numher. These they also made an attempt to maltreat. They di, mounted from their in:tchi nes upon seeing t h small party appioach and commenced to throw large stones and brick ends at the Warrineonians. Na one, however, was struck with these missiles except Mr. B. Newcomb, of Penketh. who was one of the party. Be was struck on the head with half a briek, a painful bruise being in- flieted. The police at Frodshaan were afterwards in- formed of the affair, and at once commenced to make inquiries as to the assailants.
THE EXAMINEE, SKI URDAY MAY 26, 1894.

div.head: REDUCTION OE ENTRANCE PEES.
div.p: REDUCTION OE ENTRANCE PEES.

Mr. William H3yes moved a resolution that the entrance fee to the clvtb be reduced from 53. to 2s. 61 He said that h was sure that this change would caus;" a large increase of the club membership,as the membership had decreased since the entrance fee had been increased a few years ago. They ought to have a much larger inerr- bership than 400.—Mr. T. Barnes seconded the motion. —After a lengthy discussion in which Messrs. Pember- ton, G. Smith, Davies. Critchley,and Tin nion took part, the motion was carried by a large mljority.

div.head: ALTEUATION IN THE RULES.
div.p: ALTEUATION IN THE RULES.

Mr. Fairfield Turner moved and Mr. Evans seconded that the Secretary acquaint the members of the club of the ddte of the annual meeting seventeen days before hand, in order to give the members sufficient warning to give notice el any special notice they may wish to bring forward. The motiou was carried unanimously. Mr. S. Wright, J.P., proposed that rule 4 be altered to read that the acting officers should consist of the presi- dent, hon. secretary. hon. treasurer, captain of the first, and captain of the " A " teams, and that the cc.mmitee consist of the above mentioned officers,and ten members of the club, none of whom most be players.—Mr. Critchley seconded the motion.—Aftur a long discussion, in which some z)f the playing members 'strongly opposed the motinn,on the suggestion of Mr. H. Ashton, the resolution was altered to the effect that the commit- tee should consist of the president, hon. secretary, hon. treasurer. captains of the first and " A" teams, the touch judges of the first and "A " teams. an eight non- playing members. The resolution was then unaatimously carried.

div.head: ELECTION OF CAPTAINS, ETC.
div.p: ELECTION OF CAPTAINS, ETC.

The election of officers was then proceeded with. Mr. Percy Davies was unanimously re-elected president, Mr. J. E. Warren, hon. secretary, and T. Pemberton, hon. treasurer, Mr. Fairfield Turner was elected captain of the first team, and Mr. J. Jolley sub-captain. N Mr. NV. Handles was elected-captain, and Mr. J. Lawless, jun., sub-captain of the "A " team. Mr. D. Galion was imaiiimously elected captain of the second teain. Mr. P. Barnes, jun., was appointed Ouch judge of the first team, Mr. J. Boyle of the " A " team, and Mr. T. Smith of the second team. Mr. Davies said that the election of the committee could not he prnceeded with that night in consequence of thepassing of Mr. S. Wright's motion, and the nra•,ting was accordingly adjourned for a fort• night for that litirp ..se, the meeting to he held in the Not ton Arms. Ttit, meeting closed with the usual i'otes of thanks.

div.head: DEATH OF TM?, SCOITISU STRAWVA HILTS.
div.p: DEATH OF TM?, SCOITISU STRAW- VA HILTS.

"HE COULD MAKE ANYTHING Bur MONEY." Mr. James Gilchrist, a famour Giaswegian, is dead, at rtitheerte.,siltli,n„finignevianrotilre,ilt.r the age of sixty-two. taakne natik e of Retliesay, and res al sr 4. Go 1 cEtli reirsAti d was a - began his career in Glasgow as an exceptionally promis- ing worker in metal.,?, the hardest of which were to a grt at exten.t. plastic in his hands. He was a skilled worker in woods as well as metals, and constructed the most exquisite models, many of them designed by Him- self. Be made all kinds of philosophical instruments. He taught mechanics in Allan Gl,u's school, an.i wrote excellent prose and poetry. He construeted on novel ! lines a locomotive engine and circular railway for a High land estate, which was higaly successful. He built small ' Screw and paddle steamers, one of which he sailed in Rothesay Bay. He fitted with gis and electric light some of tin' largest bails, saloons, and theatres, and sup• plied them with improved entrance lamps of his own design. He contrived and patented an ingenious ar- rangement for ship lamp hales, by which paraffin wax was kept in solution by the light acting on. an arched band of copper which communicated with the wax-.-s beautiful example of action and reaction. Mr. i;ilitlirst was an independent worker with high ideals,but like other men of his class, he was blind to self-interest. He had none of the instincts of business, and monetary matters with him were always cif ecc,miary importance. His wife, with kindly discrimination and pardonable pride, truly said of him, " Ile can make anything but money." This one sentence accurately describes the man, What- ever his head conceived his hands could execute. Gfteti as Mr. Gilchrist unque.stionably was as a mechanician of the first order, it was as a violin-milter that he achieved his latest triumphs. Be took to violin-making in 1880, comparatively late in life, but he acquired a position at once, and rapidly eclipsed his compeers in this seductive and, to him, new branch of art. He made in all eighty-six very high-class instruments (violins, violas, -violen-cellos, and celletos). Violin- making became latterly the passion of his life. He worked at his fine instruments with a child-like enders- ism, and no hand but his ()own was permitted to touch them. His timber was algrays very carefully selected, vets' mature, and of the finest quality. He did not' skimp his instrements of material, ta get false brilliancy in tone. Be fashionel all their parts with wonderfel skill, and lingered, so to spsak, over his work after the manner of the old masters. In this way he very worthily earned for himself tie title al the Scottish Reich- varins. He cut his own scrolls, bushed, alter a neW method, his own peg holes, and graduated the varying thicknesses of hacks and bellies with scrupu- lous exactitude and mathematical accuracy from. elaborate calculations and- design s woiked out by I ;insel He employed as many as fifty diagrams to insure a just and perfect gra.iluatiori of the sound board, particu!arly in relation to the sound post,bass-bar, and bridge. Not content with ordinary metlinds, he Vlevised ',eve e.lamps, moulds. and tools to secere every combination a curve. He aimed at eraert and strength. His ii4struments are full-sized, and combine in a remarkable degree beanty of outline with a certain degree it selidarity implying great durability. His IP holes, purfling, and varnish ate perfect. His model is flattish,and instills respect resew-. bles that of the famous Stradi varies. He, however. followed no master, and worked on original lines as far as this was possible. •

ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS. INQUIRER (Earlestown).—We cannot say by whose " permission" or upon what authority the tolls you re- fer to were collected on the occasion of the May Queen festival. If you think there is any encroachment upon public rights It would, we should say, be best to brim:, the matter under the notice of the -Commissioners who are the elected representatives .1 the ratepayers.

THE RECTOR AND THE DRINK TRIFFIC. Sir,—Having read the Rector's letter with much sur- prise and grief, I feel how very differently we can study the same hook, for to me the Bible seems just full of warnings against drunkenness. Let us just think of a few of them. " Wine is a mocker, strong drink is rag- ing: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise:" Prov. 20.1. "Who hath woe? Who filth sorrow? Who hath contentions? Who hath babbling? Who hath wounds wit'sout cause? Who bath redness of the eyes? They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine. Look not upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth it- self aright. At the last it biterh like a serpent, and sting,eth like an adder." Prov. 23, 29 to 32 v. "Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink." Isaiah 5: 22. "It is not for kings, 0 Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink: Last they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted." Prov. 31 :4, 5. If it is important for kings to abstain how much more so for judges and magistrates? We see from these passages the evils of wine drinking clearly pointed out and if they were the unfermented wines similar to that presented by the butler to Pharaoh, how much moredo they apply to the unfermented wines, the ales and the spirits of the present day. But we also find in the Bible that those who were seek- ing to lead a higher and nobler life or who were devoted to His service were either forbidden the use of wine or gave it up:themselven, as in the case of the Levites while engaged in the tabernacle (Lev. 10 :9) ; in that of the ifazaritea during their separation (tium.6 : 3) ; in that of the Rechabites who were accorded a special token of God's approval (Jer. 35 : 5 to end) ; and above all in the case of Daniel the prince, the statesman, the scholar and higher still, the Christian, "the man greatly beloved" (Dan. 1:3 to end). We find also in later times that the scrop!es ot Timothy were so great, that St. Paul had to exhort him to take a little wine as a medicine (would that all doctors recommended it in like quantities). Then, seeing that the best and noblest of ages have ranged themselves on the side of abstinence, surely the Church should follow their example,a.nd seek to lead the way to a higher, nobler, state of things than we find at present, when around us we see so many human wreck in consequence of this evil, surely it is time for Chris- tians not "to drink wine, nor anything whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak " (Rom. 14. : 21).—Yours truly, S. G.
Warrington, May 15th, 1894.

Sir,—ln your issue of the 12th inst. the Rector very graciously condescends, for the benefit "of those who have not studied Holy Scripture and are desirous to judge impartially," to give his views on the subject of Moderation v. Total Abstinence. Those who have endeavoured to interpret the some- what mixed statsments of the Rector, will, I am sure, be somewhat puzzled to find out what this question of Moderation v. Total Abstinence, has to do with the original statement, made by the Rector, viz. : "The drink traffic is not wrong." But it is invariably the practice with those who, having made a reckless state- ment regarding any subject, and finding themselves cornered, to jump off into another path, and start another hare. But I trust that those who are on our side, will not allow the rev, gentleman to drift away from his subject. It would be a difficult matter to fin-ri a more sweeping denunciation of the Rector's statement, viz., that" the drink traffic is not wrong," than is sup- plied by his own words. In his letter referred to above, occur the following words :—" The brewer who presses his liquor on the publican, and the publican who presses his liquor on his customer simply for the sake of money, when he knows that it is not required for necessary or innocent consumption and that shocking harm, misery, and crime are the results, is incurring a terrible respon- sibility and committing a frightful sin for which he will have to answer, if not now, at the last" (day I suppose he means). The Rector then goes on to say, he will do all in his power to aid legislative action, and further every ameliorating influence to lessen the scourge. Good! The Rector will I am sure pardon me for saying it, but, it needs be said, he should be most grateful to you, and " his critics," for giving him the opportunity of (in part) setting himself right before the public. No one I am sure would dream of charging the Rector with want of courtesy, and no doubt there most be some mis- take in the Rector's letter of the 12,h where snubs his critics, or appears to do so, by his refusal to enter into a discussion on his unfortunate panegyric on our brewing magnates. But whether ths. Rector chose to notice, in "his high and mightiness," as our friend "Spoofah Bey" would say, to notice us poor insignificant scribblers, he will, I trust, be attended to all the same. Then, let me say, that the subject deals not with the question of drink, but with the drink traffic, that is to say, the system now is vogue and countenanced by the law of the land of buying and selling intoxicating liquors. Ilse subject takes for granted that certain " evils of the Drink Traffic" do exist. These evils have been sum- marized as follows in the report on Intemperance laid before the Belgian Chamber of Representatives by M. Frese Orban, the Minister of Instruction in 1868: "Nine- tenths of the paupers ; three fourths of the criminals ; one half of the diseases ; one third of the insanity; three fourths of the depravity of children and young people ; one third of the shipwrecks." These are the results of the drink traffic of England, as given in the report. They proceed from a careful investigation by a respon- sible and impartial body of educated men, and the summary may be taken as at least fairly accurate. Let us take the Drink Bill, i.e., the amount of money spent in intoxicating liquors in the United Kingdom for the year 1890. It amounts to £139,495.470. exceeding that of the previous year by about £7.250,000. Close on 140 millions spent on intoxicating drink! averaging an expenditure of £3 13s. per head! Bat enough of this. The Rector himself says: "That the publican and brewer who make this drink traffic a matter of money," are condemned, and I should like to know the brewer or the publican who does not make it a matter of profit. Are not the public-houses made as bright, as cheerful, and enticing as possible, and if it were not for the fear of the law, what publican would refuse money no matter how drunk the offerer. Do not the brewers and publicans know full well that our people are poor and wretched because of their indulgence in drink? Does not the Rector know full well, that the young man, who falls away from t'se prac- tice of holy religion do so through drink ? Does he not know that many of our poor sisters are outcasts,because of drink ? Are your churches empty? tis the drink ; are your charities crippled for resources ? 'tis because of the drink ; are the sunny days of childhood made dark and cheerless ?' tis because of the drink. Then why in the name of common justice, do such men as the Rector, and the Rev. Dr.Binns, sing the praises of drink ? God knows it is a hard struggle for those who have the cour- age to deny thersselves for Christ's sake, to push on this temperance movement, Aye hard indeed it is! and hew sad to think, that, we should receive discouragement from those who should be our best friends, and strong- est supporters, in this movement for the regeneration of our people. Personally I owe every thins, (next to God) to the temperance party. Through the instrumentality of the Order of Good Templars I am what I am. May God bless the Good Teinplars and such associations. How many souls how many homes have been saved by such societies, as the Band of Hope, the Young Crusade, and all temperance organisations? God only knows. Then take courage ye temperance workers, rally round our banner, tis the banner of Christ, and in spite of all apposition let our cry be ever," In hoc Signo Vinces".— Yours truly, • J. C. DALTON Warrington, Whit Sunday.

. Sir,—The Rector has given us a long letter in justifica- tion of his attitude towards the drink traffic. It would appear that because certain passages in the Bible seem to support his contentions, that then the drink traffic -'receives divine sanction and approval. Now, I have no intention to handy words with him as to the meaning of certain texts of Scripture. Perscnally, I am not con- cerned about them,and leave them for your other corres- pondents to deal with. Believing,as I do,that reason and -experience and commonsense are greater authorities -than any book, I prefer to be guided by them rather than by inspired or not. But the Rector believes in the Bible and he believes in the example of "Christ. Well, we are told in Hebrew vi. 18, that "it is ; impossible tor Goa to lie," and again in Proverbs xii. 22 that " lying lips are an abomination to the Lord" ; but in 2 Chron. xviii. 19, we are told, " Behold,qhe Lord .hath pw a lying spirit in the ineuth of these thy pro- phets." Does the lit'ctor believe this? We have other passages in the Bible equally as contradictory on the question of drink—as quoted by your correspondents. And the Rectar quotes approvingly certain so-called Biblical authorities who say that Christ by a miracle converted an enormous quantity of water into wine— about 135 gallons—on the occasion of a marriage feast. - wonder it the Rector think; this was a ccmmendable • thing to do—an example worth copying? Now, in all -soberness and sineerity I wish to ask the Rectorwhether he wuuld follow this example in the case of a marriage Lin his own family? Would it be a right and proper • thing to do? I am afraid he would be scandalized at the. bare suggestion of such a thing. I fail to see how he could reconcile it with his own ideas ni moderation. Fancy the Rector's smn being. 'Daniel and 135 gallons of ferrnnted wino being provided ! IVhy, he would have • al the town drunk pretty neir. So winch f.r the Rector's I.iiblical authorit,..—sur)posing, his interpretation of the 'Bible is to he r bt.ti ,pen, which I wiestion. lint the Recnar eor,-ion t ) 'ay that " there is another side (to thk qaest ion), and I am not going to spare any. "fne brewer mile Pescea his llqiier on the publican, and %Abe publiebn •A'hil presses his liquor on his customer,

simply for the sake of money, when ho knows that it is sot required for necessary or innocent consumption, and that shocking harm, misery and crime are the results, is incurring a terrible responsibility, and committing a frightful sin, for which he will have to answer if not now, at the last. Ido not hesitate to say that the traffic is shamefully mismanaged, and that the law should step in and stop the awful abuse." These are brave words. Does the Rector know that brewers do press their liquors on the publicans? Does he know that they buy up, wherever they can, all houses possessing a license? With what obj ct ? Of compelling the tenants to buy their— the brewers' liquor. For what? For money—for the purpose of making money. And is he aware that directly they become possessed of a house they at once raise the price of beer ? That is to say, supposing that previous to their buying a house,the house has been what is known as a free house, and the publican has bePn free to buy his beer where he liked, they at once compel him to buy his beer from them, and charge him mOre than he paid before, even though he had previously bought from them. I believe it is a fact that the Rector himself can buy one or two barrels of beer direct from the brewers for lea; money than the publicans themselves— who are the brewers' tenants. And yet the Rector is not ashamed to receive gifts from the brewers for God's ser- vice. If the Rector wants to satisfy himself as to whether publicans press their liquor on their customers I would respectfully suggest to him that he should make a visit to the public houses—incognito—any Saturday night that would be convenient to him. lam afraid if he did so he would be too much upset to conduct religious services the following day. Only the other day I saw a number of the lowest and vilest women in the town dancing at the door and under the window of a public house to the strains of a barrel organ, running in from time to time to" liquar up." Would any respect- able draper or butcher tolerate such conduct at the door of his premises? Two or three days aft n.wards two drunken men were Pjected from the same house, and commenced fighting at the door in a most:l:antsl manner, hundreds of people blocking up the thoroughfare ta see the fun. The Rector says most truly that the traffic is shamefully mismanaged, resulting in ;hocking harm, and misely and crime, and those responsible for it commit a frightful sin—and yet he is publicly and gratefully thankful to receive gifts from them for God's house and service.

I am in entire sympathy with the Rector's "remedies," but will he support candidates who will carry them to practical conclusions ? Will he attond the next Brewster Sessions to urge a reduction of licenses, thus giving us a tangible evidence of his sincerity ? If he does he will render a great public service and win the respect of all who hove the well-being of the town at heart, but I am afraid he will no longer have occasion to rendor tnanks, publicly and gratefully or otherwise to the brewers for any help he will receive from them. Poor Mr. Carleton. I really thought he would have had a word or two to say about that £1,500 for St. Luke's, after his very vehement denials. But what he could say I am puzzled to know.—Yours truly..
JOHN bANDY.

div.head: SOCIALISM.
div.p: SOCIALISM.

Sir,—Mr. Flawcroft has had his last word and I will give mine as briefly as:l can. The Paraguay failure has no disturbing effect upon me I can assure you. The more we have of these attempts,the greater the manifestation, I take it, of what we are reaching forward to. The advice of Mr. Jo!en Peers that socialists should seek out some unsettled country, a mere wilderness I suppose, and leave the individualist at rest, is by no means new and while ! these experimental efforts will doubtless continue to be mada, the real work will be going on slowly but surely at home: Socialism will Ise grafted on, is being' grafted " on to the present system, however much Mr. T.Y.H. and Mr. John Peers may dislike it. It will be evolved out of the present conditions, as the capitalist system has taken the place of feudalism and slivery. These fell under after they had served their purpose, and so will capitalism and perhaps socialism which is to folloOktvhen they have served theirs. In the words of Tennyson. "let the great world go spinning down the ringing groves of change." Does Mr. John Peers think that his string of adjectives is going to arrest the progress of social development, or Mr. Howcroft believe that even his remarkable potato stories will pro duce any great effect? My paint about the railway companies has been totally misapprehended. It was merely an incidental reference to show the progress of combinationloya word which I used intny letter ot March 3, and to illustrate the untenableness of Mr. Howcreft's contention that business was best done by a single pro- prietor. Mr. H. makes another reference to the man of the middle ages, but I think I will let the poor fellow rest. As a matter of fact he is really of very little con- sequence in this discussion. Mr. Howcroft is exercised to know how a man may prove his genius under Socialism. I answer in the same way that he proves it now, only with the additional advantage that is to be derived from improved facilities in the way of education szc. Edison proved his genuis while he was poor. Nobody found him any money til he had proved his genius. How did Palis:y the potter,l evince his genius? Who found him, a poor work- ing man the money to carry on his experiments? Be found it himself, and burnt up every piece of furniture in the house to carry out his object. And by the way was it mere love of money that formed the motive of his determination? But that in passing. As I said in a ' former letter on the authority of Arthur Helps, the pre- ponderatory num!..er of inventions have come from the humble classes; as poor men they evinced the possession of great gifts and that genius was recognised while they were poor. Whether they reaped the fruits of their tga nius that, of course, is another story. Very well, then, what would prevent there cognitionolgenius under Socialism? Scholarships are provided now for talented young people Under Socialism we should be alive to the advantages to be derived from an extension of this system, and budding genius would thus find increased opportunity for expansion. Again what would prevent experiments being carried on by this state, as such experiments are in some countries carried on now, in agriculture ? I was amused at Mr. Howcroft's:extraordinary description of what a person would be compelled to do and be prevent- ed from doing, under Socialism. No man would be pre- vented from leaving his country and travelling, if he had an inclination that way. I wonder how many workers are able to accomplish that now. I shouldn't mind doing a'bit of travelling myself, but I rather fancy the Gov- ernment wonld object to stand "exes." Well, if under Socialism a man wanted to roam a bit at his own cost who would say him nay. There would,. under Socialism, says Mr. Howcroft, be a rush for the soft jobs. There would be nothing very remarkable in that. There is a rush for the soft jobs now, but perhaps under Socialism there wouldn't be any soft jobs to rush to, if by that description he means useless jobs with good salaries attached. " A man would not have the right nor the liberty to follow the bent of his inclination." He would have the same right and greater liberty than he 1.-,as now. A man must either work or starve now. The same thing would exist under Socialism, with this difference that whereas now h gets only one-third of his earnings under Socialism he would get all. As to following one's bent, if more boys wanted to be carpen- ters than the State could keep, some of them would have to follow some other occupation. Perhaps they would all want to be gentlemen, as they probably do now, and if they found they could not be this, whEre would he the hardship. Mr. Howcroft's letter does not leave me with the feel- ing that he possesses a thorough knowledge of the sub- ject. The essential difference between the present system and Socialism is this : While under the formes great in- dustries are managed by organizers of labour for the benefit of men who have practically a " soft job" of it, under Socialism these industries would be managed for the benefit of the community by the same class of or- ganizers. Thus the profit which now goes to make the fortunes of the,"soft jeb"men, would go into the pockets of the workers.

In my last letter I was unfortunate enough to indulge in a Biblical reference, referring by way ot illnstration to the walls of Jericho falling before the noise of Joshua's army. Mr. Peers " spotted " this reference instanter. Be went at it as a bull would at a red rag. and he was pleased, sarcastically, to find one who believed that the walls of Jericho did fall. If I had to quote Wordsworth, and say that I had seen "ten thou- sands of daffodils dancing in the sun."or quoting another Biblical character, declare that " the hills clapped their hands with joy," I have not the least doubt Mr. Peers would be prepared to deny that I had seen anything of the kind, or that the hills did anything so frivoloua. Yours, &c., COMMON JUSTICE.

div.head: STOCKMN HEATH.
div.p: STOCKMN HEATH.

DEATH OF MRS. WEIR, OF WALTON.-MrS. Mary Weir, wife of Mr. John Weir, of Baronet Farm, Lower Walton, died alter a brief illness on Monday morning at her residence. The deceased lady was in her 71st year, and was well known and respected in the naighbour- hood. She attended divine service at St. John's Church. Walton, on Sunday morning, and was apparently in the best of health until the evening of that day when,whilst in the act of performing her household duties, she was suddenly seized with an apopletic fit. Dr. H. Smith, of Warrington, and Dr. Willett, of Stockton Heath, were called in, but their assistance was of no avail, tiw de- ceased lady succumbing to the sudden attack as above stated. The funeral took place on Wednesday.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

MAERIB.4II.—On Wednesday morning a marriage was solemnized by licence at the Halton-road Wesleyan Church by the Rev. J. Hanby, the contracting parties being Mr. Walter Morris, farmer of Runcorn. and Miss Annie Houghton, second daughter of Mr. J Lines Hough- ton, late of Halton. The bride was attired in a dress of dove colourel cloth, with hat t ) match trimmed with plumes. She was given away at the altar by her father. The bridesmaids who attended her were the Misses Amy and Emily Houghton, sisters of the bride, who wtre robed in dresses of electric blue material with hats to match. The best man was Mr. George Yates. After the wedding breakfast had been part aken of the happy pair left Runcorn fn. Southport, where the honeymoon will be spent. Along list of handsome presents has been received.
