div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 26, 1804. NOTES ON GAMES AM) NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. ATHLETICS. BY OUR OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 26, 1804. NOTES ON GAMES AM) NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. ATHLETICS. BY OUR OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

I don't know what the officials call the work that is at present being carried out pretty nearly all over the township, on the roads. I daresay they christen it improvements, but I have heard not a few christen it a nuisance. The roads are being cut up in all directions, and macadam stones freely scattered about, but the use of the steam roller to crush them into position, is quite an absent quan- tity. There areone or two good roads, but just out- side the inner circle of the town,they are anything but inviting. I like to see things done methodi- cally, but the authorities are far too methodical in Earlestown for my liking.

The Salvation Army, at least that portion of it which has its headquarters in Earlestown, must certainly be increasing both financially and numeri- cally. This is the opinion I have gathered from the fact that they are having their barracks very much enlarged. Not only is the building being extended, but an ante-room is also being provided for the use presumably of the officers, when in council. To my mind, judging from the numbers I have seen at the nightly gatherings the place was quite big enough, but then one cannot tell what fresh attack the officers may have in view. At one time several noted places in the town were attacked and carried by storm, prisoners, who were sup- posed to be past reclamation being secured and taken to what is called the penitent form. These penitent beings however soon repented of their rashness, and finally broke through their bonds,and at, the presew, time are leading the life they were more accu-tomed to. This is a great pity, but per- haps the officers think with more commodious pre- mises, and renewed activity, they may be able to bring them again to the fold.

It was admitted on all sides that the procession in connec:ion with the Niay Queen festival was a gorgeous affair, and I am prepared to agree with that. The affair appears to have become firmly established, aid if the interest of the townspeople can only be maintained, in the course of a year or two the festival at. Knutsford will be of a second rate quality when compared with the show here. The committee who work the affair deserve a lot of congratulation, but then it must not be forgotten that if the parents of the children did not take a lively interest in it, the work of the Committee would be labour wasted. This year the Committee were very much hampered for want of a marshal- ling ground, and although the Vitriol Square turned out to be a capital place, still it was not a private spot, or enclosed, and thus the public could not be excluded, whilst the arduous task of arranging the children in processional order was proceeded with, The want of an enclosed central ground, where the committee could work unmolested was very much felt, and although there are one or two such places, the proprietors do not see their way to place them at the disposal of the committee for the purpose, unless they are prepared -to pay pretty smartly for the privilege. This they cannot do,and seeing that the affair is not for the benefit of any partie,ular in- dividual but to provide funds to supply a want for the town,l think the field proprietors might en this occasion at least, stretch a point,and meet the com- mittee more liberally.

I h6ar that a petition has been framed,and signed by some of the residents of Newton,and despatched to the Railway Company complaining of the service of trains to and fram Newton-le-Willows. If the Newton people think they are badly served, what do the Earlestown people think? There is a much larger trading population in Earlestown,and yet the train service is about as bad as it; could well be. Take Warrington as an instance. During the afternoon you can get from Newton to Warrington by several fairly convenient trains, but if you happen to get stranded at Earlestown after the 2.15 has gone, you can kick up your heels for nearly three hours before you can hope to get a train to Warrington. Of course you have the alternative of going via New- ton,or walking all the way. Several of the express trains from Liverpool in the evening rush through Earlestown, but call at Newton, as also do some of the trains to and from Chester. I think if any peti- tion is needed, it should emanate from Earlestown, although I do not grumble at Newton endeavour- ing to get more than they already have.

A PENKETH PROVISION DEALER'S CLAIM. William Lo ngshaw, provision dealer, Penketh, sued Annie Swift, also of Penketh, at the Warring- ton County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, for £l2 lls, far provisions supplied to the defendant's father. Mr. Percy Davies who represented the plaintiff said that his client was a shopkeeper in Penketh, and the busi- ness was carried on by his wife, Sarah Longshaw. The provisions had been supplied to the defendant's father who died in February. The deceased was a man of considerable means, as he had an income of abou t £l5O a year which was paid in two instalmonts, viz., in February and August. The deceased man had promised to pay the debt when he received his next instalment of salary in February,but he died before then. On February 10th Mrs. Swift, the defendant's daughter, went to Pres- ton to receive some money which belonged to her father and she brought -C49 back with her. Mr. Forshaw received the money but he died the following day before he could pay the debt. Mrs. Longshaw waited until after the funeral and then asked Mrs. Forshaw for the money which was owing to her, but Mrs. Forshaw in - formed her that Mrs. Swift,her stepdaughter had taken away the money which deceased had left, and also some furniture, and that she (the widow) could not pay the debt as she had no money. Mrs. Swift however, refused to pay the debt, and proceedings against her were now taken.—Mrs. Longshaw said the defendant had promised to pay the money if the furniture realised enough.—Mrs Forshaw the widow of Philip Forshaw,said that on Feb- ruary the 10th she received some money from Preston which was wrapped up in a handkerchief. She did not know how much there was. She put the money in a drawer, and some days • afterwards, while she was at Warrington, her stepdaughter Mrs. Swift came into the house, and took the money and also a chair, a sewing machine, and an oil painting and a piano. When wit- ness went to Mrs. Swift to ask her about taking the articles she aqsumed a threatening manner, and would not admit taking the money.—Elizabeth Mary Hould- ing also gave evidence in support of the prosecution.— Mr. Arthur Browne for the defence admitted that it was true that his client had received a chair and picture, but they were not worth much. He contended that the piano had been purchased by her, and that the sewing machine had been given to her sister by her father, before he died, and in whose possession it was at preient. His client had paid a tremendous amount of money since the funeral, and she had paid more than she received of her father's goods.—Evidence of corroboration was given by John Swift, Mrs. John Swift (the defendant), and Mrs. Joseph Swift. The defendant denied that tile took the money. Robert Lowe, auctioneer, said that he had valued the furniture alleged to have been taken out of the house of Mr. For- shaw. He valued the chair at 4s. 6d.; the picture 63. 6d. the piano £6 ; and the sewing machine 321. 6d.—Sis Honour said that he considered that the defendant had paid out more than she had received,and he must there- fore give judgment for the defendant.
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRIN.GTON.

St. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CEIURCH. On Sunday, the anniversary services in connection with the above church were held, morning and evening. There were good congregations at each service, and the preacher, ;the Rev. W. Ritnund brothers of Leeds preached two excellent sermons, which were listened to with close attention. Collections in aid of the church fund were taken at each service. Mr. Wadsworth pre- sided at the organ with his usual ability. WORKINGMEN'S MISSION. BANK QUAY. The anniversary services in co:aiection with the abovs mission were held on Sunday. In the morning Mr. James Evans of Warrin,fton, gave an address to parents and children. The preacher in the afternoon and even- ing was Mr. Richard Johnson, of Manchester, who Preached two excellent sermons to large congregations. During the evening service, a solo entitled " Pardoned," was very ably executed by Mr. S. Hassall. Special hymns went sung at each service by the children and choir. The choir was under the I,,adertiiip of Mr. James Mills, and the organist was Mr. F. Atkinson. Collections were taken at each service, the total realized being £l6 14s. 01-(1. uhich include the sum of £8 Collected by a very prominent member of the mission by private subscription.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

'The Warrington first team came out of the match with Liverpool on Saturday rather creditably. This was the first meeting between the clubs for some years,a.nd there was therefore grea'; interest shown in the match. Tne Liverpool team containing as it does such players as Steel and Roper is a formidable combinati.n ts) encounter, but Warrington managed to make a draw of it,although not altogether in their favour. It is probable that had the match been played to a conclusion the Liverpool men would have won, but it is very creditable te Warrington to be able to play out time. By the way, it is rather curious that Warrington . always make a good show against such powerful organisations as Liverpool and Manchester, and although last season was such an un- successful one, they numbered the powerful Manchester team amongst the clubs they defeated.

There was some good scoring in the match on Satur- day. Liverpool went in first, and compiled 176 runs for nine wickets, when they closed their innings. Towards this total, D.Q. Steel contributed exactly half a century before he fell a victim to the prowess of Clarke. Other good scorers were Rev. H. E. Stanley who was run out when he made 34, H. C. Harrison, whom the Warrington bowlers could not get out, and made 32, Stoddart arid Goodwin, who made 19 and 16 respectively. The field- ing of the Warrington men, and the wicket keeping of Clark is well shown when, despite the high total of 176, only two extras were scored. In fact, the fielding and wicket keeping of Warrington appear to be their strong points, and could the other departments of the game be brought up to the same standard of excellency,our local club would be a terror to all the clubs round about.

With the respectable score of 176 before their eyes, the Warrington players were not in a very hopeful frame of mind. They however, gallantly went to the task of attempting to top this se )re, and although they failed, as I said above, " time "came to their assis- tance and the match became a draw, Warrington scor- ing 115 for seven wickets. The principal scorers for Warrington were Bates with 34, Callon with 18 not out, Wadsworth with 17, and Crosfield with 16. In the bowl- ing department, the nine Liverpool wickets were divided between Crosfield and Clarke with thiee each, and Bates with two. Harrison claimed four of the Warrington wickets. Warrington are evidently good " drawists " on their own grou ucl.for both matches tney have played, have resulted in this fashion.

The second team have yet to taste defeat, and on Sat- urday they disposed of the Penketh Friends by almost two to one, or to be more exact by 101. to 53. The team as a whole however, were very poor in the batting line, the only double figure man being Bibby, the Friends' bowlers being un- able to find the w.iy to his wicket, and he carriad his bat through for 63. But for him, the victory might have been on the other side. There was no tremendous scoring on the other side to balance Bibby, the highest being Pollard with 12 runs. This player also claimed six of the Warrington wickets.

The Sankey Wire Mills gained a victory over Hough Green away from home on Saturday. The batting on either side was only so-so, not one attaining double figures. The match was principally noticeable for the good bowling of Simpson and Hobson,the former taking tour wickets for seven runs, and the latter five for 15. Hobson also performed the hat trick.

The C.L.C. Engineers of Warrington and Birkenhead tried conclusions at Warrington on Saturday, and the Warrington men overcame their brethren of Birkenhead by 43 to 19. '[he Birkenhead innings was chiefly Teinark- able for the number of "ducks," there being seven of tOem. 'The Warrington men also contributed three " ducks," so that this species of fowl was rather com- mon at the match. The two players who were solely responsible for the wholesale destruction of the Birken- head wickets were Monks and Harrison. Monks clean bowled two,Harrison clean bowled three,the same player c and b two,and of the remaining three wickets, Harrison caught two off Monks' bowling, and Monks caught one off Harrison's bowling. This is almost an unique per- fortnance.

div.head: BOWLS.
div.p: BOWLS.

The first engagement of the Warrington Liberal Club team in the Warrington and District Bowling League ended in a victory for them by 15 points. Their oppon- ents were the Bull's Head team and the match through- out was evenly contested. The scores were Liberal Club 145, Bull's Head 130. The first-named club had of course an advantage in playing on their own ground,but never- theless they can take soine credit for beating last year's chanspions,ot the league.

The green was in splendid orier and some excellent bo wiing was witnessed. The surprise of the afternoon was the game between A.Jones and D. Snaw both noted trundlers, the former by some very excellent bowling beating his opponent by 12 points. 'l'. Locker also played a sterling game, and beat J. Shaw by 3 points. J.E.Warren created a surprise by running away from his opponent P. Dutton, and winning by a majority of 13 points. Although tile number of wins on each side was rqual, the home team kept a slight lead throughout the game.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Messrs. H. Hellier and J. K. Thompson, of the Anfield Cycling Club, have been breaking records recently. A few days ago they started on a 24-hours' ride from Stockton Heath. The first-named mounted on a tricyle while Mr. Thompson rode a safety bicycle. Mr. Hellier finished his ride—twelve minutes under the allotted time —with a total of 317 miles to his credit, and Mr. Thomp- son, who rode out full time, completed 320 mi!es. Mr. HeHier's performance beats the previous northern tri- cycle record made by himself last July, by no fewer than 36 miles, and is witle,ut doubt one of the best perform- ances ever accomplished on a three-wheeled machine. The ride of Mr. Thompson breaks the northern record for safety bicycles by 5i miles.

Dr. R. H. Carlisle, of the AnfiOd C.C., who is again trying to lower the Land's End to John O'Groat's record, arrived at Warrington about 12.30 on TueAday . Dr. Carlisle started from Land's End .at 6.30 on Monday morning, and has been going ever since and intends going through without sleep from Whitchurch. The record break.,,r was paced to the Norton Arms by the Brothers Deakin. After a stay of about fifteen minutes at the hotel for food, Carlisle left the town, paced by fleonan, of Manchester, and Binns, of the Irish Road Club. The record breaker was within his time, and well ahead of the record. Two hundred and ninety miles were covered in the 24 hours.
BASEBALL.

Still another victory for the Warrington Baseball Club! Their chances for securing the coveted position of first place in the Liverpool and District Baseball Gsmpetitiou are becoming more and more rosy each week. Their op- ponents on Saturday were the Emmanuel (Liverpool). Warrington were the first to take the bat at 3 15,anci com- piled the respectable total of 95. l'he visitors followed on but they were only able to put together 37 runs. This being more than 30 runs behind, the visitorb had to take the inevitable " follow on." Owing to desultory play on the part of the ‘Varrington fielders, the visitors were enabled to scrire 69, which mad them 11 runs ahead of the Warrington team's first innings. Warring- t-in again went in and scored 18, without the loss of a single player, which gave them a victory of 7 runs and eleven men to b it. For Warrington the best scorers were Plicenix, (16) ; Gallop, (16) ; Blackmore, (14). For Emmanuel,G. Brown was far and away the best,seoring 22 runs in the two innings.

div.head: RAC [NG BETWEEN ATLANTIC STEAMERS. A PERILOUS MANCEUVRE.
div.p: RAC [NG BETWEEN ATLANTIC STEAMERS. A PERILOUS MANCEUVRE.

It is stated that great indignation was on Wednesday expressed by the passengers who landed at Liverpool from the %S bite Star line steamer Majestic at the treat- ment their steamer experienced from the American liner Paris on the voyage from New York. The Majestic left Sandy Hook half an hour later than the Paris last Wed- nei-day. when the latter was out of sight. The Majestic, however, overhauled her rival on the second day, and the two steamers ran neck and neck almost till Monday noon, when the Majestic was slightly ahead of the Paris. At this time the latter steamed up astern, and passed the Majestic on the port side, subsequently signalling that she intended crossing the Majestic's bows. This she did at no greater distance than 200 or 300 yards, so close that there was no difficulty in reading the Paris's name withcut glasses. Fortunately Captain rarsell, of the Majestic, slowed down ; otherwise ft disaster second only to that which overtook the ironclad Victoria when ram- med by the Camperdown might have happened. As it was, the Majestic's passengers say that shortly after this startling incident, fog suddenly obscured the horizon. They state that this crossing of the Majestic's course was gratuitous, for the Paris subsequently returned to the southerly course from which she had deviated with such risk.

div.head: PHEASANTS nun
div.p: PHEASANTS nun
HOW AGRICULTURE IS HANDICAPPED.

It seems that the lease in connection with the Sluth Eastern Agricultural College at Wye, which has been established by the Bent and Surrey County Councils, in combination with the Charity Commissioners, contains a clause providing that for each pheasant's nest des- trayed on the estate, a sum of twenty pounds—not twenty shillings—shall be ferfeited. If there are many pheasant's nests on the college land, tillage and scientifi- experiments:are likely to prove somewhat costly on these terms. People therefore are asking why the Governors have agreed to a provision which may prove very detrimental to the purposes for which the land has been acquired.

div.head: THREATENED COAL STRIKE AT ST. HELENS. THE NOTICES WITHDRAWN.
div.p: THE THREATENED COAL STRIKE AT ST. HELENS. THE NOTICES WITHDRAWN.

A meeting of the miners employed at the Ashton's Green Collieries, St. Meng, was held on Wednesday night, at the Bull's Head Inn, Parr Stocks, when the question of the notices sent in for a revision of the field prices, &c., was discussed. Mr. Thomas Glover, J.P., miners' agent was present, and there was a large atten- dance. It was decided—" That,under the circumstances seeing that there was not a ballot taken of the men before notices were sent in, we agree to withdraw the present notices. and to bal!ot the men on the question of a standard price list." The ballot will be taken in about a fortnight.

div.head: JUVENILE GOOD TEMPLARY ANNIVERSARY.
div.p: JUVENILE GOOD TEMPLARY ANNIVERSARY.

The fourteenth Anniversary of the Juvenile Order of Good Templars was held on Saturday at the Good Templar Hall, Hindley. A nicely served tea was thoroughly enjoyed, by a large muster of juvenile and adult members. After tea a public meeting vi as held, presided over by Bro. E. Newman D.S.J.T. who gave an encouraging opening address. The Rev. W. F. Meyers also spoke, and complimented Bro. Houghton S.J.T., on the work accomplished during the existence of the G.T. lodge, and temple in Himiley, and urged the importance of training the boys and girls in right and true principles. Bro. R. Johnson S J.T., jun. read an excellent report of the years' work, after which a good programme of melodies, songs, recitations, and dialogues, was sub- mitted. Bro. D. Houghton afterwards presented book prizes to several successful competitors for singing, reciting, attendance,good conduct &c. Bro. Joynson seri., gave a short address, and the usual thanks brought a very successful g thering to:a close.

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

The usual weekly meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon was presided over by Mr. Joseph Owen. In the course of a short address he urged upon young men the necessity of aspiring to something higher. The Rev. D. W. Roberts, minister at Golborne-street Baptist Chapel, delivered the address. He referred to the depra- vity of Corinth at the time of Paul's visit, and contrasted it with the condition of Warrington at the present time and ask his hearers whether Warrington was not in a similar condition. He contended that it was, and said if society was to be transformed it could only be done by men who were imbued with .the same spirit which animated Paul who was "determined not to know any- thing save Jesus Christ and Him crucified." Mr. R. H. Pearson admirably rendered a violin solo. Messrs. T. Wallington, J. Haviour and W. Lowe also took part in the meeting.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The annual Sunday School sermons in connection with the above place of worship were held in the chapel on Sunday, The preacher in the morning and evening was the Rev. Herbert Waterworth of Edinburgh, and formerly ot the Warrington circuit. In the morning, a flute solo was ably rendered by Mr. W. H. Podmore. In the afternoon a sacred cantata entitled " Pentecost," was rendered by an augmented choir, with orchestral accompaniment. The pieces were very efficiently exe- cuted, and in the solos, dueti, ism., the following artistes took part :--Mrs. Bailey, Misses A. Morrell, Jones, and Kelly, Messrs. A. Scattergood, L. Richardson, Bailey and Entwistle. Mr. W. Brough was the conductor, and Mr. T. Brough acted as organist. Mr. W. H. Podmore again gave as a solo upon the flute the well-known piece "With verdure clad." At the evening service, the chapel was crowded to the doors, many persons being unable to obtain admission. The Rev. H. Waterworth's sermon was listened to with great attention. During the service, Mr. Kirk contributed a clarionet solo,which he did with his usual ability. Special hymns were sung by the choir and children during the day, and two, in which the children alone sang, were much appreciated. Collections on behalf of the school fund were taken at each service, and the total amount realised was over £l9.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

JUMBLE SALE AT THE CIIRIST CBURCH SCITOOLS.—As a means of augmenting the funds of the liquidation of the debt at present on the Christ Church Day and Sun- day Schools, Weston Point, a jumble sale was held in the school on Friday afternoon. The articles for s +le which were numerous and varied had all been presented by different members of the congregation and other inter- ested persons. Donations had been received, amongst the list of donors being :—Mr. Joseph Verdin and Mr. W. H. Verdin (North wich), Messrs. W. Whittaker, Moss, Orrell,Skone, and Branch. The goods were arranged on stalls superintended by Mesdames Rezenberg, W. F. Clarke, R. It. Clarke, W. McLear, Miss MeLear, &c., all of whom did their best to find purchasers. There was a large number of persons present when the opening cere- mony was performed by the Rev. D. Saunders Bowen, who undertnok that duty in the absence of Mr. P.Speak- man,J.P.,C.C. In a letter sent by the latter gentleman, he expressed his regret for not being able to attend and enclosed a donation of £2 2s. Tee sale then proceeded. The total amount of the takings exceeds £25, which is considered by all interested in the venture as highly satis- factory. BRAVE RESCUE FROM DROWNING : HAD SAVED SIXTEEN LIVES.—An instance of gallantry was witnessed on Tuesday evening at Weston Point, when Mr. Murphy, who is the pier head master of the Manchester Ship Canal, at Weston Marsh Lock, susceeded in rescuing a boy named William Morris from drowning. The boy, who is the son of Mr. Thomas Morris, and is only four years of age, was playing on the bridge, which crosses the Runcorn and Weston Canal at Weston Point, at about seven o'clock on Tuesday evening, when he sud- denly fell into the canal. Mr. Murphy, who, at, the time, was working in his garden, which is not far from the bridge, heard the boy's screams, and running towards the spot dived into the canal. He succeeded in landing the boy safely and was then helped from the water himself. A man named John Griffiehs, stone- cutter, of South-road also jumped into the water but, fortunately, the boy was already in good hands. P.C. Hatnmersley took charge of the lad and conveyed him to his home where after a little nursing he recovered from the shock he had received by the fall into the water, and appeared to be none the worse for the immersion. Much praise is due to Mr. Murphy for the plucky conduct he displayed in entering the water so readily, and more especially is he deserving of the praise when it is con- sidered that he has now saved the lives of sixteen per- sons from drowning. This is certainly worthy of some little recognition fcom the Royal Humane Society,if such has not already been extended. The matt John Griffiths is also to be complimented upon his action in the matter.

PRESINTATION TO MR. AND Mns. JOFIN LUCAS.—On Wednesday evening at the Weaver Hotel, an interesting ceremony took place in the form of a presentation. Mr. John Lucas, who has been the walking ganger of No. 3 section of the Manchester Ship Canal works at Weetmn Point is about to leave the district as the section is now completed. His wife will accompany him, and conse- quently their friends in the neighbourhood took the opportunity of raising a subscription fund out of which they purchased an elegant black marble timepiece awl a handsome silver teapot, beautifully chased. The for- mer bore the following inscription :—" Presented to Mr. John Lucas by his fellow-workmen of the No. 3 section, Ship Canal, Weston Point, May, 1894." On the teapot was inscribed :—" Presented to Mrs.. John Lucas by her friends of Weston Point, May, 1894." Previous to the ceremony a sumptuous supper was partaken of by the company at the Weaver Hotel, and supplied by Mr. Peter Coyle. Subsequently an adjournment was made to another room, where Mr. Vergniand, time- keeper of No. 3 section, presented the timepiece and tea pot to Mr. and Mrs. Lucas respectively. In doing so,he said that they were all very sorry to part with Mr. and Mrs. Lucas, both of whom had proved themselves good friends to them. These presents were small tokens of the esteem in which they held Mr. and Mrs. Lucas, whom they sincerely hoped would live lont; to enjny them. (Applause.)—Other remarks followed by diff- rent friends, after which Mr. and Mrs. Lucas made fit- ting acknowledgments of the presents, expressing their thanks for the kindness of their friends, and the regret they felt in taking their departure from them. The re- mainder of the evening was spent in conviviality.

CONTINUATION OF THE CHURCH SCHOOL FETE.-Ow- ing to the inclement nature of the weather on Whit-Wed- nesday, the latter portion of the proceedings of this fete was postponed and given on Saturday when the favour- able weather attracted many visitors. Subsequently the Wes- ton Brass Band played for dancing which was indulged in by a large number on the green.
SANITARY INSPECTOR'S A sSOCIATION, LIVERPOOL
CENTRE.

On Saturday, at a meeting of the above Associa- tion, held in the Free Library, William Brown-st., Liverpool, Mr. Ralph Norman, chief sanitary inspec- tor, of Warringim, was unanimou-ly elected a delegate to represent the Association at the Con- gress of the Sanitary Institute, to be held in Liver- pool next September.

div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S EYESIGHT.

THE OPERATION PERFORMED. The Press Association telegraphs that the operation on Mr. Gladstone's right eye for cataract was successfully performed at Lord Rendel's house on Thursday morning, and the following bulletin was issued :—" Mr. Glad- stone's eye was operated upon for cltaract quite success- fully this morning at half-past nine. Mr. J. B. Lawford assisted at the operation. Mr. Gladstome's health is well raaintained.—(Signed) E. NETTLESHIP, S. H. HABERSHON, M.D." Mr. Gladstone remains in good spirits.

div.head: QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.

The Queen completed her seventy-fifth year on Thurs- day, having been born at KensiFigton Palace on the 24,b of May, 1819. This age has been exceeded by two only of the occupants of the English throne—namely Georg, 11, who lived seventy-seven years, and G?orge 111, woo nearly attained the age of eighty-two. On the 20th of June next,her Majesty will have reigned over the United Kingdom for fifty-seven years. This length of reign has been exceeded by one of her predecessors only. George lll,who occupied the Throne for nearly sixty years. The Queen has now been a widow over thirty-two years,the Prince Consort having died on December 14, 1861. tier Majesty is the oldest crowned head in Eorope, with te exception of the King of Denmark, who is about one year her senior.

div.head: FICKLE PUBLICAN. "THE FIRST STEP TOWARDS HOUSEFURNISHING."
div.p: A FICKLE PUBLICAN. "THE FIRST STEP TOWARDS HOUSE- FURNISHING."

In the Queen's Bench Division on Thursday, before Mr. Jubtice Lawrance, Lily Sailing, a tradeuman's daughter at Tottenham, sued H. C. DePape, publican,of Gateshead, for damages for breach of promise of mar- riage. The defendant was the girl's suitor for eighteen months, promised her marriage, and arrangements were made for the wedding; but in the meantime the defend- ant attended a funeral, met another young woman,Rose Smith, and, finding "she had a bit of money on her own account," married her, though he had sworn be true to Lily Sailing, to whom hc had sent a kitten in a basket as " the first step towards furnishing a houso." It was stated during the hearing that the defendant had considerable property. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £135. '

div.head: LATEST RUSSIAN PLOT.
div.p: THE LATEST RUSSIAN PLOT.
A DESPERATE SCHEME.

The "Times" St. Petersburg porrespondent telegraphs that in connection with the recent arrests, the gravest news is that the authorities lately discovered attempts to undermine a house and an Orthodox Church close to the railway line between Trel and Vitibsk. Between these two towns lies the large city of Smolensk, which was to be the scene of extensive military manceuvres this autumn in the presence of the Czar. It is itated that the house which was being undermined had been selected as the residence of the Emperor during the mili- tary movements, a church near the railway being also included in the operations of the conspirators. A !arg,e number of the railway servants were arrested, many of them being engineers. One of the latter shot himself on being arrested. There is little doubt that the capture of the late General Andreiff's son and daughter led to many o: the arrests. Another son of the General has been also arrested, and on him was found a book in cipher.

div.head: IMPERIAL PA RLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PA RLIAMENT.
'THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons, on Thursday evening, Mr. FOWLER repls ing to a question, said the recent military insubordination at Agra was confined to two cowponies and not soricus in its character, and was unconnected with caste or religion. As to the suggestions with regard to the existence of disaffection in India, the Government had received no information which in any way either confirmed or supported them. Mr. Monr..E.y. in answer to Mr. Ross, said he was ad- vised that there %vaR no ground for a prosecution against Mr. Dillon in respect of his speech at liallyProod last Sunday. Mr. H. GARDNER informed Mr. J. W. Lowther that he proposed to introduce next Monday a measure dealing with the importation of foreign and colonial meat. Mr. A. MORLEY, in reply to Mr. Field, said the eiovern- merit had decided to terminate the existing American mail contract aid Queenstown. Mr. MIINDELLA made an explanatory statement about his resignation of the Presidency of the Riani of Trade. He said that when his name was first mentioned in con- nection with certain legal proceedings he at once Placed his official position at the disposal of the Prima Minister, who was, however, reluctant to accept it. Now that he had determined to give up office his colleagues could no longer be attacked through lihn,and sospicion for gide!) there was never the slightest foundation could no longer attach to his Department. He felt fully assured that throughout his life he had preserved his character free from stain of dishonour.

On the motion to go into Committee on the Budget Bill Sir J. LUBBOCK moved that it be an instruction to the Committee that they have power to divide the bill into two parts, and in the first place to report to the House the portion relating to Customs and Inland Revenue. Sir W. Harcourt opposed and Mr. Gosehen supported the instruction, which on a division was re- jected by 161 to 121. The other proposed instructions were ruled out of order, and the House went into Coin- mittee on the bill. The Chairman ruled out of order Sir J. Lubbock's amendment to the clause relating to estlte duty, which proposed to leave out the word "estate" and insert "legacy." Thereupon Mr. BALFOUR moved to report progress. Sir W. HARCOURT said the Opposi- tion had never dared to face this Budget fairly. This was the worst method he had ever seen of wasting the time of the House. Mr. BALFOUR asked the Government to bring in their resolution on the ,first day when thi s matter should be taken up again, so that the Opposition might move their amendment. After the closure had been applied the motion to report progress was defeated by 239 to 195. Mr. BANBURY moved that clause 1 be postponed. The motion was defeated by 258 to 222. Mr. T. BOWLES then moved an amendment to clause 1 to define more exactly the nature of the duty. Aft.r an animated debate this amendment was rejected by 212 to 181, and progress was reported.

The medals won by the "A " team of the Runcorn Football club, in connection with the Liverpool and Di - trict Junior Rugby League are now on view at the shop of Mr. T. Whinyates, High-street. They are of an ex- ceedingly pretty design and have been supplied by Messrs. Alexander Bros. Liverpool. On the front of the medals is inscribed the word " Runcorn," and on the back the initials of the League champions, 1893-94, as well as the name of the recipients. It is understno d that a social evening will be organized for the benefit of the" A "team on the occasion of the presentation of the medals.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
SUCCESS OF A WARRINGTON MUSICIAN.
Mr. John H. Hudson, baritone, of Latchford, War- rington, has been appointed to the vacancy in the Liverpool Cathedral choir.

ALL SAINT'S MISSION. The distribution of prizes to the scholars attend- ing the Sunday school connected with the above named Mission, took place on Sunday afternoon. Amongst those present were the Vicar (Rev. H. V. Pigot) Mr. and Mrs. T. Morris, and Mrs. Orr. Mr. Morris made the presentation of prizes which con- sisted of useful books. WYCLIFFE COCICHEDGE MISSION.

The anniversary sermons in connection with the above named mission were preached on Sunday, afternoon and evening. The preacher at the after- noon service was Mr. W. Light, of Warrington, and Mr. James Evans preached at the evening service. The services were well attended, the room being crowded at the evening service. Special hymns and anthems were sung. Collections were taken on behalf of the mission fund, and realised a satis- factory amount.

The County Council for the County Palatine of Lancaster. " THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT, 1888" AND "THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT, 1894." THE WARRINGTON UNION. XTOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that a Committee of .11 the County Council will hold an INQUIRY at the COUNTY POLICE COTIRT, in WARRINGTON, ON FRIDAY, the Ist day of JuNE, 1894. at 10 o'clock in the FORENOON, for the purpose of making such Inquiries as may be necessary for carrying into effect the previsions of" The Local Government Act, 1894," within the District of the Warrington Union, and especially with regard to the following matters, namely- 1. The division of the district of the Haydock Local Board into wards. 2. The division of any Rural Township into wards for the Election of Parish Councillors. 3. The number of Parish Councillors to be elected for each of the townships entitled to a Parish Council. 4. Any other matter and thing which under the said Act may be necessary to be enquired into. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN, that all persons interested in all or any of the foregoing matters may attend the said Inquiry and be heard. Dated this 19th day of May 1894. FRED. C. HULTON, Clerk of the County Council.

IS MARRIAGE A FAILURE? What a question to ask, but how often could it be answered in the affirmative, the nrin-ipal cause beinpthe improvidence of Furnishing on the Hire System. Since 9.1 r advertisements have appeared pointing out I,llr disadvantages. we lime re- ceived several le:ters agreeing with our denunciations of this pernicious system. Each Hire Agreement specifies that after the deposit is paid, so many weekly payments shall be made and that until the whole of the sum mentioned is paid the goculs shall not become the property of the would-be pur- chaser, and that if any of the payments are neglected to the exact time specified the goods may be forcibly taken away and the whole of the payments forfeited. County Court judges have denounced the sy,tem, inasmuch as the vendor gets both money and goods. Again, the pri es charged are enormous, without any respect being paid to the quality, in many eases being worn out before they are paid for. To com- bat this system, and open the eyes ot the public, Worsley's of " The Pantheon," Gayt horn, Manchester. the Largest Retailers of Second-hand Furniture in the worlsl, have determined to wpm, all respectable householders to have furniture at the ticketed marked cash price, a small percentage being charged for the conven'ence of payment by the week, month, or quarter. On the fourth page of the " Exsminer" •we advertise a list of Bargains every week, any of which can be had and paid for by convenient intervals, the articles being delivered upon the first payment being reads. Furniture from £5 to £1 000 may be arranged for in this way. To give an idea of the equity of our proposals we are prepared to supply for a working man a House of Furniture complete, thoroughly good aud substantial (every article warranted), price £2O cash down, not a penny less, or 10 I or cent extra if credit is given, making £22. THE LARGEST FURNISHING HOUSE IN THE NORTH. W. H. WORSLEY. Est,b. 1841„ " The Pantheon," Gay thorn. Manchester. WEEKLY CHAT, SUBJE( T NEW LONDON FURNITURE. Good Furniture is the one absolute necessity of a comfort- able home, but how often is the purchaser victimised by the showy flimsy rubbish manufactured in the East End of Lon- dAr. and now largely retailed by drapers, who have not the slighest knowledge of the cabinet trade. The lowest ticketed price may be all very well in ribtons and lace, but this will not prove a good investment when applied to furniture, the lowest priced furniture is not the cheapest ry any means. The Fast End of London is swarming with Jews.
